(Anglo-Saxon England).text: Anglo-Saxon England was formed by Germanic settlers, Angles, Saxons and Jutes, who arrived after Roman Britain's end. It began as many small kingdoms, slowly joined into one English kingdom in the 10th century, and ended with the Norman Conquest in 1066.

(Brythonic Kingdoms).text: The Brythonic kingdoms were the Celtic-speaking realms of post-Roman Britain, in Wales, Cornwall, and northern England and southern Scotland. Anglo-Saxon pressure shrank them over centuries, until Wales fell to Edward I of England in 1283.

(Chenla).text: Chenla is the Chinese name for the Khmer lands that followed Funan in Cambodia and nearby areas between the late 500s and the early 800s. Many historians think it was a loose set of principalities rather than one kingdom, and Chinese records say it split into Land and Water Chenla soon after 706.

(Commonwealth of Nations).text: A voluntary association of 56 countries, most of them former British territories, including India, Canada and Nigeria. Members work together on trade, education and democracy. King Charles III is its head.

(Kingdom of Bohemia).text: A medieval kingdom in central Europe, the forerunner of today's Czech Republic. Its kings were prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire. This entry groups the lands of the Bohemian crown.

(Kingdom of Denmark).text: A Viking-age kingdom that took shape in the 900s. Gorm the Old ruled from Jelling from c. 936, and his son Harald Bluetooth won all of Denmark and made it Christian. Its crown later led the Kalmar Union of 1397 with Norway and Sweden.

(Mahajanapadas).text: The Mahajanapadas, meaning great realms, were sixteen kingdoms and tribal republics of northern India, c. 600-345 BCE, during the second wave of Indian cities. Magadha eventually swallowed most of its rivals.

(Phoenician Empire).text: The Phoenicians were seafaring Canaanite city-states along today's Lebanese coast, at their height from about 1200 to 332 BCE. They were great traders and shipbuilders, founded colonies such as Carthage, and spread an alphabet that Greek and later scripts descend from.

(Taifas of Iberia).text: The independent Muslim kingdoms, called taifas, that arose in Spain when the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in the early 1000s. Rich courts and poetry flourished, but their weakness let Christian kings take land, and later Berber empires took over.

Abasgia.text: A principality of the Abasgians on the north-eastern Black Sea coast, in today's Abkhazia, c. 550-777 CE. Its own princes ruled under Lazic and then Byzantine overlordship; Justinian had them converted and built forts at Pityus and Sebastopolis.

Achaean League.text: A federation of Greek city-states in the northern Peloponnese, which grew under Aratus of Sicyon to include most of the peninsula. It opposed Sparta and Macedon, but lost to Rome in 146 BCE, when Corinth was destroyed.

Adal Sultanate.text: A Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa, founded in 1415 on the Harar plateau after the fall of Ifat, with trading ports such as Zeila. From 1529 Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim overran much of Christian Ethiopia, until he was killed at the Battle of Wayna Daga in 1543.

Adiyaman chiefdom (Tagadur).text: A chiefdom of the Sangam age in the Dharmapuri area of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-190 CE. Its chiefs, the Adiyamans, are praised in early Tamil poems, and Anji is the best known of them.

Aetolian League.text: A confederation of tribes and cities in central Greece that became a major power after helping beat back Gallic raiders at Delphi in 279 BCE. It sided with Rome against Macedon, then fought Rome alongside the Seleucids and ended up as a client of Rome in 188 BCE.

Aghlabid Dynasty.text: An Arab dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia) from 800 to 909 under the Abbasid caliphs. From Kairouan it conquered Sicily from Byzantium, starting in 827, before the Fatimids overthrew it.

Ahi Republic.text: A brotherhood of craftsmen and tradesmen around Ankara in central Anatolia in the 1200s and 1300s, linked to Ahi Evran. Historians call it the Ahi Republic because its guilds held much local power in place of a ruling dynasty.

Ahlatshahs (Shah-Armens).text: An Armenian-Turkic Muslim dynasty based at Ahlat on Lake Van in eastern Turkey, also called the Shah-Armens, ruling c. 1100 to 1207. Ahlat passed to the Ayyubids in 1207.

Ahmadnagar Sultanate.text: One of the five Deccan sultanates of India that arose when the Bahmani Sultanate broke up. Founded in 1490 by Ahmad Nizam Shah, it held off the Mughal emperor Akbar for years, thanks to its queen Chand Bibi, before falling in the 1600s.

Ahom kingdom.text: A Tai kingdom founded by Sukaphaa in the upper Brahmaputra valley in Assam, India. It began small in 1228 and lasted to 1826, growing to hold much of modern Assam.

Ahom kingdom (Assam).text: A kingdom in Assam's Brahmaputra valley founded by Tai-speaking Ahom people. It fought the Mughals for the western frontier and won at Saraighat in 1671, but the Moamoria rebellion and Burmese invasions of 1817-1826 shattered it before British annexation.

Ainu and Nivkh peoples (Sakhalin).text: The Ainu and Nivkh, indigenous peoples of Sakhalin island in Northeast Asia. They fished and hunted, and the island was later claimed by both Russia and Japan.

Ajmer (British).text: A British-held district in Rajputana, taken over in 1818 after Daulat Rao Scindia ceded Ajmer to the East India Company on 25 June. Francis Wilder was its superintendent; in 1823 it was joined with Merwara.

Ajmer (British): Kekri tract.text: A detached tract of the British district of Ajmer in Rajputana, held by the East India Company after Daulat Rao Scindia ceded Ajmer to it in 1818. The Kekri area was one of the pieces of the district, shown for 1818-22.

Ajmer (held by the Scindias).text: The district of Ajmer in Rajasthan while held by the Scindias, one of the great chiefs of the Maratha confederacy. Scindia took it in 1752, and Daulat Rao Scindia gave it to the British by treaty in 1818.

Ajmer (held by the Scindias): Kekri trac.text: The Kekri area, a part of the Ajmer district in Rajasthan, held with the rest of it by the Maratha Scindias from 1752. The district passed to the British in 1818.

Ajmer-Merwara (British).text: A British-run district in Rajputana, 1823-57, formed when Ajmer, ceded by Scindia in 1818, was joined with the Merwara hills, part of which Udaipur gave up in 1823. Its seat was at Ajmer, with Beawar the centre for Merwara.

Ajmer-Merwara (British): Kekri tract.text: A detached tract of the British district of Ajmer-Merwara in Rajputana. The Kekri area was one of the pieces of the district, which the East India Company formed in 1823 by joining Ajmer to the Merwara hills.

Ajuran Sultanate.text: A Somali Muslim sultanate led by the Garen dynasty, controlling the Shabelle and Jubba river lands and the ports of the Benadir coast in the 16th and 17th centuries. It resisted Portuguese and Oromo pressure before breaking up in the later 1600s.

Akwamu.text: An Akan state in the Atewa hills north of Accra, Ghana, first recorded on a Dutch map of 1629. It then conquered the coast from Accra to the Volta, and was destroyed by Akyem and its allies in 1730.

Alans.text: The Alans were nomadic Iranian-speaking horsemen from the steppe north of the Caucasus. Some were pushed west by the Huns and joined the Vandals in crossing into Spain in 409 CE, while others stayed and became ancestors of the Ossetians.

Albania.text: A Balkan country that declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1912. Between the wars it came under the strongman Zog, who turned the republic into a monarchy in 1928 and ruled as king until Italy invaded in 1939. Its capital is Tirana.

Albanian Principalities.text: A set of small Albanian-ruled states in the western Balkans in the 1300s and early 1400s, led by noble families such as the Thopias and Balshas. They were often rivals, and the Ottomans took most of them in the 1400s.

Alodia.text: Alodia, or Alwa, was a Christian Nubian kingdom of central Sudan, south of Makuria. Its capital Soba sat near where the Blue and White Niles meet. It lasted over a thousand years until Soba fell around 1500, either to Arab tribes or to the Funj.

Alwar State.text: A Rajput state in north-east Rajasthan, founded in 1775 when Pratap Singh of the Naruka Kachhwaha clan broke away from Jaipur's overlordship and took Alwar fort. In 1803 it became the first Rajputana state to sign a permanent alliance with the East India Company.

Amathus.text: A city-kingdom on the south coast of Cyprus, c. 600-312 BCE. It was tributary in turn to Assyria and Persia but kept its own kings, such as Androcles, until Ptolemy of Egypt took over the island.

Ambrosian Republic.text: A short-lived republic in Milan, set up in 1447 after the last Visconti duke died. It was named after St Ambrose, the city's patron. It collapsed in 1450 when Francesco Sforza took Milan and became its duke.

American zone.text: The American occupation zone of Germany, 1945-49, one of four zones in Germany west of the Oder-Neisse line. The Allied Control Council in Berlin governed Germany jointly, and the western zones became the Federal Republic in May 1949.

Ammon.text: An Iron Age kingdom east of the Jordan River in modern Jordan, c. 1000-582 BCE, with its capital at Rabbath Ammon, today's Amman. It paid tribute to Assyria from 734 BCE and ended after a Babylonian campaign in 582 BCE.

Andamanese peoples.text: The indigenous hunter-gatherer peoples of the Andaman Islands in the Bay of Bengal, including the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese. Isolated for thousands of years, they were devastated by outside diseases after sustained contact began in the late 1700s and British penal colonies were set up in the mid-1800s.

Angevins.text: The counts of Anjou in western France, whose lands here are shown c. 1126-1146. Geoffrey Plantagenet married the English king's daughter Matilda and conquered Normandy in 1144, and their son became Henry II of England.

Angles.text: The Angles were a Germanic people from Angeln, in what is now northern Germany, who crossed the sea and settled in Britain in the 400s CE. They founded East Anglia, Mercia and Northumbria, and England is named after them.

Anglo-Saxon England.text: This entry shows the early Anglo-Saxon settlements in eastern and southern England, when Germanic newcomers from across the North Sea first carved out territory in former Roman Britain in the 5th and 6th centuries CE. Later they merged into larger kingdoms.

Angola.text: A country on the southwest coast of Africa, ruled by Portugal until 1975. After the MPLA dropped Marxism, elections were held in 1992, but war with UNITA resumed and only ended in 2002. It is rich in oil and diamonds.

Ankole (Nkore).text: A Bantu kingdom in south-western Uganda, ruled by a king called the Omugabe and known for its cattle herds. It dated from about the 15th century and was folded into the British Uganda Protectorate by an agreement in 1901.

Antigua and Barbuda.text: A two-island country in the eastern Caribbean. It became a self-governing state in association with Britain in 1967 and fully independent in 1981. Nelson's Dockyard at English Harbour, an old naval base, is a World Heritage Site.

Anurādhapura.text: The first great kingdom of Sri Lanka, based at the city of Anuradhapura, which was its capital for some 1,500 years. Buddhism took root there early, and its kings built huge reservoirs and stupas. Chola invaders from South India sacked the city in 993 CE, and power shifted to Polonnaruwa.

Aquitaine.text: Aquitaine was a duchy in southwest France, quasi-independent within the Frankish realm from the late 7th century CE. Its dukes often clashed with the Frankish rulers, and later it passed by Eleanor's marriages to English kings.

Arab Federation.text: A short-lived union joining the two Hashemite kingdoms, Iraq and Jordan, formed in February 1958 as a rival to the union of Egypt and Syria. It collapsed when a revolution overthrew Iraq's King Faisal II in July 1958 and was formally dissolved that August.

Arab Republic of Egypt.text: The modern state of Egypt, in the Nile valley, which took this name in 1971. Under Anwar Sadat it fought Israel in 1973 and then made peace in 1979. Its history stretches back to the pharaohs.

Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party.text: Syria as drawn for 1967 to 1972, under the Arab nationalist Ba'ath Party. Israel captured the Golan Heights in the 1967 war, and in 1970 defence minister Hafez al-Assad took power, founding a ruling family that lasted decades.

Aram-Damascus.text: An Aramaean kingdom around Damascus in Syria, c. 950-733 BCE. Under King Hazael it dominated neighbouring Israel and took Gilead and Bashan. Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered it in 732 BCE.

Archbishopric of Riga.text: The northern lands of the archbishop of Riga, in what is now Latvia, part of medieval Livonia. The see became an archbishopric in 1255, and the archbishop shared power with the Livonian Order and other bishops.

Arghun dynasty (Sindh).text: A Turko-Mongol dynasty from Kandahar that ruled in Sindh, in today's Pakistan. Shah Beg Arghun, pushed out of Kandahar by Babur, took Thatta c. 1520, and his son Shah Husayn conquered Multan in 1528. Their rule ended under the Mughals.

Armenia.text: The first Armenian republic, declared in 1918 after the Russian Empire collapsed, was based in Yerevan and lasted until 1920, when it was taken over by the Soviets. Armenia became independent again in 1991.

Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.text: An Armenian state on the southern coast of Anatolia, begun around 1080 by refugees from the Seljuk invasion of Armenia. It became a kingdom in 1198, allied with the Crusaders, and the Mamluks conquered it in 1375.

Artuqids.text: A Turkmen dynasty with branches at Hasankeyf, Mardin and Harput (in southeast Turkey) from 1102. The Ayyubids took Hasankeyf and Amid in 1232, leaving only the Mardin branch, which survived under Mongol overlordship.

Aruva Nadu (lower Pennai valley).text: A region of early Tamilakam in the lower Pennai valley of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-190 CE, ruled by chiefs called the Aruvalar. Sangam poems mention them, but no ruler is named in the map data.

Aruva Nadu under Chola overlordship.text: Aruva Nadu, the lower Pennai valley of Tamil Nadu, drawn c. 190-300 CE under Chola overlordship. A poem tells that the Aruvalar submitted to Karikala; the date depends on one historian's dating of him.

Arzawa.text: A group of Bronze Age lands in western Turkey, c. 1450-1320 BCE; this map shows Arzawa Minor, its chief state, whose king Tarhundaradu wrote to the pharaoh Amenhotep III. Mursili II of the Hittites conquered it and split it into vassal kingdoms.

Ashikaga Shogunate.text: The military government of Japan from 1336 to 1573, started when Ashikaga Takauji became shogun. Also called the Muromachi shogunate after its Kyoto district, it was weak in later years and ended when Oda Nobunaga expelled the last shogun.

Asir.text: A mountainous region in southwest Arabia, now a province of Saudi Arabia. From about 1907 it was the emirate of the Idrisi family, with its capital at Sabya, until it came under the Saudi kingdom and was formally annexed in 1934.

Astrakhan Khanate.text: A Tatar successor state of the Golden Horde near the mouth of the Volga. Its khans controlled river trade to the Caspian Sea, and Russia under Ivan the Terrible conquered it in 1556.

Athenian Coalition.text: Athens and its allies, who tried to throw off Macedonian rule: first in the Lamian War of 323-322 BCE after Alexander died, and later in the Chremonidean War of the 260s BCE. Both revolts failed and Athens stayed under Macedonian influence.

Atropatene.text: A kingdom in northwestern Iran and Azerbaijan, founded by the Persian governor Atropates after Alexander's conquest. It kept its independence under Seleucids and Parthians, and its name lives on in the word Azerbaijan.

Austral Islands chiefdoms.text: Chiefdoms on the southernmost islands of French Polynesia, such as Tubuai and Rurutu. Each island had its own ruling chiefs until France took over in the late 19th century.

Ava Kingdom.text: A kingdom of upper Burma founded in 1365 by Thado Minbya, who built its capital at Ava (Inwa). It saw itself as heir to the Pagan Empire and fought long wars with Hanthawaddy. A confederation of Shan states sacked Ava in 1527, and Toungoo finally conquered it in 1555.

Ay chiefdom (Podiyil and Nanjil Nadu).text: A Sangam-age chiefdom at the southern tip of India, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, in the southern Western Ghats and the coast near Kanyakumari. Its chiefs, such as Ay Andiran, are praised in early Tamil poems.

Azerbaijan Democratic Republic.text: Azerbaijan's first republic, declared in 1918, was the first parliamentary democracy in the Muslim world. It gave women the vote but lasted only until the Red Army took Baku in 1920.

Ba'athist Syria.text: Syria after the March 1963 coup that brought the Arab nationalist Ba'ath Party to power. The party built a one-party state, and a further coup in 1966 handed control to a more radical wing of the party.

Baekje.text: Baekje was one of Korea's Three Kingdoms, in the southwest, founded around 18 BCE. A strong sea power, it helped carry Buddhism and continental culture to Japan, and fell in 660 CE to Silla and the Chinese Tang.

Bagratid Armenia.text: An Armenian kingdom founded in the 880s by Ashot I of the Bagratuni family, after Armenia had been under foreign rule for about two centuries. It later made Ani its capital, and Byzantium took it over in 1045.

Bahawalpur.text: A Muslim princely state on the Sutlej in present-day Punjab, Pakistan. Its Nawab signed accession to Pakistan on 5 October 1947, making it the first princely state to join Pakistan.

Bahawalpur State.text: A princely state in the Punjab of present-day Pakistan, founded in 1748 by the Daudpotra nawabs, who came from Sindh. They ruled a strip along the Sutlej and the desert behind it, and signed a treaty with the British in 1809.

Bahmani Sultanate.text: The first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan in India, founded in 1347 by Hasan Gangu during a revolt of Deccan nobles against the Delhi Sultan. Its capital moved from Gulbarga to Bidar, and in the late 1400s and early 1500s it broke up into five smaller sultanates.

Bahrain.text: An island group in the Persian Gulf, long known for pearling. The Bani Utbah, led by the Al Khalifa family, took Bahrain in 1783 and have ruled it since. Bahrain gained independence from Britain in 1971.

Bahrani Dynasty.text: The map shows the Al-Ahsa oasis region of eastern Arabia, a fertile area near the Persian Gulf, c. 1260-1520. Local Arab dynasties ruled it in these centuries: the Usfurids from 1253, then the Jarwanids, and from 1417 the Jabrids.

Baku Khanate.text: A khanate on the Caspian coast at Baku, self-governing after Nader Shah's death in 1747 under nominal Iranian suzerainty. Russia took control of it in 1806.

Balasagan.text: A historical region between the Kura and Aras rivers beside the Caspian Sea, in today's Azerbaijan, bordering Atropatene. It lay within the Sasanian world and later the Arab-ruled caliphate, but few details survive.

Balhae.text: Balhae was a kingdom founded in 698 CE by Dae Joyeong, covering parts of Manchuria, northern Korea and the Russian Far East. It adopted Tang-style government offices and later had friendly ties with Tang, until the Khitan Liao conquered it in 926.

Bali.text: The island of Bali, Indonesia, divided among rival rajas such as those of Klungkung and Badung. Dutch forces conquered the island between 1906 and 1908, when several courts chose a ritual mass death known as puputan.

Balinese Kingdom.text: The Hindu kingdom of Gelgel, which held sway over Bali, Indonesia, in this period. Many Javanese nobles, priests and artists took refuge on Bali after Majapahit fell, and under Dalem Baturenggong in the mid-1500s Gelgel also ruled Lombok and western Sumbawa. It broke apart after 1651, and a new court arose at nearby Klungkung in 1686.

Balinese kingdom of Lombok.text: A Balinese-ruled kingdom on Lombok, built up from the 1600s as rulers from Bali took the island from the Sasak, and holding all of it by about 1750. It ended in 1894 when the Dutch invaded.

Bamana Empire.text: A West African state also called the Ségou Empire, on the middle Niger in today's Mali. It grew under the founder Biton Coulibaly after about 1712, and fell to the jihad of El Hadj Umar in 1861.

Banaban people.text: The Banabans are the people of Banaba, a lone raised coral island in the Pacific, now part of Kiribati. Their island was rich in phosphate, and from 1900 mining by outside companies reshaped their lives and land.

Banate of Bosnia.text: A medieval state in what is now Bosnia and Herzegovina, ruled by bans. Nominally under the Hungarian crown but largely independent, it became a kingdom under Tvrtko I in 1377.

Bandanese chiefdoms.text: The Banda Islands in eastern Indonesia, for centuries the only place on Earth where nutmeg and mace came from. Councils of rich men called orang kaya ran the trade until the Dutch conquered the islands in 1621, and only about a thousand Bandanese stayed on as forced labourers.

Bani Khalid Emirate.text: An Arab emirate in eastern Arabia, led by Barrak ibn Ghurayr, who drove the Ottomans out of al-Hasa in 1669-70. It ruled al-Hasa and al-Qatif until the Emirate of Diriyah conquered al-Hasa in 1793-95.

Banswara State.text: A Rajput princely state in southern Rajasthan east of the Mahi river, split from Dungarpur after 1527. By the late 18th century it paid tribute to the Maratha Raja of Dhar, and it accepted British protection in 1818.

Baol.text: A Wolof kingdom in Senegal between Cayor and Sine, ruled by the Teigne. It became independent of Jolof after 1549, was tied to Cayor from 1697 to 1756, and France conquered it between 1874 and 1895.

Barbados.text: A small, flat island in the eastern Caribbean that stayed under British rule for centuries as a sugar colony. It became independent in November 1966 and a republic in 2021, when it removed the British monarch as head of state.

Barghawata Conference.text: A Berber confederation in the Tamesna plain on Morocco's Atlantic coast, c. 744 to 1058. Its leader Salih ibn Tarif declared himself a prophet and founded a new faith mixing Berber beliefs with Islamic elements, with its own scripture. It held out against the Almoravids, whose leader Ibn Yasin died fighting it in 1058.

Baroda (Amreli).text: The Amreli division, a detached piece of Baroda, the Maratha state of the Gaekwads, whose land lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Baroda was a princely state under the British until it acceded to India in 1947.

Baroda (Baroda division).text: The Baroda division, the central block of Baroda, the Maratha princely state of the Gaekwads in Gujarat. The state's land lay in separate parts across Gujarat and Kathiawar, and it acceded to India in 1947.

Baroda (Kadi division).text: The Kadi division, a northern piece of Baroda, the Maratha princely state of the Gaekwads in Gujarat. The state's land lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar; it acceded to India in 1947.

Baroda (Kodinar).text: The Kodinar division, a detached piece of Baroda, the Maratha princely state of the Gaekwads, whose land lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Baroda acceded to India in 1947.

Baroda (Navsari division).text: The Navsari division, a detached piece of Baroda, the Maratha princely state of the Gaekwads, whose land lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Baroda acceded to India in 1947.

Baroda (Okhamandal).text: The Okhamandal division, a detached piece of Baroda, the Maratha princely state of the Gaekwads, whose land lay in separate blocks across Gujarat and Kathiawar. Baroda acceded to India in 1947.

Baroda State (Gaekwad; Baroda district).text: The core of the Gaekwad state of Baroda, a Maratha state in Gujarat, shown 1818-57. Allied with the East India Company from 1802, it became a protected state after 1818; its land lay in separate blocks, and the Baroda and Kadi districts were the largest.

Baroda State (Gaekwad; Kadi district).text: The northern block of the Gaekwad state of Baroda, a Maratha state in Gujarat, around Kadi and Patan. After 1818 the state was protected by the British, and Kadi was its northern district.

Basotho Kingdom.text: A kingdom in present-day Lesotho and nearby South Africa, drawn 1824-68. Moshoeshoe I gathered refugees from the Difaqane at the mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu; it fought wars with the Orange Free State until Britain annexed it as Basutoland in 1868.

Bastar.text: The largest of the Chhattisgarh feudatory princely states in central India, a forested plateau ruled from Jagdalpur. It joined India and was merged into the Central Provinces on 1 January 1948.

Bastar (Kakatiya kingdom).text: A forest kingdom in the Dandakaranya region of central India, ruled by rajas who claimed descent from the Kakatiyas of Warangal. It became a tributary of the Bhonsles of Nagpur in the late 18th century, and after 1818 it was a British-protected state.

Bavand dynasty.text: An Iranian dynasty ruling Tabaristan (Mazandaran, on Iran's Caspian coast), sometimes independent and sometimes a vassal. The map shows two of its lines: the Ispahbadhiyya of 1074 to 1210 and the Kinkhwariyya of 1238 to 1349.

Bavarians.text: The Bavarians were a people first recorded around the 550s, living in the land between the Danube and the Alps. Ruled by dukes of the Agilolfing family under Frankish overlordship, they lost their last such duke, Tassilo III, when Charlemagne deposed him in 788.

Belize.text: A small country on the Caribbean coast of Central America, formerly British Honduras, which became independent in September 1981. English is its official language, the only Central American country where this is so, and it has a huge barrier reef.

Berar (Hyderabad Assigned Districts).text: Berar, the Hyderabad Assigned Districts in central India, 1858-1903. They belonged to the Nizam of Hyderabad but were run by the British under an 1853 treaty; leased permanently in 1902, they joined the Central Provinces in 1903.

Berar Sultanate.text: A Deccan sultanate of central India founded in 1490 by Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, governor of Berar, as the Bahmani Sultanate broke up. Ruled by the Imad Shahi dynasty from Ellichpur (Achalpur), it was invaded and annexed by neighbouring Ahmadnagar in 1574.

Bessarabia.text: A historical region between the Prut and Dniester rivers, now mostly in Moldova with a southern part in Ukraine. Russia took it from the Ottoman-ruled principality of Moldavia in 1812, after a war that ended with the Treaty of Bucharest.

Betsimisaraka Confederation.text: A confederation of east-coast peoples of Madagascar, formed c. 1712 by Ratsimilaho, son of an English pirate and a local princess. It stretched from the Bay of Antongil south toward Vatomandry, with its centre at Foulpointe and Fénérive.

Beylik of Alaiye.text: A beylik centred on Alanya (Alaiye) on Turkey's south coast, semi-independent after the Seljuk defeat at Köse Dağ. It was at times under the Karamanids, passed briefly to the Mamluks in 1427, and fell to the Ottomans in 1471.

Beylik of Aydin.text: A Turkish principality on the Aegean coast of Anatolia, founded around 1300 and famous for its raiding fleet. Its capital was first Birgi and later the port of Selçuk, and it was finally absorbed into the Ottoman state in the 1420s.

Beylik of Dulkadir.text: A Turkish principality in southeastern Anatolia, based first at Elbistan and later Maraş, founded in the 1330s. It sat between the Ottomans and the Mamluks, and the Ottomans conquered it in 1515, finally annexing it in 1522.

Beylik of Erzincan (Emirate of Erzincan).text: An emirate centred on Erzincan in eastern Turkey, autonomous after Eretna's death in 1352 under Ahi Ayna and his successors. Mutahharten was a vassal of Timur, and the Qara Qoyunlu annexed it c. 1410.

Beylik of Hamid.text: A Turkish principality in southwestern Anatolia around Eğirdir and Isparta, one of the small states that rose from the decline of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. Founded by Dündar Bey, it lasted from about 1280 until the 1390s.

Beylik of Isfendiyar.text: A Turkish principality on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, also called the Candar dynasty, founded about 1291. Its lands included Kastamonu and Sinop, and it survived until the Ottomans, led by Mehmed II, took it in 1461.

Beylik of Karaman.text: A powerful Turkish principality in south-central Anatolia, founded in the 1250s by the Karamanlu clan. Its capital was Karaman, and for a time Konya. It was a long rival of the Ottomans, who finally absorbed it in 1487.

Beylik of Karasi.text: A Turkish principality in northwestern Anatolia around Balıkesir, founded around 1300 by Karasi Bey. Its sea raiders troubled the Byzantines, but in the 1330s or 1340s (sources disagree) the Ottoman sultan Orhan took its lands and gave them to his son Suleiman.

Beylik of Lâdik (İnançoğulları).text: A small Turkish beylik around Lâdik, now Denizli, in south-west Turkey, which emerged as Seljuk power collapsed in the 1260s. It later depended on the Germiyanids and was absorbed c. 1368.

Beylik of Menteshe.text: The first of the Turkish beyliks of Anatolia, in the southwest around ancient Caria, named for its founder Menteshe Bey. It had its capital at Milas, used its harbours for sea trade and raiding, and lasted until the Ottomans took it over in the early 1400s.

Beylik of Saruhan.text: A Turkish principality in western Anatolia centred on Manisa, founded in the early 1300s by Saruhan Bey in the Gediz valley. Under him it grew into a sea power on the Aegean, and the Ottomans absorbed it for good in 1412.

Beylik of Sinop.text: The Black Sea port of Sinop in northern Anatolia. It was ruled by the Pervane family, Seljuk officials, until the early 1320s, when the Candar dynasty of Kastamonu took it over and made it a base on the coast.

Beylik of Tacettin.text: A small Turkmen principality of Niksar and the coast at Ünye and Çarşamba in northern Turkey, 1348 to 1428. It lay between Trebizond, the Ottomans and Kadi Burhan al-Din's state at Sivas (once Eretnid).

Beylik of Teke.text: A Turkish principality on the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia, founded in 1321 by a branch of the Hamid dynasty. Its capital was the port of Antalya, and it lasted until the Ottomans took it in the 1420s.

Beylik of Tunis.text: The Husainid monarchy of Tunisia, ruled by hereditary beys from 1705, who were nominally Ottoman but largely independent. It lasted until the French protectorate in 1881.

Bharatpur (Jat kingdom).text: A Jat kingdom of the Sinsinwar clan in Rajasthan, which under Suraj Mal (1755-63) ruled far beyond its later borders, including Agra, held 1761-74. It resisted Lord Lake's siege in 1805 but fell to the British in 1826.

Bhauma-Kara kingdom (Toshala).text: A dynasty of coastal Odisha, c. 736-839 on this map, ruling Toshala north of the Mahanadi from Jajpur. Its kings include Shivakara I and Shubhakara. Its start date is uncertain, since historians disagree whether its era began in 736 or 831.

Bhopal.text: A Muslim-ruled princely state in central India, governed for much of the 1800s by women rulers known as begums. Its capital, Bhopal, is now the capital of Madhya Pradesh.

Bidar Sultanate.text: A Deccan sultanate of central India, ruled by the Barid Shahi dynasty from the city of Bidar. One of the five states that took the place of the Bahmani Sultanate, it was ended by Bijapur around 1619.

Bijago people.text: The Bijagós are some 88 islands and islets off Guinea-Bissau in West Africa, home to the Bijago people. Their isolation from the mainland gave them considerable autonomy, and Portugal did not formally annex the islands until 1937.

Bijapur Sultanate.text: One of the five Deccan sultanates of India, founded in 1490 by Yusuf Adil Shah and ruled by his Adil Shahi dynasty. At its peak it was among the most powerful states in India, and it left famous buildings like the domed Gol Gumbaz. The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb conquered it in 1686.

Bikaner.text: A Rathore Rajput princely state in the Thar Desert of north-west Rajasthan, part of the Rajputana Agency under British rule. It acceded to India in 1947.

Bikaner State.text: A Rajput princely state in the desert of north-west Rajasthan. Once a Mughal vassal, it paid tribute to Maratha armies in the 18th century, and signed a protection treaty with Britain in 1818.

Bikaner kingdom.text: The Rathore kingdom of Bikaner in Rajasthan, India. Rao Kalyan Mal, restored with Sher Shah's help in 1544, ruled it after the Sur collapse and submitted to Akbar at Nagaur in 1570.

Bishopric of Ösel–Wiek (Dagö).text: The island of Dagö (Hiiumaa), Estonia, part of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek, a church-ruled territory of medieval Livonia under a prince-bishop from 1228 to 1560.

Bishopric of Ösel–Wiek (Wiek).text: The Wiek (Läänemaa), the western Estonian mainland coast, part of the prince-bishopric of Ösel-Wiek of 1228 to 1560, with Lihula and Hapsal as its bishop's seats.

Bishopric of Ösel–Wiek (Ösel).text: Ösel (Saaremaa), the biggest Estonian island, conquered in 1227 and made part of the prince-bishopric of Ösel-Wiek, with Arensburg (Kuressaare) as its seat. It was an autonomous part of the bishopric from 1241 to 1343.

Bit Adini.text: An Aramaean kingdom on the Euphrates in northern Syria, c. 1000-856 BCE, with its capital at Til Barsip. Its king Ahuni lost it to Shalmaneser III of Assyria in 856 BCE, who renamed the city Kar-Shalmaneser.

Blambangan Kingdom.text: The last Hindu kingdom on Java, based in the island's far eastern corner around Banyuwangi. It outlasted Majapahit's collapse in the late 1400s and survived into the 1700s, and is remembered through the Javanese folk tale of Menak Jingga and Damarwulan.

Boina Kingdom.text: A Sakalava kingdom in north-west Madagascar, founded from Menabe and rich from the Mahajanga trade. Merina forces took Mahajanga in 1824, and the kingdom was occupied after 1832 and annexed in 1840.

Bolivia.text: A landlocked Andean country named after Simón Bolívar, which became independent from Spain in 1825. It has two capitals: La Paz holds the government, while Sucre is the constitutional capital and seat of the courts.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.text: A Balkan country that declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1992, which led to a brutal war until 1995. The Dayton Agreement then split it into two self-governing parts under a shared national government.

Breton Kingdoms.text: The Breton kingdoms were Celtic realms in Brittany, northwest France, founded by Britons who migrated from Britain around the 5th and 6th centuries CE. They stayed independent under Frankish pressure, and united under Nominoë in the 9th century.

British Bencoolen.text: A British East India Company pepper post on the southwest coast of Sumatra, centred on Fort Marlborough. Britain handed it over to the Netherlands under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824.

British Crown Dependencies.text: The Isle of Man, Jersey and Guernsey. These self-governing islands belong to the British Crown but are not part of the United Kingdom, and each has its own parliament that makes laws on local matters.

British zone.text: The British occupation zone of Germany, 1945-49, one of four zones set up after the May 1945 surrender, under the Allied Control Council in Berlin. In May 1949 the western zones became the Federal Republic of Germany.

Brythons.text: The Brythons, or Britons, were the Celtic-speaking people of Britain, who kept their independence in the west and north after Roman rule ended. They split into the Welsh, Cornish, Bretons and the Cumbrians of the Old North, and their tongue lives on in Welsh, Cornish and Breton.

Buganda.text: A Bantu kingdom on the north-west shore of Lake Victoria in present-day Uganda, ruled by the Kabaka. Small at first beside Bunyoro, it grew in the 18th century into the strongest lake state, and became a British protectorate in 1894.

Bundi State.text: A Rajput princely state in south-east Rajasthan. Formerly a Mughal vassal, it paid tribute to the Marathas in the 18th century and came under British protection by treaty in 1818.

Bundu.text: A Fula Muslim state in Senegal and Mali between the Falémé and upper Gambia rivers, founded in 1690 by the Torodbe cleric Malick Sy. By 1716 it was the most powerful state on the upper Senegal. It became a French protectorate in the 1850s.

Bunyoro (Bunyoro-Kitara).text: A kingdom in western Uganda ruled by the Babiito Omukama, the leading lake power of the 16th and 17th centuries. Toro broke away c. 1830, and Kabalega's resistance to the British ended with his capture in 1899.

Burgundian Kingdom.text: The Kingdom of the Burgundians grew from a Roman resettlement of Burgundians around Lake Geneva in 443, after their earlier kingdom on the Rhine was crushed. It spread across today's western Switzerland and southeast France, moved its capital from Geneva to Lyon, and passed to the Franks in 534. Burgundy still bears its name.

Burgundians.text: The Burgundians were a Germanic people first recorded near the Vistula in present-day Poland between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. By the 3rd century some lived by the Main river in Germany, and around 406 they crossed the Rhine into the Roman Empire, where they went on to found a kingdom.

Burid dynasty (Emirate of Damascus).text: A Turkic dynasty founded by the atabeg Toghtekin, who took Damascus after the Seljuk ruler Duqaq died in 1104. It governed the emirate of Damascus as subjects of the Seljuks until Nur ad-Din of Aleppo took the city in 1154.

Burkina Faso.text: A landlocked West African country that became independent from France in 1960 as Upper Volta. In 1984 the young leader Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso, meaning land of upright people.

Byeonhan.text: One of the Samhan, the three loose confederations of chiefdoms in southern Korea, on the southwestern side of the Nakdong River valley. Its chiefdoms produced growing numbers of iron weapons, and most of them later joined the Gaya confederacy.

Cai.text: A small Chinese state of the Zhou period, in the area of modern Henan, founded for Cai Shu Du, a younger brother of King Wu, the first Zhou king. It moved its capital several times and was finally destroyed by Chu in 447 BCE.

Calicut (Zamorin's kingdom).text: The kingdom of the Samoothiri (Zamorin) of Kozhikode, which made Calicut the chief port of the Malabar coast in Kerala, India. It was rising to prosperity by 1342, when Ibn Battuta wrote of the Zamorin.

California Republic.text: A tiny breakaway state, known as the Bear Flag Republic, declared by American settlers in Sonoma in June 1846 during the war with Mexico. It lasted only about three weeks before the United States flag replaced it.

Cambodia.text: The Khmer kingdom after Angkor, squeezed between Siam and Vietnam as both grew stronger in these years. Both neighbours repeatedly interfered in Cambodian royal succession, and the court sat at Oudong for much of this period.

Cao.text: A small Zhou-dynasty state in what is now western Shandong, founded in the eleventh century BCE by Shu Zhenduo, a brother of King Wu. Its capital was Taoqiu and it was conquered by Song in 487 BCE.

Capetian House of Anjou.text: A royal house, a branch of the French Capetian dynasty, founded by Charles I of Anjou, who took the Kingdom of Sicily in 1266. The Sicilian Vespers revolt cost them the island of Sicily in 1282, but they held Naples.

Caquetío chiefdoms.text: The Caquetío were an Indigenous people of northwestern Venezuela and of Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire. Spanish contact from about 1500 brought them heavy losses, including the deportation of some 2,000 islanders to Hispaniola in 1515.

Carantania.text: Carantania was an early Slavic principality in the eastern Alps, in today's Austria and Slovenia. It was an ancestor of Slovene statehood, famous for its prince-installation ritual on a stone throne, and fell under Bavarian and Frankish rule.

Carnatic Sultanate.text: A state in southeastern India ruled by a Muslim nawab, at first at Arcot, under the nominal overlordship of the Nizam of Hyderabad. It lasted until the British ended it in 1855.

Caroline Islands chiefdoms.text: Before European rule, the scattered Caroline Islands of the western Pacific were home to many separate chiefdoms and clan groups, now mostly in Micronesia and Palau. Spain claimed the islands in the 1880s, ending that independence.

Catalan Company.text: A band of mercenaries from Aragon and Catalonia, hired by the Byzantine emperor in 1303 under Roger de Flor. After he was murdered in 1305 they turned on their employers, won the Duchy of Athens in 1311, and held it until about 1388.

Catalonia.text: A brief independent Catalonia in 1640-41, born in the Reapers' War against the Spanish crown. Catalan leaders declared a republic under French protection in January 1641, and days later recognised Louis XIII of France as their Count of Barcelona.

Caucasian Albania.text: An ancient kingdom of tribes in the eastern Caucasus, in today's Azerbaijan, with no link to Albania in the Balkans. It had its own language and alphabet and was an early Christian land, before Persia and then Arabs took over.

Caucasian Iberia.text: The Georgian kingdom of Kartli in the east of Georgia, called Iberia by the Greeks and Romans. Caught between Rome and Persia, it made Christianity its state religion in the fourth century under King Mirian III.

Caucasian Imamate.text: A Muslim resistance state in Dagestan and Chechnya that fought Russian conquest during the Caucasian War. Led by imams, most famously Shamil, it ran under Islamic law until Shamil's capture in 1859.

Cayor.text: The largest Wolof kingdom of Senegal, which broke from the Jolof empire at the battle of Danki in 1549. It lay between Waalo, Jolof and Baol and included the Cap-Vert peninsula. France began annexing it in 1879.

Central African Republic.text: A landlocked country at the heart of Africa, independent from France in 1960. Its first leader, Barthélemy Boganda, died in a plane crash before independence. Later rulers included Jean-Bédel Bokassa, who crowned himself emperor in 1977.

Central India Agency (other states): Cha.text: A grouping on the map of small princely states of the Central India Agency, here the Bundelkhand state of Charkhari, under British rule. The agency was a patchwork of small states, and all of them acceded to India in 1947-48.

Central India Agency (other states): Dat.text: A grouping on the map of two small Bundelkhand princely states, Datia and Samthar, which belonged to the Central India Agency under British rule. Like all the agency's states they acceded to India in 1947-48.

Central India Agency (other states): Dew.text: A grouping on the map of many small princely states of the Central India Agency in Malwa and Bhopawar, such as Dewas, Dhar and Ratlam, with detached Gwalior districts. The agency was a patchwork of tiny states and enclaves, all of which acceded to India in 1947-48.

Central India Agency (other states): Orc.text: A grouping on the map of Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand princely states of the Central India Agency, among them Orchha, Panna, Chhatarpur and Maihar. They were small states under British protection and all acceded to India in 1947-48.

Central India Agency (other states): sma.text: A grouping on the map of small Bundelkhand princely states of the Central India Agency near Baoni. The agency was a patchwork of small states under British protection, all of which acceded to India in 1947-48.

Ceylon.text: The island now called Sri Lanka, drawn here c. 1236-1506 for its medieval kingdoms, Sinhalese and Tamil. Ceylon was the name used by Europeans and later the British; the country became independent in 1948.

Chahamanas of Jalor.text: A branch of the Naddula Chahamanas in southern Rajasthan, first vassals of the Chaulukyas and then independent, ruling from Jalor. Alauddin Khalji's siege of Jalore in 1311 ended it.

Chahamanas of Naddula.text: A branch of the Chahamana Rajputs ruling Marwar from Nadol in Rajasthan, c. 1056-1197. A junior branch held Jalore from the 1160s, and Qutb al-Din Aibak's invasion of 1197 ended the kingdom.

Chahamanas of Ranthambore.text: A kingdom in Rajasthan, India, founded in 1192 by Govindaraja, son of Prithviraja III, as a Ghurid vassal. It alternated between being subject to Delhi and independent until Alauddin Khalji's siege ended it in 1301.

Chalukya Dynasty.text: The Chalukyas of Badami ruled much of the Deccan from about 543 CE. Their king Pulakeshin II beat the north Indian emperor Harsha, and they built rock temples at Badami and Aihole. The Rashtrakutas replaced them in 753.

Chamorro chiefdoms.text: The communities of the Chamorro people on the Mariana Islands, including Guam, in Micronesia, organised in a caste society with a ruling upper caste. Their way of life was upended after Spain annexed and colonized the islands in the late 1600s, but the Chamorro people still live there today.

Champaner (Khichi Chauhans).text: Khichi Chauhan chiefs who held the hill fort of Pavagadh above Champaner in Gujarat, India. Mahmud Begada captured it in 1484 after a 20-month siege, and Champaner then briefly became Gujarat's capital.

Chanda (Gond kingdom).text: A Gond kingdom in the Wardha-Wainganga country of central India, in Maharashtra, with its capital at Chanda (Chandrapur). It ended in 1751 when the Maratha leader Raghoji I Bhonsle conquered it.

Chandela Kingdom.text: A Hindu kingdom of central India, from c. 831 into the early 1300s. Its kings built the temples of Khajuraho, famed for their carved sculptures, but their power faded after attacks by the Chahamanas and Ghurids around 1200.

Chandela Kingdom (Jhansi country).text: The western part of the Chandela kingdom of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand), around Jhansi, Orchha and Datia in central India, c. 1040-1201. It lay between the Kachchhapaghatas of Gwalior and the Chandela heartland at Mahoba and Khajuraho.

Chandra Dynasty.text: A Buddhist dynasty of southeastern Bengal, based in the Samatata region, with its centre later at Bikrampur. It ruled in the 10th and 11th centuries, until about the mid 1000s.

Chang-shan.text: A short-lived kingdom in central Hebei, China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE when the Qin dynasty collapsed. Its king Zhang Er allied with Liu Bang, and the kingdom was destroyed in 205 BCE.

Characene.text: A kingdom at the head of the Persian Gulf, in southern Iraq, c. 141 BCE-222 CE. Hyspaosines founded it after the Seleucid collapse; it was often a Parthian vassal with its own coins until Ardashir I took it.

Chauhan Dynasty.text: Rajput ruling families of the Chauhan clan in Rajasthan and northern India. The best-known ruler was Prithviraj Chauhan of the Ajmer line, whose defeat at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 was a major setback for the clan.

Chauhan Dynasty (Delhi and Hansi).text: The Shakambhari Chahamanas (Chauhans) of Rajasthan, who took Delhi and Hansi from the Tomaras around 1152 under Vigraharaja IV. Chahamana rule there ended when Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraja III in 1192.

Chaulukya Dynasty.text: A dynasty ruling Gujarat and parts of Rajasthan, western India, c. 940 to 1244, also known as the Solankis. They built the Rani ki Vav stepwell and rebuilt the Somnath temple, with Anahilavada Patan as their capital.

Chen.text: A small state of ancient China on the plains of eastern Henan, founded by Duke Hu of Chen, a descendant of the sage-king Shun. Chu absorbed it in 479 BCE, and Chen is still a common Chinese surname.

Cheng Han.text: Cheng-Han was a Sixteen Kingdoms state in Sichuan, founded in 304 CE by Li Xiong of the Ba-Di people. After a few decades of rule it was conquered in 347 by the Eastern Jin general Huan Wen.

Chenla.text: Chenla was the early Khmer kingdom that rose after Funan in Cambodia, in the 6th and 7th centuries CE. Its capital Ishanapura, now Sambor Prei Kuk, has brick temples. It is a stepping stone toward the later Khmer Empire.

Chera Perumal kingdom (Mahodayapuram).text: The medieval Chera Perumal kingdom of Kerala, c. 1000-1123, ruled from Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur). At its height it ran from the Chandragiri river to Nagercoil; Chola invasions did not end it, but its break-up around 1124 left Venad, Kolathunadu and others.

Chera Perumal kingdom (Makotai).text: A kingdom of central Kerala, c. 844-1000 on this map, ruled from Mahodayapuram, today's Kodungallur. Its kings included Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara, and most of its revenue came from maritime spice trade; recent scholars see it as a looser state than once thought.

Chera kingdom (Kuda Nadu, Malabar coast).text: One of the three great Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam age, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, on the Malabar coast of Kerala. Its kings are known from Sangam poems and Graeco-Roman accounts, which attest a pepper and spice trade with Graeco-Roman merchants; Senguttuvan is among its rulers.

Chhattisgarh feudatory states: Kanker.text: Kanker, one of the Chhattisgarh feudatory states in central India, small princely states under the British Central Provinces. It was merged into the Central Provinces on 1 January 1948.

Chhattisgarh feudatory states: Kawardha.text: Kawardha, one of the Chhattisgarh feudatory states in central India, small princely states under the British Central Provinces. It was merged into the Central Provinces on 1 January 1948.

Chhattisgarh feudatory states: Nandgaon,.text: A grouping on the map of two Chhattisgarh feudatory states in central India, Nandgaon and Khairagarh, small princely states under the Central Provinces. They merged into the Central Provinces on 1 January 1948.

Chhattisgarh feudatory states: Raigarh,.text: A grouping on the map of Chhattisgarh feudatory states in central India: Raigarh, Sarangarh, Sakti, Korea, Jashpur and Udaipur (Dharamjaigarh). These small princely states, subject to the British Central Provinces, merged into it on 1 January 1948.

Chiangmai.text: The northern Thai kingdom of Chiang Mai, retaken from Burma in 1775 with Siamese help and rebuilt by Chao Kawila from 1797. Siam made him a tributary king in 1802 and gradually absorbed the state, ending its separate existence in 1899.

Chindaka Nagas of Chakrakota.text: A dynasty of the Nagas ruling Bastar, Koraput and Kalahandi in central India from 1023 to about 1176. The Kalachuri king Jajalla-deva I invaded in 1114; the last known ruler appears in an inscription of 1324.

Chitral.text: A mountain princely state in the far north-west of present-day Pakistan, ruled by a Mehtar and allied with the British from 1885. Its Mehtar signed the Instrument of Accession to Pakistan on 6 November 1947.

Chobanids.text: A dynasty descended from a Mongol family that took over Azerbaijan and nearby lands after the Mongol Ilkhanate fell apart in the 1330s. They ruled from Tabriz until 1357, when an army of the Golden Horde captured the city and ended their rule.

Chola kingdom (Chola Nadu).text: One of the three great Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam age, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, in the Kaveri delta of Tamil Nadu. Karikala and Kocengannan are its best-known early kings, and its port Puhar (Poompuhar) lay near the delta.

Chu.text: The big southern power of Zhou-era China, centered on the Yangtze middle valley, whose rulers took the title of king. Famed for its shamanic poetry and lacquerware, it fought Qin for centuries before falling in 223 BCE.

Chudasama kingdom (Sorath).text: A Rajput kingdom in Sorath, south-western Saurashtra in Gujarat, c. 1000-1471, with the fortress of Uparkot at Junagadh and Mount Girnar. Often tributary to the Chaulukyas, it fell to Mahmud Begada of Gujarat in 1472.

Chutia kingdom.text: A kingdom on the north bank of the Brahmaputra around Sadiya in Assam, India, prominent from the 14th century. The Ahoms annexed it in 1523-24.

Chámpa.text: Champa was a group of Cham kingdoms along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, lasting from about the 2nd century CE to 1832. Its ports grew rich from the spice trade, and the Cham worshipped Hindu gods. Vietnam slowly absorbed it.

Chüzan.text: One of three small kingdoms on Okinawa in the 1300s, in the middle of the island, with its capital at Urasoe. Its ruler eventually conquered the other two, and in 1429 it united the island as the Ryukyu Kingdom.

Cimmerian Bosporus.text: A Greek and Scythian kingdom on the Crimean peninsula and the Taman peninsula by the Black Sea, c. 438 BCE to c. 527 CE. It grew rich shipping grain to Athens, and sat on the Strait of Kerch.

Circassia.text: The land of the Adyghe (Circassian) princes and free communities between the Kuban river, the Black Sea and the Caucasus, with Kabarda in the east. Tradition credits Inal the Great with uniting the principalities in the 15th century.

Cisalpine Republic.text: A French client republic in northern Italy, set up by Napoleon in 1797, with Milan as its capital. It became the Italian Republic in 1802.

Cispadane Republic.text: A French client republic south of the Po in northern Italy, founded in 1796 under Napoleon's protection. Its Reggio Emilia congress adopted the green, white and red tricolour, and it merged into the Cisalpine Republic in 1797.

Classic Veracruz Culture.text: Classic Veracruz was a culture of Mexico's Gulf coast, c. 100 to 1000 CE, famed for the city of El Tajín and its Pyramid of the Niches. They played the ball game, and carved stone yokes and smiling clay figures.

Cochin.text: A small princely state on the south-west coast of India around Ernakulam and Trichur, north of Travancore. It acceded to India in 1947 and merged with Travancore on 1 July 1949; today it forms part of Kerala.

Colchis.text: A land on the eastern Black Sea coast in today's western Georgia, famous in Greek myth as where Jason and the Argonauts sought the Golden Fleece. In reality it was an early Georgian state of mixed peoples that sold gold, iron, timber and honey to Greek cities.

Commonwealth of Dominica.text: A mountainous, forested island in the eastern Caribbean, independent from Britain in 1978. It is not to be confused with the Dominican Republic, and is known as the Nature Island.

Commonwealth of The Bahamas.text: An island chain of about 700 islands in the Atlantic southeast of Florida, independent from Britain in July 1973. Columbus first landed in the Americas on one of its islands in 1492.

Commune of the Zealots.text: A radical faction that ran the Byzantine port of Thessaloniki from 1342 until 1349, during the civil war between the regents of John V and John VI Kantakouzenos. The Zealots seized and shared out aristocrats' property, until the townspeople rose against them and Kantakouzenos entered the city in 1350.

Communist Cuba.text: Cuba under Fidel Castro's one-party socialist government, a close ally of the Soviet Union in the Caribbean. The island survived the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961 and sat at the centre of the 1962 Missile Crisis, which nearly sparked nuclear war.

Communist Laos.text: The Lao People's Democratic Republic, a one-party communist state proclaimed in December 1975 after the Pathet Lao movement took power and ended the monarchy. It was a close ally of Vietnam.

Comorian chiefdoms.text: The small chiefdoms and sultanates of the Comoro Islands, in the Indian Ocean between Africa and Madagascar. The islands were first settled c. 800 to 1000, and later ruling houses with Persian Gulf and Hadhrami Arab roots tied them to the Swahili coast, until France took over in the 1800s.

Comoro sultanates.text: The islands of the Comoros, between East Africa and Madagascar, divided among rival small sultanates with strong ties to Swahili coast trade. France took the islands in the 1800s, starting with Mayotte in 1841, and in 1975 the Comoros declared independence, though Mayotte stayed French.

Comoros.text: A small group of volcanic islands in the Indian Ocean between Madagascar and Africa. Three of them declared independence from France in 1975, while the fourth, Mayotte, chose to remain French.

Comtat Venaissin.text: A small papal territory in southern France, around Carpentras, held by the popes from 1274 until the French Revolution annexed it in 1791. Though surrounded by French lands, it was never part of the kingdom of France, and it sheltered Jews long after they were expelled elsewhere.

Confederation of the Rhine.text: A union of German client states created by Napoleon in 1806 after the end of the Holy Roman Empire. It supplied troops to France and collapsed in 1813 after Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig.

Cook Islands chiefdoms.text: The island chiefdoms of the Cook Islands in the South Pacific, led by paramount chiefs called ariki. Britain declared a protectorate in 1888 at the request of a leading ariki, Makea, and since 1965 the islands have governed themselves, with New Zealand handling defence and foreign affairs.

Cornwall.text: Cornwall in this period was the Brittonic kingdom at the southwest tip of Britain, a remnant of old Dumnonia. West Saxon armies pushed Cornwall back, and tradition says King Athelstan set the Tamar as its border in the 10th century.

Corsican Republic.text: An independent Corsica proclaimed in 1755 by Pasquale Paoli in a revolt against Genoa. It had its own written constitution, until Genoa sold its claim to France and French forces conquered the island in 1769.

County of Ampuria.text: A medieval Catalan county around the town of Empúries in the Empordà region of northeast Catalonia. It split from Roussillon in 989 and was ruled by its own line of counts until 1322; from 1341 it was held by members of the royal house of Aragon.

County of Anjou.text: A French county in the Loire valley, with Angers as its capital. Its counts, the Plantagenets, became kings of England, and Henry II inherited it. The French king Philip II took it in 1204.

County of Aragon.text: A small Frankish border county in the Pyrenean valley of the Aragon river in northern Spain, founded in the early 800s. Its counts grew its lands, and in 1035 it became the Kingdom of Aragon under Ramiro I.

County of Armagnac.text: A county in Gascony in southwestern France, between the Adour and Garonne rivers, split off as a separate county in 960. Its counts grew into one of the three great lordships of the French south, adding Rodez and other lands by marriage and purchase.

County of Artois.text: A county in northern France around Arras, near the Belgian border, created in 1237 for Robert, brother of King Louis IX. It later passed to the Dukes of Burgundy and the Habsburgs, and France took it in 1659.

County of Auvergne.text: The county of Auvergne in the volcanic highlands of central France. Philip II joined most of it to the royal lands, but the counts held on to a remnant around Vic-le-Comte, which passed to the crown only in the 16th century through Catherine de' Medici.

County of Barcelona.text: The leading Catalan county, set up after the Franks took Barcelona in 801. Its counts gathered other counties under their rule and became effectively independent around 988, and from 1137 a royal marriage tied the county to Aragon, a personal union completed in 1162.

County of Berga.text: A small medieval county in the Pyrenean foothills of Catalonia, around the town of Berga. It was created in 988 out of Besalú for a son of Count Oliba Cabreta, and later passed to the counts of Barcelona.

County of Besalú.text: A small landlocked Catalan county in the northeast of Catalonia, around Besalú. It was ruled by its own counts until the last count died in 1111 and it passed to Barcelona.

County of Blôis.text: A feudal county centred on Blois in the Loire valley, south of Paris. Its counts were also lords of Champagne for a time and ranked among the strongest nobles of the French kingdom.

County of Boulogne.text: A French county on the Channel coast around Boulogne-sur-Mer, first under Flanders and later with its own counts. Philip II merged it with Artois in 1212 and it joined the French crown in 1477.

County of Brabant.text: The Duchy of Brabant, an imperial state in the Low Countries, created in 1183 from the small Landgraviate of Brabant west of Brussels. Its dukes won Limburg after their victory at Worringen in 1288, and in 1430 Brabant passed by inheritance to Philip the Good of Burgundy.

County of Béarn.text: A small Pyrenean lordship in southwest France. In 1347 its viscount Gaston Fébus declared that he held Béarn from God alone, and it became in practice a sovereign principality. Its rulers shifted their court to Pau, away from Orthez, in 1464, and under Henry IV it passed to the French crown.

County of Champagne.text: A medieval county in northeast France known for its trade fairs, which made it an international trading centre. Count Henry the Liberal made Troyes its capital, and after Joan I married the future Philip IV in 1284 it passed to the French crown.

County of Edessa.text: The first Crusader state, founded in 1098 around Edessa (Şanlıurfa, Turkey) in Upper Mesopotamia. Its capture by the Muslim commander Zengi in 1144 led directly to the Second Crusade.

County of Flanders.text: A wealthy county on the North Sea in modern Belgium and France, known for cloth-making and cities such as Bruges. It was a fief of France, and passed to the dukes of Burgundy in 1384.

County of Foix.text: A medieval county in southern France, roughly the eastern part of today's Ariège department, ruled by counts from their castle above the town of Foix. In the 13th and 14th centuries they ranked among the most powerful French nobles, and after gaining Béarn in 1290 they mostly lived there.

County of Holland.text: A county of the Holy Roman Empire in the Low Countries, covering today's North and South Holland. It passed to the Dukes of Burgundy in 1433, and much later became the most important province of the Dutch Republic.

County of Luxembourg.text: A county that grew from the castle which Count Siegfried acquired in 963, in today's Luxembourg. The title count of Luxembourg dates from Conrad I in 1059. It later became a duchy in 1354.

County of Maine.text: A French county around Le Mans, between Normandy and Anjou. Its location made it a battleground between the Norman and Angevin rulers, and eventually it joined the French crown.

County of Namur.text: A small county on the Sambre and Meuse rivers in present-day Belgium, c. 981-1421, between Brabant, Liège and Hainaut. John III sold it to Philip the Good of Burgundy in 1421, taking effect at his death in 1429.

County of Nevers.text: A county in central France around Nevers, roughly today's Nièvre department, dating from about 900. It was often tied to the neighbouring Duchy of Burgundy and passed through several families, including the counts of Flanders, before becoming a duchy in 1539.

County of Oldenburg.text: A county on the Hunte and Jade in north-west Germany, held by the House of Oldenburg, whose Christian I became king of Denmark in 1448. It added Jever in 1575 and passed to the Danish crown in 1667.

County of Osona.text: A Catalan county of the old Spanish March, centred on Vic in northeast Spain. It was ruled with Barcelona's counts and was eventually absorbed by them.

County of Pallars.text: A small Pyrenean county in Catalonia, nominally part of the Frankish empire but in practice independent. It was ruled by its own counts for several centuries and was later split into two parts.

County of Pallars Jussà.text: Lower Pallars, a Catalan county in the Pyrenees of northeastern Spain, created in 1011 when Count Sunyer's lands were split between his sons. Richer than its mountain neighbour, it suffered long feuds with it, and in 1192 its last countess handed it to the Crown of Aragon.

County of Pallars Sobirà.text: Upper Pallars, a poor and remote county high in the central Pyrenees of Catalonia, formed in 1011 when the old county of Pallars was divided. Its counts raided their richer lowland cousins; around 1199 it passed by marriage to the house of Comminges, and it survived until 1487.

County of Poitou.text: A county in western France around Poitiers, covering today's Vienne, Deux-Sèvres and Vendée. Long held by the dukes of Aquitaine and then the kings of England, it was seized by Philip II of France in 1205, and Henry III of England failed to win it back.

County of Portugal.text: A medieval county around Guimarães and Porto in northern Portugal, where the Portuguese identity formed. In 1139 its ruler Afonso Henriques took the title of king, and it became the Kingdom of Portugal.

County of Provence.text: A county in south-east France between the Rhone, Durance and Var, c. 972-1245. It was ruled by the Bosonid counts after William the Liberator drove out the Saracens of Fraxinetum, and later by the House of Barcelona; it passed to Charles of Anjou in 1245.

County of Périgord.text: A county in southwestern France, the land of the Petrocorii tribe, with Périgueux, Bergerac and Sarlat as its main towns. It was held as a fief under the dukes of Aquitaine and was fought over in the Hundred Years' War.

County of Ribagorza.text: A medieval county in the Pyrenees of northeast Spain, on the border of Aragon and Catalonia. It began as a Frankish border county and was later absorbed by the Kingdom of Aragon.

County of Rosellón.text: The medieval county of Roussillon, in the far south of France next to Catalonia, with Perpignan as its main town. It was ruled by local counts for centuries and was linked to Catalonia and Aragon.

County of Rouergue.text: A medieval county in southern France, roughly the modern department of Aveyron, with Rodez as its chief town. It lay between Auvergne, Languedoc and Quercy and changed hands several times during the Middle Ages.

County of Savoy.text: A feudal county of the Holy Roman Empire in the western Alps, which grew up as the old Burgundian kingdom fell apart in the 11th century. Its counts made Chambéry their capital after 1220, gained Nice in 1388, and were raised to dukes in 1416.

County of Toulouse.text: A powerful county in southern France, c. 778 to 1271. Count Raymond IV led the largest army of the First Crusade, but the Albigensian Crusade broke his heirs, and in 1271 the county passed to the French crown.

County of Touraine.text: A county in the Loire valley of west-central France, with Tours as its capital. King Philip II of France took it from the English crown around 1204-05, and it became part of the French royal lands.

County of Tripoli.text: A Crusader state on the coast of present-day northern Lebanon. Raymond of Toulouse began the siege in 1102, and his heirs ruled it as vassals of Jerusalem until the Mamluks conquered it in 1289.

County of Urgell.text: A medieval county in the Catalan Pyrenees, bordering Pallars and Cerdanya, carved out by the Franks around 785 to 790. One of the old Catalan counties, it kept its own counts until 1413, when it was absorbed into the Crown of Aragon after its last count rebelled.

County of Vermandois.text: A French county in Picardy, named after an ancient tribe, the Viromandui. Count Herbert II grew its power and kept King Charles the Simple captive for six years, and from 1191 the French crown took over its lands step by step.

County of Vexin.text: A county in northern France on a plateau north of the Seine, on the border between Normandy and the French crown. Both the dukes of Normandy and the kings of France fought to control it.

County of Württemberg.text: A county in south-west Germany named for the Wirtemberg hill, where Conrad I is first recorded about 1081. Stuttgart came to the county through the marriage of Ulrich I in 1251, and the county became a duchy in 1495.

County, later Duchy of Bar.text: A county between Champagne and Lorraine in north-eastern France, 1033-1430, made a duchy in 1354. Part of it was a French fief. René of Anjou inherited it in 1430 and married the heiress of Lorraine.

Cretan State.text: An autonomous state on Crete formed in 1898 after revolts against the Ottomans, with a Greek prince as high commissioner. Officially still Ottoman, it was effectively led by Greeks and joined Greece in 1913.

Crown of Aragon.text: A medieval composite monarchy whose king of Aragon was also Count of Barcelona and later King of Valencia, each land keeping its own laws. It began in 1137 with the union of Aragon and Barcelona, and in the 14th-15th centuries built a sea empire including the Balearics, Sardinia, Sicily and southern Italy.

Crown of Castile.text: A medieval kingdom in the Iberian Peninsula formed in 1230, when Ferdinand III united Castile and León. It later joined Aragon by marriage and led Spain's overseas empire.

Cuba.text: The Caribbean island nation ruled by the Communist Party since 1959. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 it lost its main trading partner and entered a harsh economic time known as the Special Period.

Cuban Communists.text: A small rebel-held zone of eastern Cuba, drawn for 1958 to 1959, during the revolution against dictator Fulgencio Batista. Fidel Castro's guerrillas, based in the Sierra Maestra mountains, took power in January 1959. The Communist Party of Cuba itself was only formed in 1965.

Cuban Nationalists.text: Cubans fighting Spain for independence in the war of 1895 to 1898, inspired by writer José Martí. The conflict drew in the United States in 1898, and Spain gave up Cuba. The article linked here is about Fidel Castro, which does not fit.

Cuman-Kipchak Confederation.text: A loose alliance of Turkic nomad tribes, the Cumans and Kipchaks, who spread over the steppe north of the Black Sea in the 11th century. They were skilled horse archers, often allies or enemies of Rus princes, and lost power to the Mongols in the 1230s-40s.

Cundinamarca.text: A short-lived state centred on Bogotá in what is now Colombia. Proclaimed in 1811, it was led for years by Antonio Nariño and refused to join the federal United Provinces. Simón Bolívar forced it into the union in December 1814, and Spain reconquered the region in 1816.

Cutch.text: A princely state on the Kutch peninsula in Gujarat, ruled by a Rao. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Cutch (Kingdom of Kutch).text: A kingdom in Kutch, western Gujarat, ruled by the Jadeja Rao dynasty from Bhuj, a city founded in 1549. The Raos paid tribute to the Mughals from the 1590s but ruled themselves, and accepted British protection in 1819.

Cuzco.text: The Cusco region in the Peruvian Andes, where the Inca began as one small chiefdom around the 1200s. From this valley they later grew into the biggest empire in the Americas, and Cusco stayed their sacred capital.

Cyprus Condominium.text: From around 688 CE, Cyprus was shared by the Byzantine Empire and the Arab caliphate, a rare arrangement where both taxed the island. Byzantium retook full control in 965, before Cyprus became an independent republic in 1960.

Cyrenaica.text: The eastern coast of today's Libya, settled by Greeks from Thera who founded Cyrene in about 631 BCE. Rich in wheat, wine and the rare herb silphium, it came under Ptolemaic Egypt in this period until its last ruler, Ptolemy Apion, left it to Rome in 96 BCE.

Czech Republic.text: A country in central Europe that became independent on 1 January 1993, when Czechoslovakia was peacefully dissolved. It covers the historic lands of Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia.

Czechoslovakia.text: A Central European country created in 1918 from Czech and Slovak lands, with Tomáš Masaryk as its first president. Nazi Germany dismantled it between 1938 and 1939. Restored after the war, it later split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia at the end of 1992.

Dabuyid Dynasty.text: The Dabuyids were a Zoroastrian dynasty of Tabaristan, on Iran's Caspian coast. They held out against the Arab conquest from the 640s CE, and survived in their forests and mountains until the Abbasids ended them in 760.

Dacia.text: The Dacian kingdom of c. 43 BCE-106 CE in the Carpathians of present-day Romania. Decebalus reunified it in the 80s CE, fought the emperors Domitian and Trajan, and lost it to Rome in 106 CE.

Dacia under Burebista.text: The Geto-Dacian kingdom of Burebista, c. 82-44 BCE, which briefly ruled from the middle Danube to the Black Sea in modern Romania and Bulgaria. It broke apart after his death in 44 BCE, according to Strabo.

Dai.text: A short-lived kingdom in northern China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by the warlord Xiang Yu when the Qin dynasty collapsed in 206 BCE. It disappeared during the civil war that ended with the founding of the Han dynasty.

Danelaw.text: The part of eastern and northern England where Danish settlers lived under their own customs, from the late 800s. Vikings took land there after the 870s, and English kings gradually won it back in the following decades.

Danish Magnates.text: A name for the broken state of Denmark after King Christopher II died in 1332. Parts of the country were held by foreign counts and local nobles for years, until Valdemar IV rebuilt the kingdom in the 1340s and 1350s.

Danishmendids.text: A Turkish dynasty that held central and northeastern Anatolia from about 1071 to 1178, around Sivas, Tokat and Niksar. They fought both Byzantines and Crusaders, and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum absorbed them.

Dauphiné.text: A province of southeastern France, roughly today's departments of Drôme, Isère and Hautes-Alpes. Its rulers were called dauphins; in 1349 it went to the French crown, and the heir to the throne then took the title.

Deccan states: Akalkot.text: Akalkot, one of the small Maratha-ruled princely states of the Deccan under the Bombay government. Along with the other Deccan states, it acceded to India in 1947.

Deccan states: Bhor.text: Bhor, one of the small Maratha-ruled princely states of the Deccan under the Bombay government, near Pune. Along with the other Deccan states, it acceded to India in 1947.

Deccan states: Phaltan.text: Phaltan, one of the small Maratha-ruled princely states of the Deccan under the Bombay government, in present-day Maharashtra. Along with the other Deccan states, it acceded to India in 1947.

Deccan states: Sangli, Miraj, Jamkhandi,.text: A grouping on the map of Southern Maratha Country princely states under the Bombay government: Sangli, Miraj, Jamkhandi, Mudhol, Ramdurg and Jath. These small Maratha-ruled states acceded to India in 1947.

Deccan states: Savantvadi.text: A small princely state in the south of present-day Maharashtra, near the Konkan coast, under the Bombay government. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Deccan states: small tract near Kurundva.text: A small tract near Kurundvad, one of the little Maratha-ruled princely states of the Southern Maratha Country under the Bombay government. Like the other Deccan states, it acceded to India in 1947.

Deccan states: small tract south of Kolh.text: A small tract south of Kolhapur, one of the little Maratha-ruled princely states of the Southern Maratha Country under the Bombay government. Like the other Deccan states, it acceded to India in 1947.

Deheubarth.text: A realm of south-west Wales ruled by the House of Dinefwr, c. 920-1093, formed when Hywel Dda joined Dyfed and Seisyllwg. The name was a regional label more than a fixed kingdom. The Normans overran it after Rhys ap Tewdwr was killed in 1093.

Deheubarth (the Lord Rhys).text: Deheubarth, the realm of south-west Wales, was rebuilt from 1155 by Rhys ap Gruffydd, the Lord Rhys, after the Normans overran it in 1093. His house of Dinefwr traced back to Hywel Dda.

Demak Sultanate.text: The first Muslim state on the island of Java, Indonesia, on the north coast. It began as a vassal port of the Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit and grew strong in the early 1500s as Islam spread, then faded by the middle of that century.

Democratic People's Republic of Korea.text: North Korea, a communist state founded in 1948 in the north of the Korean peninsula under Kim Il Sung. Pyongyang is its capital, and the Kim family has ruled it as a hereditary dictatorship ever since.

Democratic Republic of Vietnam.text: North Vietnam, the communist state led by Ho Chi Minh and based in Hanoi. After 1954 it fought the south and the United States in the Vietnam War, and united the country in 1976.

Democratic Republic of the Congo.text: A huge country in central Africa that won independence from Belgium on 30 June 1960, with Patrice Lumumba as its first prime minister. Its early years brought chaos and civil war. It was called Zaire from 1971 to 1997.

Dendi Kingdom.text: The free Songhai kingdom of the Askias on the lower Niger, set up after Morocco conquered Gao in 1591. Its northern parts broke into separate chiefdoms later; the French deposed the last askia in 1901.

Denkyira.text: An Akan gold state in south-western Ghana that dominated the Gold Coast hinterland in the 17th century, until Asante defeated it at Feyiase in 1701. That defeat opened the way for the rise of the Asante empire.

Denmark.text: A Nordic country in northern Europe, a constitutional monarchy with its capital at Copenhagen. It was liberated from German occupation in May 1945. Greenland and the Faroe Islands are self-governing parts of the Danish realm.

Denmark-England.text: A North Sea realm in which Danish kings also ruled England, drawn here c. 1040-1045. It ended with the death of Cnut the Great's son Harthacnut in 1042, when Edward the Confessor, of the old English royal line, became king of England.

Deogarh (Gond kingdom).text: A Gond kingdom in central India on the Chhindwara plateau and Nagpur plain. After a succession dispute it passed under the Bhonsle ruler Raghoji I, who founded the Maratha state of Nagpur.

Derbent Khanate.text: A short-lived khanate based at Derbent on the Caspian coast in Dagestan, set up in the Afsharid period after Nader Shah's death in 1747. It was later merged with the neighbouring Quba Khanate.

Despotate of Arta.text: A state in northwestern Greece, created in the 1350s by Albanian chiefs after they beat the Despot of Epirus at the Battle of Achelous in 1359. It lasted until 1416, when it was taken over by the Tocco family.

Despotate of Dobruja.text: A breakaway Bulgarian principality in Dobruja, on the Black Sea coast of today's Bulgaria and Romania, that split from the Second Bulgarian Empire in the 1340s. Under despots such as Dobrotitsa it kept its own navy and traded grain through Varna and Kaliakra, until the Ottomans took Varna in 1389.

Despotate of Epirus.text: A Greek successor state formed in 1204-05 after the Fourth Crusade, founded by Michael Komnenos Doukas, a relative of the Angelos emperors. It claimed to be the true heir of Byzantium, ruling parts of western Greece and Albania from Arta.

Despotate of Vidin.text: A Bulgarian state in the northwest, on the Danube, ruled by Tsar Ivan Sratsimir after the Second Bulgarian Empire split. The Ottomans destroyed it in 1396, after the crusader defeat at Nicopolis.

Dholpur State.text: A small Jat state in northern India, in what is now eastern Rajasthan, founded in 1805. Rana Kirat Singh of Gohad gave up Gohad to the British and received Dholpur, Bari and Rajakhera instead; it came under British protection in 1818.

Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom.text: The Dimasa Kachari kingdom of Assam, India. After the Ahoms occupied Dimapur in 1536, its kings abandoned it and later ruled from Maibang in the North Cachar hills.
