Domain of Rhodes.text: The Aegean island of Rhodes, which in the early and mid-1200s, as Byzantine power broke apart, was ruled as a self-governing domain by Leo Gabalas and his brother John. Genoa seized it in 1248-1250, and the Empire of Nicaea then made it one of its provinces.

Dominican Republic.text: A Caribbean country on the eastern part of Hispaniola, sharing the island with Haiti. It won independence from Haitian rule in 1844. Its capital, Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, was Europe's first permanent settlement in the New World.

Don Cossacks.text: A free military community of Cossacks living along the middle and lower Don in southern Russia, who chose their own leaders. They guarded Russia's southern frontier in return for broad self-government, and in 1637 they captured the Ottoman fortress of Azov at the mouth of the Don.

Dong-okjeo.text: A tribal state on the northeast coast of Korea, in the Hamgyong region of today's North Korea. It was a small land of farmers and fishermen that paid tribute to Goguryeo, which absorbed it.

Dongye.text: The Dongye, or Eastern Ye, were a chiefdom on the northeastern Korean coast, from about the third century BCE. They were farmers and fishers who held a yearly dance festival, and they were absorbed by Goguryeo.

Duchy of Anhalt.text: A small German duchy between the Harz Mountains and the Elbe, with Dessau as its capital. Its ruling family's lands had long been split into branch states such as Anhalt-Dessau and Anhalt-Bernburg, which were reunited in 1863; Anhalt remained a duchy until 1918.

Duchy of Aquitaine.text: A large duchy in southwest France, held for centuries by the counts of Poitiers. Eleanor of Aquitaine brought it first to the French and then to the English crown, and France finally won it back from England in 1453.

Duchy of Athens.text: A Crusader state in Attica and Boeotia in Greece after the Fourth Crusade, ruled by the French de la Roche family from 1205. Later the Catalans and then the Italian Acciaioli family held it, until the Ottomans conquered it in 1458.

Duchy of Athens (Acciaioli).text: The Duchy of Athens under the Acciaioli family: Nerio Acciaioli, a Florentine, took Athens from the Catalans in 1388. His family ruled Attica and Boeotia, paying tribute to the Ottomans, until Turahanoğlu Ömer Bey conquered the duchy in 1456.

Duchy of Bavaria.text: A duchy in southern Germany, one of the old stem duchies of the East Frankish kingdom and the Holy Roman Empire. The Wittelsbach family ruled it from 1180, and it became an electorate and later a kingdom.

Duchy of Benevento.text: The southernmost of the Lombard duchies in Italy, Benevento was set up around 571 (some say about 590) by Duke Zotto. Cut off from the Lombard north by papal lands, it was always partly independent, and after Charlemagne took the Lombard kingdom in 774 it lived on as the Principality of Benevento, in practice independent for almost three centuries.

Duchy of Bohemia.text: A medieval state in the present-day Czech Republic ruled by the Přemyslid dynasty, famous for Duke Wenceslas, later the patron saint. It was a duchy within the Holy Roman Empire and later became a kingdom.

Duchy of Brabant.text: A duchy of the Holy Roman Empire in the Low Countries, with Leuven, Brussels and Antwerp, ruled by dukes (from 1183/1190) descended from the counts of Leuven. Limburg was added in 1288 and the duchy passed to Burgundy in 1430.

Duchy of Brittany.text: A medieval duchy in northwest France, from about 939 to 1547, formed after the Vikings were driven out. Its heiress Anne of Brittany married two French kings in turn, and in 1532 the duchy was united with the French crown.

Duchy of Brunswick.text: A small duchy in northern Germany, set up in 1815 after the Congress of Vienna from the old lands of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. It belonged to the German Confederation and then the German Empire. Its monarchy ended with the revolution of 1918.

Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg.text: The Welf duchy created in 1235, when Otto the Child ceded his lands to Emperor Frederick II and was enfeoffed with the new imperial duchy, in northern Germany. It was divided in 1269 into Lüneburg and Brunswick.

Duchy of Burgundy.text: A wealthy French duchy centred on Dijon, whose Valois dukes became among the most powerful rulers in Europe. After Charles the Bold died in 1477, France took the duchy.

Duchy of Bytom.text: A small Upper Silesian duchy in southern Poland, formed about 1281 when the sons of Duke Władysław of Opole divided his lands. Its seat was Bytom, and it was one of many Piast principalities in a Poland broken into pieces.

Duchy of Cleves.text: A county on both banks of the lower Rhine around Kleve, Wesel and Emmerich, in Germany. Its first count dates from 1092, and it became a duchy in 1417. It joined with Jülich and Berg in 1521.

Duchy of Courland.text: A duchy in what is now Latvia, set up in 1561 as a vassal of Poland-Lithuania. Under Duke Jacob it even founded colonies in Tobago and the Gambia, and it was absorbed by Russia in 1795.

Duchy of Croatia.text: A medieval Slavic state on the eastern Adriatic coast, in present-day Croatia, from about the 700s to c. 925. It was founded by Croats who settled the old Roman province of Dalmatia, and it became a kingdom when Tomislav took the royal title.

Duchy of Gaeta.text: A small coastal duchy between Rome and Naples in Italy, c. 839-1140. It was nominally Byzantine but ruled independently by the Docibilian dynasty, then by Lombard and Norman lords, before Roger II of Sicily absorbed it in 1140.

Duchy of Gascony.text: A medieval duchy in southwest France, first set up by the Frankish Merovingian kings in 602 as a frontier march to control the Basques. Under a line of Basque dukes from 864 it became largely independent, but by 1053 it had passed to the dukes of Aquitaine.

Duchy of Greater Poland.text: A Polish duchy in the west-central heartland of Poland around Poznań, formed after Bolesław III Wrymouth's 1138 will split the kingdom among his sons. It was divided and reunited more than once before being absorbed into the restored Kingdom of Poland in 1320.

Duchy of Guelders.text: Guelders (Gelre) joined with the County of Zutphen in 1138, covering the Veluwe, Betuwe, Nijmegen and Zutphen in the Netherlands, plus lands around Geldern in Germany. It became a duchy in 1339 and fell to Charles V in 1543.

Duchy of Głogów.text: A Silesian duchy in Lower Silesia, in southwestern Poland, centred on Głogów. It was ruled by the Silesian Piasts and later by the Jagiellonian family.

Duchy of Holstein.text: A duchy in northern Germany, in today's Schleswig-Holstein, ruled by the Danish king but a member of the German Confederation. The fight over it and Schleswig caused wars, and Denmark lost both in 1864.

Duchy of Jawor.text: A small duchy in Lower Silesia, in today's southwestern Poland, split off from the Duchy of Legnica in 1274. It was ruled by the Silesian branch of the Piast dynasty, had its capital at Jawor, and lasted until 1392 as one of many fragments of medieval Poland.

Duchy of Jülich.text: A county, a duke's realm from 1356, west of Cologne around Jülich and Düren in Germany. It was joined with Berg in 1423 and with Cleves in 1521.

Duchy of Kalisz.text: A Polish duchy in Greater Poland around the city of Kalisz, founded in 1177 after a rebellion against Mieszko III. Its first ruler was Casimir II the Just.

Duchy of Kuyavia.text: Kuyavia, a region of central Poland between Greater Poland and Masovia, once centred on Kruszwica by Lake Gopło. After Bolesław III Wrymouth's 1138 will it was attached to Masovia, and in 1233 it became a separate Piast duchy under Duke Casimir I.

Duchy of Legnica.text: A Silesian duchy in southwestern Poland, carved out in 1248 by Bolesław II the Bald while Poland was split into provincial duchies. Ruled from Legnica by a branch of the Piast dynasty, it later accepted Bohemian overlordship and lasted until its last Piast duke died in 1675.

Duchy of Limburg.text: A small duchy on the Vesdre river between Liège and Aachen, in present-day Belgium, 1065-1288. After the War of the Limburg Succession, decided at Worringen in 1288, it passed to Brabant.

Duchy of Lorraine.text: A duchy in northeastern France, part of the Holy Roman Empire, that gave its name to the modern region. Charles the Bold of Burgundy, who tried to seize it, was defeated and killed at the Battle of Nancy in 1477. France annexed the duchy in 1766.

Duchy of Lucca.text: A small Italian state around the city of Lucca in Tuscany, 1815-47. The Congress of Vienna made it a duchy for the Bourbon-Parma family, and in 1847 Charles Louis handed it to Tuscany just before inheriting Parma.

Duchy of Luxembourg.text: A small state of the Holy Roman Empire and home territory of the House of Luxembourg, which gave the empire several emperors and Bohemia its kings. Raised to a duchy in 1353 to 1354, it passed in the 1440s to Philip the Good of Burgundy, who bought out its heiress Elisabeth.

Duchy of Mantua.text: A north Italian state ruled by the Gonzaga family, who had held Mantua as lords since 1328 and became marquesses in 1433. Emperor Charles V made it a duchy in 1530, and it ended in 1708 when Austria took it.

Duchy of Masovia.text: A Polish duchy in the northeast of the kingdom around the Vistula, created in the partition of 1138. Its capital moved from Płock to Czersk and Warsaw, and it kept a separate duke until 1526.

Duchy of Mecklenburg.text: The Mecklenburg lands on Germany's Baltic coast, divided in 1701 between Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz. The Congress of Vienna raised the duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin to grand duke in 1815, and his line ruled from Schwerin until the German Revolution of 1918.

Duchy of Milan.text: A north Italian state created in 1395 when Gian Galeazzo Visconti obtained the title of duke from Wenceslaus, King of the Romans. After the Visconti line died out, the Sforza family ruled it and brought in silk-making, and in the 1500s it passed to the Spanish Habsburgs.

Duchy of Modena and Reggio.text: A small duchy in northern Italy, in today's Emilia-Romagna, ruled by the Este family. After Napoleon's fall it was returned in 1814 to an Austrian branch of the family, and it was absorbed into the new Italy in 1859.

Duchy of Montferrat.text: A duchy in Piedmont, north-west Italy, formerly a marquisate. The Gonzaga of Mantua held it from 1536 and it became a duchy in 1574. Savoy took part of it in 1631 and the rest in 1708.

Duchy of Naples.text: A small state around Naples in southern Italy, c. 661 to 1137. It began as a Byzantine province, became effectively independent, and survived as a duchy until the Normans under Roger II absorbed it into their kingdom.

Duchy of Nassau.text: A German state formed in 1806 in the area of today's Hesse and Rhineland-Palatinate. It joined the Confederation of the Rhine, and Prussia annexed it in 1866.

Duchy of Normandy.text: A French duchy that began in 911, when Charles III gave Viking leader Rollo land at the mouth of the Seine. In 1066 Duke William conquered England, and the duchy was long held by the English kings.

Duchy of Oldenburg.text: A state in northwest Germany named after the city of Oldenburg, which had been Danish-ruled until 1773 and was raised to a duchy in the 1770s. It was later made a grand duchy, joined the German Empire in 1871 and lasted until 1918.

Duchy of Opole.text: A Silesian duchy ruled by a branch of the Polish Piast dynasty, centred on Opole in Upper Silesia, southwestern Poland. It was created in 1172 for Duke Jarosław, later merged with Racibórz more than once, and its Piast line died out in 1532.

Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.text: An Italian duchy in Emilia-Romagna. Napoleon's wife, Marie Louise, ruled it as duchess after his defeat until her death in 1847, when the Bourbon-Parma family returned. It was abolished in 1859 when it joined the new Italian state.

Duchy of Pomerania.text: The Griffin dukes' duchy on the Baltic coast of what is now Poland and Germany, a fief of the Empire from 1181, often split between Stettin and Wolgast lines. After Bogislaw XIV died in 1637 it was occupied by Sweden, and in 1648 it was divided between Sweden and Brandenburg.

Duchy of Racibórz.text: A duchy in Upper Silesia, southern Poland, first created in 1172 for a Piast prince and absorbed into a larger duchy in 1202. It was revived in 1281 when Duke Władysław's sons divided his lands, ruled from Racibórz, and lasted until 1521.

Duchy of Saint Sava.text: A small state in today's Herzegovina and Bosnia, founded in 1448 by the Kosača family. The title of herzog (duke) that its ruler took is the origin of the name Herzegovina. The Ottomans absorbed it in 1482.

Duchy of Sandomierz.text: A Polish district duchy in southeastern Poland, formed in 1138 when Bolesław III divided his kingdom, and centred on the town of Sandomierz. It was merged back into the Kingdom of Poland in 1320.

Duchy of Saxe-Lauenburg.text: An Ascanian duchy north of the lower Elbe around Lauenburg and Ratzeburg in Germany, split from Saxony in 1296. It was occupied by Celle and passed to Hanover when its last duke died in 1689.

Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg.text: An Ascanian duchy on the middle Elbe around Wittenberg in Germany, whose duke became an elector under the Golden Bull of 1356. When the line died out in 1422, Emperor Sigismund gave it to the Wettin margrave of Meissen.

Duchy of Silesia.text: A medieval duchy in the region of Silesia, formed under the Piast dynasty after 1138. It was later split into many smaller duchies, and Silesia drifted toward the Bohemian crown.

Duchy of Spoleto.text: Spoleto was a Lombard duchy in the mountains of central Italy, founded under Duke Faroald I during the 570s. Its dukes often acted on their own, and some later rose to be kings or even emperors. Beginning in the late 1100s the popes slowly took it over, and under Innocent III it ceased to be a separate state.

Duchy of Styria.text: A duchy in southern Austria and northern Slovenia, part of the Holy Roman Empire and later Austria-Hungary. Its capital was Graz, and the Habsburgs held it from the late 13th century.

Duchy of Thuringia.text: Thuringia, the old homeland of the Thuringians in central Germany, came under Frankish kings in the 500s and became an eastern frontier of Merovingian Austrasia. Around 631 King Dagobert I made a local noble, Radulf, its first duke; Radulf guarded the Saale border against the Slavs and later rebelled, keeping near-independence.

Duchy of Tuscia.text: Tuscia, first called the Duchy of Lucca, was a Lombard duchy covering much of today's Tuscany, set up in the 570s CE after the Lombards seized Byzantine lands there. Its dukes lived at Lucca, a town on the Via Francigena pilgrim road, and the duchy also took in Florence.

Duchy of Urbino.text: A duchy in the northern Marche of Italy, ruled by the Montefeltro and later della Rovere families as a papal fief. Its court was famous under Federico da Montefeltro, and it passed to the Papal States in 1631.

Duchy of Warsaw.text: A Polish client state of Napoleon set up in 1807, after the Treaties of Tilsit. It was ruled by the King of Saxony and collapsed in 1813-15 after France's defeat.

Duchy of Wrocław.text: A medieval duchy in Silesia, southwestern Poland, centred on Wrocław and ruled by the Piasts after 1138. It was splintered into many duchies and passed to the Bohemian crown by 1327.

Duchy of Württemberg.text: A south-German state in the Holy Roman Empire, raised from a county to a duchy in 1495. It turned Protestant in 1534, spent 1520-1534 under Habsburg rule, and also held the exclave of Montbéliard in France. It lasted until Napoleon's reshaping of Germany.

Duchy of the Archipelago.text: A Venetian-founded Crusader state in the Cyclades of the Aegean, centred on Naxos and Paros. It was set up in 1207 by Marco Sanudo and survived until the Ottomans took it in 1579.

Duchy of Łęczyca.text: A small Polish duchy around the town of Łęczyca in central Poland, a separate Piast land after Bolesław III Wrymouth's 1138 testament divided the kingdom. King Władysław the Short later reunited it with Poland as the Łęczyca Voivodeship.

Dumnonia.text: Dumnonia was a Brittonic kingdom in southwest Britain, covering Devon and Cornwall. It stayed independent against the West Saxons for centuries, losing its eastern lands in the 7th century, and Wessex's later campaigns left a rump state in Cornwall.

Dungarpur State.text: A Rajput princely state in southern Rajasthan, the elder Sisodia line of Vagad, west of the Mahi river. It was under Maratha control from the 1730s and accepted British protection by treaty in 1818.

Dál Riata.text: Dál Riata was a Gaelic kingdom spanning the sea between northeast Ireland and western Scotland. Its people, the Scots, gave Scotland its name, and the monks of Iona were part of its world. Vikings and Picts weakened it by the 9th century.

Earldom of Desmond.text: A lordship in southwest Ireland, with the title Earl of Desmond granted in 1329 to Maurice FitzGerald. The Geraldines, a Norman family who became deeply Irish, ruled Munster as semi-independent lords from here for centuries.

Earldom of Ulster.text: An Anglo-Norman earldom in northeast Ireland, whose first earl, John de Courcy, was made earl in 1181. In 1333 its third earl, William de Burgh, was murdered at age 20, setting off a civil war and leaving the lordship to pass through the female line.

Early Bahmani Sultanate.text: The first years of the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan of India, founded in 1347 by rebel Tughluq officers at Daulatabad under Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah. Its capital was Gulbarga from 1347 to 1425.

Early Balinese Kingdoms.text: A series of Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms on the island of Bali, Indonesia, before Majapahit troops landed in 1342 and conquered it. Their court culture blended local spirit and ancestor worship with Hindu ideas that came from India by way of Java.

Early Cheras.text: One of the three great Tamil kingdoms of Sangam-age South India, alongside the Cholas and Pandyas, ruling parts of today's Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It grew rich selling pepper to Roman merchants through ports such as Muziris.

Early Lý Dynasty.text: The Early Lý dynasty was a short-lived Vietnamese state founded by Lý Bí in 544 CE after rebelling against Chinese rule. He named it Vạn Xuân, meaning myriad springs, and the Chinese Liang and Sui reconquered it by 602.

Early Pandyas.text: One of the three great Tamil kingdoms of Sangam-age South India, in the far south of today's Tamil Nadu. Known for its pearls and for patronizing Tamil poets, it traded with Egypt and Rome. Its capital moved from Korkai to Madurai.

Early Vijayanagara (Sangama brothers).text: The first years of Vijayanagara in Karnataka, India, when the Sangama brothers Harihara and Bukka took over the former Kampili kingdom around Hampi. The 1336 founding date is traditional.

East Timor.text: A country covering the eastern part of Timor island. A Portuguese colony, it was occupied by Indonesia from 1975. After a 1999 referendum it became fully independent in May 2002.

East Turkestan.text: A historical name for the Tarim Basin and nearby oases in today's Xinjiang, western China. In the 1460s it was divided among local Muslim rulers and Mongol-descended khans, living off Silk Road trade.

East Turkestan Republic.text: A short-lived state in Xinjiang in northwest China, proclaimed in November 1944 by Uyghur and other rebels with Soviet backing. Based in Ghulja, it dissolved into a coalition provincial government in 1946, and its army was folded into China's communist army in 1949.

Eastern Chalukya kingdom of Vengi.text: A South Indian dynasty ruling the Krishna-Godavari delta in Andhra Pradesh from 624. It began as a viceroyalty of the Badami Chalukyas under Kubja Vishnuvardhana I and became independent, probably after 642; Rashtrakuta armies overran it more than once.

Eastern Ganga Kingdom.text: A Hindu dynasty ruling Kalinga, today's Odisha and nearby coast of eastern India. They are best known for building the huge Jagannath temple at Puri and the Sun Temple at Konark.

Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga.text: The early Eastern Ganga kingdom of southern Kalinga, in coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, c. 498-655 CE. Its first kings, such as Indravarman I, ruled from Dantapura and later Kalinganagara. The imperial phase over all of Odisha began in 1077.

Eastern Hungarian Kingdom.text: A modern label for the part of Hungary held by John Zápolya and then his son John Sigismund, who contested the throne with the Habsburgs between 1526 and 1570. Backed by the Ottomans, it developed into the Principality of Transylvania.

Eastern Moghulistan.text: The eastern branch of the Moghul khans, Muslim descendants of Chagatai who, after their khanate split, held the oasis towns of today's Xinjiang, China, ruling from Turpan and from Yarkand or Kashgar. Torn by rivalries between princes and religious factions, their lands fell to the Dzungars in the late 1600s.

Eastern Wei.text: Eastern Wei was one of two successors of Northern Wei, in northeast China, from 534 CE. The general Gao Huan held the real power behind a puppet emperor, and his son took the throne in 550, founding Northern Qi.

Ebla.text: A Bronze Age kingdom in north-western Syria, c. 2400-2300 BCE, near modern Aleppo. Its palace archive of some 20,000 clay tablets shows a rich trading state, destroyed around 2300 BCE; the Akkadian kings Sargon or Naram-Sin are one suspected culprit, though scholars disagree.

Edom.text: An Iron Age kingdom south of the Dead Sea, in today's southern Jordan and Israel, c. 850-553 BCE. It broke away from Judah, paid tribute to Assyria, and fell to Nabonidus of Babylon around 552 BCE.

Elam.text: An ancient civilization in southwestern Iran, around the lowlands of Khuzestan and the highlands of Anshan, with its own language and scripts. Its cities, above all Susa, rivalled Mesopotamia for centuries until Assyria's Ashurbanipal sacked Susa in 646 BCE; a weakened Elam was later absorbed by the Persians.

Eldiguzids (Atabegs of Azerbaijan).text: Atabegs (regents) of Azerbaijan founded by Shams al-Din Eldiguz, who controlled the Seljuk sultans of Iraq. After 1194 they held Azerbaijan and Arran until the Khwarazmshah Jalal al-Din took Tabriz in 1225.

Electoral Palatinate.text: The Rhenish Palatinate of the Wittelsbachs, ruled from Heidelberg and one of the seven electorates after the Golden Bull of 1356. The Upper Palatinate was added in 1329 and lost to Bavaria after Frederick V's defeat in Bohemia.

Electorate of Baden.text: A short-lived state of the Holy Roman Empire that arose in 1803 when Margrave Charles Frederick was made an elector. It lasted only until 1806, when the Empire ended and Baden became a grand duchy.

Electorate of Hanover.text: A state of the Holy Roman Empire in northwest Germany, officially Brunswick-Lüneburg, with its capital at Hanover. Its elector became King George I of Britain in 1714, linking the two realms.

Electorate of Hesse.text: The German state of Hesse-Kassel, which became an electorate in 1803 when its ruler was raised to elector rank. Its capital was Kassel, and Prussia annexed it after winning the war of 1866.

Electorate of Mainz.text: The lands of the archbishops of Mainz, who were arch-chancellors of the Empire and senior electors. They covered the Rhine and Main areas around Mainz and Aschaffenburg and the Eichsfeld and Erfurt in Thuringia, until France took the left bank of the Rhine.

Electorate of Salzburg.text: A state of the Holy Roman Empire created in 1803 from the lands of the former prince-archbishopric of Salzburg. It lasted only until 1805, when it passed to Austria.

Electorate of Saxony.text: A German state of the Holy Roman Empire, raised to an electorate in 1356 so its ruler could help choose the emperor. Its rulers protected Martin Luther in the 1500s, and its capital eventually moved from Wittenberg to Dresden.

Electorate of Trier.text: A church state on the Moselle in western Germany, ruled by the archbishop of Trier, who was also one of the seven electors choosing the Holy Roman emperor. It dated from about 900 and was ended by French conquest and secularisation in the early 1800s.

Electorate of Württemberg.text: The Duchy of Württemberg raised to the rank of elector in 1803, in the reorganisation of the Holy Roman Empire. On 1 January 1806 its ruler took the title of king, so the electorate lasted barely three years.

Elmet.text: A Brittonic kingdom in West Yorkshire, England, c. 500-617 CE, one of the last British kingdoms in the east. Edwin of Northumbria drove out its king Ceretic around 617. Its extent is known mostly from place-names.

Elymais.text: A kingdom in the foothills of south-western Iran, c. 147 BCE-221 CE, in Khuzestan. It was often a vassal of Parthia but kept its own kings, such as Kamnaskires, and at times held Susa; Ardashir I conquered it.

Emirate of Bari.text: A short-lived Muslim emirate in Apulia in southern Italy, c. 847-871, founded when Khalfun seized Bari. Mufarrag ibn Sallam won recognition from the Abbasid caliph, and the Carolingian emperor Louis II ended it in 871.

Emirate of Brakna.text: A Moorish emirate of the Awlad Abdullah in south-western Mauritania, independent of other Beni Hassan from 1674, on the middle Senegal river east of Trarza. It was nomadic and became a French protectorate in 1903.

Emirate of Crete.text: A Muslim state on the island of Crete, c. 824 to 961, founded by Andalusi exiles who had earlier held Alexandria for a time. Its corsair fleets raided the Byzantine shores of the Aegean until Nikephoros Phokas took the island back for Byzantium.

Emirate of Granada.text: Western Europe's last independent Muslim state, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty over southern Spain. Its Alhambra palace still stands, and the emirate fell to Castile and Aragon in 1492.

Emirate of Jabal Shammar.text: A state in northern Arabia ruled by the Rashidi family from Ha'il. At its height it controlled much of the Najd and reached toward Iraq and Jordan. It lost its long rivalry with the Saudis and fell to Ibn Saud in 1921.

Emirate of Multan.text: A Muslim emirate in southern Punjab, in present-day Pakistan, c. 855-1000, ruled from Multan. The Banu Munabbih emirs ruled first, then Isma'ili rulers, who took power in the 10th century; Mahmud of Ghazni conquered it in 1010.

Emirate of Nekor.text: A small Muslim emirate in the Rif of northern Morocco, founded c. 710 by Salih ibn Mansur and ruled by his Banu Salih family. Around 1015 it passed to the Azdaja tribe, and the Almoravids destroyed its last stronghold in 1080-81.

Emirate of Sicily.text: The Muslim-ruled emirate of Sicily, with Palermo as its capital, which flourished from the 9th to the 11th century. Arabs conquered the island from Byzantium starting in 827, and the Normans completed its conquest in 1091.

Emirate of Tbilisi.text: An Arab emirate centred on Tbilisi in Georgia, drawn here c. 830-1122. It declared independence from the caliph under Ishaq ibn Isma'il in the 830s, was ruled partly by a city council in the later 11th century, and fell to King David IV of Georgia in 1122.

Emirate of Trarza.text: A Moorish Hassaniya emirate in south-western Mauritania, north of the lower Senegal river, with no fixed capital. It controlled the gum trade with Saint-Louis and came under French protection after treaties in 1902.

Empire of Great Fulo (Denianke kingdom).text: A Fula kingdom in the middle Senegal valley, in Senegal and Mauritania, won in 1513 by Koli Tenguella after Songhai destroyed his father's state. Ruled by the Denianke dynasty, it dominated the region until the 1770s, when Muslim clerics overthrew it.

Empire of Thessalonica.text: A short-lived Greek state centred on Thessalonica, 1224-1246, founded by Theodore Komnenos Doukas of the Epirote dynasty, who claimed the title of emperor. After his defeat by Bulgaria in 1230 it shrank, its rulers gave up the imperial title in 1242, and Nicaea annexed the city in 1246.

Empire of Trebizond.text: One of three Byzantine successor states formed after the Fourth Crusade, in northeastern Anatolia on the Black Sea. It was founded in 1204 by Alexios and David Komnenos and fell to the Ottomans in 1461.

Equatorial Guinea.text: A small country in central Africa, made of a mainland region and islands including Bioko, independent from Spain in 1968. It is the only Spanish-speaking nation in Africa, and oil has brought it wealth since the 1990s.
Equatorial Guinea.capital: Malabo; later Ciudad de la Paz

Eretnids.text: A Turkish sultanate in central Anatolia (now Turkey) founded by Eretna, a viceroy who took the title of sultan in 1341 and secured his rule at the Battle of Karanbük in 1343. After his death in 1352 the east fell away, and Kadi Burhan al-Din took over in 1381.

Erivan Khanate.text: A khanate based at Erivan (Yerevan) in present-day Armenia, self-governing after Nader Shah's death in 1747 under nominal Iranian rule. Russia took it in 1827, and Yerevan is now Armenia's capital.

Eshrefids.text: A Turkish principality in southwestern Anatolia, centred on Beyşehir and its lake, in the late 1200s and early 1300s. It was one of several small states that appeared as the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum faded, and it ended around 1326.

Este state: Ferrara, Modena and Reggio.text: The lands of the House of Este in northern Italy: Ferrara, a papal fief, plus Modena and Reggio. Ferrara was a duchy from 1471, and the Este lost it to the pope in 1597 but kept Modena.

Estonia.text: A Baltic country that declared independence in 1918 after the Russian Empire fell. The Soviet Union took it over in 1940, and Estonia became free again in 1991. Its capital is Tallinn.

Eswatini.text: A small kingdom in southern Africa, independent from Britain in 1968 as Swaziland. It is the last absolute monarchy in Africa, and in 2018 King Mswati III renamed it Eswatini.

Ethiopia.text: A country in the Horn of Africa, heir to the ancient kingdom of Aksum, and with Liberia the only African land never fully colonised. Italy occupied it from 1936 to 1941. Emperor Haile Selassie ruled until 1974, and today it is a federal republic with Addis Ababa as capital.

Etruscans.text: The Etruscans built a civilization of self-governing city-states in Etruria, roughly today's Tuscany, western Umbria and northern Lazio, whose rich families filled great tombs with imported luxuries. From the late 300s BCE the expanding Roman Republic conquered their cities one by one.

Federal League.text: A loose alliance of provinces in the Río de la Plata region, covering parts of today's Uruguay, Argentina and Brazil. Led by José Gervasio Artigas, it wanted a confederation of equal provinces and declared independence from Spain in 1815. It broke up by 1820.

Federal Republic of Nigeria.text: The most populous country in Africa, independent from Britain in 1960 and a republic from 1963. A civil war over the breakaway region of Biafra raged from 1967 to 1970. The capital moved from Lagos to Abuja in 1991.

Federal Republic of Somalia.text: A country on the Horn of Africa, formed in 1960 when former British Somaliland joined the Italian-run territory to the south. The government collapsed in 1991 and civil war followed; Somalia is now a federal republic still rebuilding its state.

Federation of Malaya.text: A country on the Malay Peninsula, made of nine Malay sultanates plus Penang and Malacca. It began as a British-run federation in 1948, became fully independent on 31 August 1957, and in 1963 joined Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia.

Fihrids.text: The Arab family of the Fihr clan that ran Ifriqiya (Tunisia) and Muslim Spain in the mid 700s. Yusuf al-Fihri governed al-Andalus until 756, when the Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman I defeated him and founded the emirate of Córdoba.

First Hellenic Republic.text: The provisional Greek government during the war of independence against the Ottoman Empire, lasting from 1822 to 1832. The name is a later label, used by scholars to stress the regime's constitutional and democratic character. The Kingdom of Greece succeeded it.

First Islamic state (Medina).text: The first Islamic state, founded by Muhammad at Medina in Arabia in 622 and lasting to his death in 632. It began with the Medina oasis under the Constitution of Medina, then grew after the conquest of Mecca in 630 to hold the Hejaz and western Najd, with looser allegiance from the rest of Arabia.

First Sealand Dynasty.text: A line of kings in the marshy far south of Mesopotamia, near the Persian Gulf, that broke away from the Old Babylonian kingdom. Known mostly from brief king-list entries, it lasted until a Kassite army from Babylon conquered the Sealand, very roughly around 1475 BCE.

Former Jin.text: A state in Shanxi, northern China, ruled by Shatuo Turks, in the years of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. In 923 its ruler Li Cunxu declared the Later Tang dynasty and conquered the Later Liang.

Former Liang.text: Former Liang was a Sixteen Kingdoms state in the Gansu corridor of northwest China, built up from 301 CE by the Han Chinese Zhang family, governors who never fully declared independence. For years they kept a Western Jin era name, ruling from Guzang until Former Qin conquered them in 376.

Former Yan.text: Former Yan was a state of the Xianbei Murong clan in northeast China, founded in 337 CE. At its height it ruled the North China Plain, but Former Qin conquered it in 370.

Former Zhao.text: Former Zhao was founded in 304 CE by Liu Yuan, a Xiongnu noble who claimed descent from Han royalty. Its armies sacked the Western Jin capitals, Luoyang and Chang'an. It lasted until 329, when rival Later Zhao destroyed it.

Formosan peoples.text: The Austronesian indigenous peoples of Taiwan, who lived there for thousands of years and traded across Southeast Asia long before outsiders arrived. Dutch and Han Chinese settlement from the 1600s reshaped their lands, and the plains peoples were largely assimilated by the early 1900s.

Fortriu (northern Picts).text: The leading Pictish kingdom of northern Scotland, c. 430-684 CE, now thought to lie around the Moray Firth. After Bridei son of Beli beat Northumbria at Dun Nechtain in 685, its kings ruled all the Picts.

Free City of Bremen.text: A self-governing port city on the Weser in northern Germany, recognised as a Free Imperial City in 1646 and long at the heart of the Hanseatic League. Napoleon annexed it to France in 1811, but after 1813 it regained its freedom alongside Hamburg and Lübeck.

Free City of Danzig.text: The Baltic port of Danzig, now Gdańsk in Poland. Napoleon made it a free city from 1807 to 1814, and after 1920 it was a semi-autonomous city-state under the League of Nations until Germany invaded Poland in 1939.

Free City of Frankfurt.text: A small independent city-state on the Main in Germany, once the place where Holy Roman emperors were elected. It was the seat of the German Confederation's assembly until Prussia annexed it in 1866 after the Austro-Prussian War.

Free City of Hamburg.text: Hamburg, a great trading port on the Elbe in northern Germany, was a fully sovereign city-state with its own government and Hanseatic traditions. It joined the North German Confederation in 1866 and became a self-governing state of the German Empire in 1871.

Free City of Krakow.text: A tiny city-state around Kraków, set up by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and nominally independent but overseen by Russia, Prussia and Austria. It became a hub of Polish patriots until Austria annexed it in 1846 after a failed uprising.

Free City of Lübeck.text: A German Hanseatic city-state on the Baltic coast, free from 1226 until it lost its status in 1937. It had been the leading city of the Hanseatic League.

Free County of Burgundy.text: A county in eastern France, later called Franche-Comté, that belonged to the Holy Roman Empire. Counts ruled it from 982, and from 1330 to 1361 it shared a ruler with the neighbouring Duchy of Burgundy. France finally annexed it in 1678.

Free Imperial City of Nuremberg.text: A self-governing city of the Holy Roman Empire in Franconia, Germany, answerable only to the emperor. Rich from trade and crafts, it won the biggest territory of any imperial city after the Landshut war of 1504-05, and kept its freedom until 1806.

Free Territory of Trieste.text: A small state on the Adriatic between Italy and Yugoslavia, created by the 1947 peace treaty with Italy. Its UN governor was never appointed; Zone A with Trieste was run by British and American forces and Zone B by Yugoslavia. A 1954 agreement divided it between them.

French zone.text: The French occupation zone of Germany, shown 1945-46, one of four zones set up after the May 1945 surrender, under the Allied Control Council in Berlin. In 1947 the Saar was detached from it as a protectorate.

Frisia.text: The coastal Frisian lands of the North Sea in the present-day Netherlands and Germany. The map shows them for a few years in the 780s, when Charlemagne's Franks were taking over the region and ending Frisian independence.

Frisia Kingdom.text: This map entry shows Frisian lands in the Low Countries and northern Germany, c. 612 to 717. The Frisians were traders who sailed the North Sea coast, and their kingdom was later cut down by the Franks under Charles Martel.

Frisians.text: The Frisians were a seafaring people of the North Sea coast in the present-day Netherlands and Germany. They were famed traders, and by the end of the 700s the Franks under Charlemagne had brought their lands under Frankish rule.

Funan.text: Funan was an early network of Indian-influenced states around the Mekong delta, in today's Cambodia and southern Vietnam, from about the 1st to the 7th century. Roman, Chinese and Indian goods dug up at its port of Oc Eo show it was a rich trading power, and Indian religion and writing spread through it.

Funj Sultanate.text: An Islamic kingdom on the Blue Nile in what is now Sudan, founded in 1504 by Amara Dunqas, who built its capital at Sennar. It followed the old Christian Nubian kingdoms, was at its height in the late 1600s, and its last sultan surrendered to Turco-Egyptian invaders in 1821.

Gabon.text: A small, forested country on the equator on Africa's Atlantic coast, independent from France in 1960. Oil wealth made it one of the richer states in the region, and it was ruled by the Bongo family for over half a century.

Gahadavala Dynasty.text: A Rajput dynasty ruling parts of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in northern India c. 1089-1197, with a capital at Banaras (Varanasi) and for a time Kannauj. Their kingdom ended with the advance of the Ghurid armies.

Gajapati Empire.text: An Odisha-based empire founded when Kapilendra Deva took power after the last Ganga king died in 1434. It held Odisha and northern Kalinga, ruled from Cuttack.

Gajapati Empire (peak).text: The Gajapati Empire at its widest, when its armies carried down the Coromandel coast to the Kaveri in the 15th century. Much of this southern conquest was later lost to Vijayanagara and Golconda.

Galatia.text: A region of central Anatolia, around modern Ankara, named after Celtic Gauls who crossed from the Balkans in the 270s BCE as hired soldiers and then raided Greek cities. It later became a kingdom, and Augustus made it a Roman province in 25 BCE.

Galicia-Volhynia.text: A medieval East Slavic state in what is now Ukraine and nearby countries, formed in 1199 by joining two principalities. Its ruler Daniel was crowned king in 1253 with the pope's blessing. It broke up in the mid-1300s, split among Poland and Lithuania.

Gallic Empire.text: The Gallic Empire was a breakaway part of the Roman Empire, covering Gaul, Britain and for a time Spain, from 260 to 274 CE. It began when Postumus rebelled during Rome's crisis, and Emperor Aurelian reconquered it.

Galuh Kingdom.text: Galuh was a Sundanese kingdom in the east of West Java and the Banyumas area, formed around 669 to 670 when the old lands of Tarumanagara were split with Sunda along the Citarum River. Known mostly from later chronicles and folk tales, this Hindu kingdom was later joined with Sunda.

Ganja Khanate.text: A khanate around the city of Ganja in present-day Azerbaijan, self-governing under nominal Iranian suzerainty after Nader Shah died in 1747. Russia took Ganja by force in 1804, ending the khanate.

Ganzhou Kingdom.text: A Uyghur kingdom in the Hexi Corridor of northwest China, around the city of Ganzhou (modern Zhangye), founded c. 894 (some sources say 848) and lasting to 1036. It sat on a key route linking China with Central Asia until the Tanguts of Western Xia conquered it.

Gao Empire (Kingdom of Gao).text: A Songhai kingdom on the Niger bend in Mali, c. 800-1299, known to Arab geographers from the 9th century and from funerary inscriptions from 1042 that name kings and queens. It lost its independence to Mali in the late 13th century; the exact date and extent are uncertain.

Gao Kaidao.text: Gao Kaidao was a rebel warlord who rose against the failing Sui dynasty in northeast China, holding the area around Yuyang, near today's Beijing. He later submitted to the Tang. In 624 his own general turned on him, and he hanged himself.

Garha kingdom (Garha-Mandla).text: The Gond kingdom of Garha in central India, which under Rani Durgavati held the upper Narmada valley around Jabalpur and Mandla. She died fighting Akbar's general Asaf Khan in 1564.

Garha-Mandla (Gond kingdom).text: A Gond kingdom in central India, which after 1564 kept a smaller territory around Mandla as a tributary of the Mughals and later the Marathas. The Marathas of Saugor annexed it in 1781.

Garhwal Kingdom.text: The kingdom of the Panwar kings in the upper Ganges and Yamuna hills of Uttarakhand, India, with Dehradun. Nepal conquered it in 1803-04, and Pradyumna Shah died at Khurbura in 1804.

Gauda Kingdom.text: Gauda was a kingdom in Bengal, known from the 4th century CE or earlier, that reached its height under King Shashanka, who ruled roughly 593 to 636 from Karnasuvarna and united much of Bengal. Soon after his death it was divided between Harsha and Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa.

Gaza Empire.text: A state founded by Soshangane in southern Mozambique after the Mfecane, 1824-95. At its height in the 1860s it dominated southern Mozambique and south-eastern Zimbabwe between the Limpopo and the Zambezi; its last ruler was Gungunhana.

Geledi Sultanate.text: A Somali sultanate of the Gobroon dynasty on the lower Shabelle river, from the late 17th century, which dominated the Benadir hinterland in the 19th century. Italy made treaties from 1889, and it was incorporated into Italian Somaliland in 1911.

Georgia.text: Georgia is a country in the South Caucasus with its capital at Tbilisi, rooted in the ancient kingdoms of Colchis and Iberia. It became a medieval power under David the Builder and Queen Tamar, was ruled by Russia, and regained independence in 1991.

Germiyanids.text: A Turkish dynasty ruling western Anatolia from about 1300 to 1429, with its capital at Kütahya. It was among the larger beyliks, and the Ottomans gained much of its land through marriage and inheritance before taking the rest.

Ghana.text: A West African country that was the first in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from Britain, in 1957, under Kwame Nkrumah. It was called the Gold Coast before that. Its capital is Accra.

Ghassanids.text: The Ghassanids were an Arab Christian kingdom that served as Byzantium's desert allies in Syria and Jordan, guarding the frontier against Persia's Lakhmids. They lasted until the Muslim conquest around 636 CE.

Giudicato of Arborea.text: One of the four independent judicates, or kingdoms, of medieval Sardinia, and the one that lasted longest. Its best-known ruler, Eleonora, issued the Carta de Logu law code, and it fell to Aragon in 1420.

Giudicato of Cagliari.text: A medieval judicate in southern Sardinia, one of four that split the island, lasting from c. 1020 to 1258. Its capital Santa Igia was besieged by Pisa and allied judicates in 1258, and the territory was then divided.

Giudicato of Gallura.text: A medieval judicate in northeastern Sardinia, one of four that split the island, ruled from Civita (modern Olbia). Pisa took control after the Visconti judge Nino was deposed in 1287.

Giudicato of Logudoro.text: A medieval judicate in northwest Sardinia, also called Torres, one of four independent kingdoms of the island. Its seat moved from Porto Torres to Ardara and then Sassari, and it ended in 1259 when Queen Adelasia died without an heir.
Giudicato of Logudoro.capital: Porto Torres; later Ardara and Sassari

Gobir.text: A Hausa kingdom of the north-west, in the Sahel of today's Niger in this period. Usman dan Fodio's jihad began in Gobir in 1804, and its capital Alkalawa fell in 1808.

Goguryeo.text: One of Korea's Three Kingdoms, Goguryeo rose from the far north around 37 BCE and at its peak held much of Manchuria and the northern peninsula. It beat back Sui invasions, then fell in 668 CE to a Silla and Tang alliance.

Gojoseon.text: Old Joseon, the first kingdom of the Korean peninsula, covering northern Korea and part of Manchuria. Korean legend says it was founded by Dangun, and it fell to the Han empire of China in 108 BCE.

Golconda Sultanate.text: A Deccan sultanate in southeastern India, in today's Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, founded in 1518 by Quli Qutb Shah. It was rich from diamonds, patronised Persian culture, and ended in 1687 when the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb captured its last sultan.

Gonja.text: A kingdom of the Mande Ngbanya people in northern Ghana between the Black and White Volta rivers, ruled by a paramount chief, the Yagbongwura, by 1675. Asante conquered it in 1751-52.

Gorkha Kingdom.text: A hill kingdom in central Nepal founded in 1559 by Dravya Shah, one of the old twenty-four Chaubisi states. Under Prithvi Narayan Shah it began conquering its neighbours from 1743 and took the Kathmandu Valley in 1768, laying the base of modern Nepal.

Gothia.text: The name Gothia fits several Gothic lands; this map entry shows the region north of the Black Sea held by the Goths in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. Their power there broke when the Huns swept in from the east around 375.

Goths.text: The Goths were a Germanic people. The Gutones, probably early Goths, lived by the lower Vistula in what is now Poland in the 1st century CE; by the 3rd century Goths had moved south toward the Black Sea and lower Danube, from where they raided Rome. Later Gothic kingdoms rose in Italy and Spain.

Grand Duchy of Baden.text: A state east of the upper Rhine in southwest Germany, raised to a grand duchy in 1806 with Napoleon's help. It joined the German Empire in 1871, and its monarchy ended in 1918.

Grand Duchy of Berg.text: A French client state on the lower Rhine created by Napoleon in 1806 after Austerlitz, and first ruled by Joachim Murat. It lasted until 1813.

Grand Duchy of Hesse.text: A west German state formed in 1806 from the Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt, with Darmstadt as its capital. It became a grand duchy under Napoleon's reorganisation of Germany and lasted until 1918.

Grand Duchy of Kraków.text: The Duchy of Kraków in Lesser Poland, the most prized of the provincial duchies of a divided Piast Poland. Leszek II the Black ruled it from 1279, rival dukes fought over it after his death in 1288, and Wenceslaus II of Bohemia took it in 1291. The Grand Duchy title of this name came much later, in 1846.

Grand Duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach.text: A small Thuringian state formed in 1809 by uniting Weimar and Eisenach, and made a grand duchy in 1815. Goethe and Schiller worked at its court in Weimar. It lasted until 1918.

Grand Duchy of Tuscany.text: An Italian state in the centre of the peninsula with its capital at Florence, ruled by the Medici and later the Habsburg-Lorraine family. It was interrupted by Napoleonic rule, and it joined Italy in 1860.

Grand Duchy of Würzburg.text: A German grand duchy in the Napoleonic era, centred on Würzburg, created in 1806 for Ferdinand, the former Grand Duke of Tuscany. It joined the Confederation of the Rhine and was given to Bavaria in 1814.

Grand Principality of Serbia.text: A medieval Serbian state, also called Rascia (Raška), that emerged in the later 11th century and grew in the 12th. Its capital was Stari Ras, and in 1217 it became the Kingdom of Serbia.

Great Moravia.text: A Slavic state in central Europe in the 9th century, centred on Moravia, now the eastern part of the Czech Republic, and neighbouring western Slovakia. The missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrived in 863 and gave the Slavs a written language, and the Hungarians overran the state around 907.

Great Principality of Duklja.text: A medieval South Slavic state in what is now southern Montenegro, here drawn at its high point in the 1050s-1070s under Prince Mihailo Vojislavljević. It started as a Byzantine vassal, then won independence and a royal crown from the pope.

Great Yuan.text: Dayuan, Chinese for Great Yuan, was a state of the Ferghana Valley in Central Asia, famed for its tall heavenly horses. Han China sent armies against it in 104-101 BCE to obtain them, after which it accepted Han overlordship.

Greek Dark Ages.text: The centuries after the Mycenaean palaces fell, c. 1180-800 BCE, when Greece had fewer, smaller and poorer settlements and no writing. Out of this age grew new ways of organising society, and by about 800 BCE Greeks had adopted the alphabet from the Phoenicians.

Greek junta.text: The military dictatorship that ruled Greece from the colonels' coup of April 1967 until 1974. It banned political parties and jailed opponents, and collapsed after its failed attempt to take over Cyprus led to the Turkish invasion.

Greenland.text: The Danish colony of Greenland, settled from 1721 and now self-governing within the Danish realm. It is the largest island in the world, and its capital is Nuuk.

Grenada.text: A small island nation in the southeastern Caribbean, called the Island of Spice for its nutmeg and mace. It became independent from Britain in February 1974. In 1983 a coup was followed by a US-led invasion.

Guatemala.text: A country in Central America whose land was the core of the ancient Maya civilization. It broke from Spain and Mexico in 1821, joined the Central American federation, and declared itself separate from it in 1839. Its capital is Guatemala City.

Guayaquil Junta.text: The Free Province of Guayaquil, created when the port city declared independence from Spain on 9 October 1820. It then sought help from Gran Colombia to free the highlands around Quito and joined it in 1822. The dates drawn on this map, 1812 to 1813, do not match.

Guge kingdom.text: A western Tibetan kingdom on the upper Sutlej, c. 1000-1550, sometimes holding Spiti, Kinnaur and Zanskar. Its ruins at Tsaparang survive. Its line was interrupted in the 12th-14th centuries when Khasa Malla kings held sway.

Guinea.text: A West African country on the Atlantic coast. In 1958 it was the only French territory to reject the new French constitution and choose immediate independence, with Ahmed Sékou Touré as president. He ruled it until his death in 1984.

Gujarat Sultanate.text: The sultanate of Gujarat in western India, ruled from Ahmedabad. In its last years the sultans ruled under regent nobles until Akbar's conquest of 1572-73.

Gujarat Sultanate (with Malwa).text: The Gujarat Sultanate at its widest, when Sultan Bahadur Shah annexed Malwa in 1531 and sacked Chittor in 1535. Humayun's Mughal army then overran Gujarat, though Bahadur soon regained it; the Portuguese had been given Bassein in 1534.

Gujarat states: Dharampur and Bansda.text: A grouping of two small Gujarat princely states, Dharampur and Bansda, under the Bombay government in the south of Gujarat. Both acceded to India in 1947.

Gujarat states: Palanpur, Radhanpur, Ida.text: A grouping of Gujarat princely states under the Bombay government: Palanpur, Radhanpur, Idar, Rajpipla, Lunavada and Chhota Udaipur, in the Palanpur, Mahi Kantha and Rewa Kantha agencies. All acceded to India in 1947.

Gujarat states: tract near Cambay.text: A small princely tract near Cambay in Gujarat, one of the Gujarat states under the Bombay government. These states acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty.text: A medieval dynasty of northern India, c. 730 to 1036. After winning the long Tripartite Struggle it held Kannauj, and it reached the height of its power under Mihira Bhoja. It also helped block Arab armies pushing east of the Indus.

Gutian Dynasty.text: A line of kings from the Gutian people who ruled much of Mesopotamia after the Akkadian empire collapsed, c. 2100 BCE. Later Sumerian writers cast them as barbarian destroyers, but they had settled in the region long before. Utu-hegal of Uruk drove them out.

Guyana.text: A country on the northeast coast of South America, independent from Britain in May 1966. It is the only English-speaking nation on the continent, and most of its people live on a thin strip of coast.

Gwalior.text: The Maratha princely state of the Scindias in central India. Its northern block held Gwalior, Bhind, Sheopur, Narwar and Isagarh, while its Malwa districts around Ujjain and Mandsaur lay among other states. It acceded to India in 1947.

Gwalior State (Scindia's Malwa districts.text: The Malwa districts of the Gwalior state, around Ujjain, Shajapur and Mandsaur, held by the Scindia dynasty in central India, 1846-57. They formed a southern block of the Maratha state, separate from its northern core.

Gwalior State (Scindia).text: The northern block of Gwalior, the Maratha state of the Scindias in central India, including Gwalior, Narwar, Guna and Bhind, 1846-57. A British campaign in 1843 brought British-officered troops into the state but cost it little land.

Hadhramaut.text: An ancient kingdom in southern Arabia, in the area of today's Yemen and Oman, known for producing frankincense. Its main city was Shabwa. It was repeatedly rival and ally of Saba, and finally fell to Himyar around 300 CE.

Hafsid Dynasty.text: A Sunni Berber dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya (Tunisia and neighbouring lands) from 1229. Founded by Abu Zakariya Yahya, a former Almohad governor, it ruled from Tunis until the Ottomans took over in 1574.

Haihayas of Ratanpur.text: A Haihaya dynasty of Ratanpur, with a Raipur branch from about the late 14th century, ruling the Chhattisgarh plains of India. The record is thin; Maratha suzerainty began in 1740 and the kingdom was annexed in 1758.

Halych-Volhynia occupation.text: The lands in western Ukraine that later formed the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia (1199-1349), one of the great Rus successor states. This entry shows the area in the 1000s-1230s, when it was split among several Rus principalities.

Hammadid Dynasty.text: A Berber dynasty in present-day Algeria, a branch of the Zirids, founded when Hammad ibn Buluggin broke away and took the title of emir in the early 11th century. Its first capital was Qal'at Bani Hammad, it later moved to Béjaïa, and the Almohads annexed it in 1152.

Han.text: One of the seven big Warring States of ancient China, around Henan and Shanxi, and the smallest and weakest of them. Its thinker Han Fei wrote on Legalism. Qin conquered it in 230 BCE, first of the six states to fall.

Hanthawaddy Kingdom.text: A Mon kingdom of lower Myanmar, founded in 1287 by King Wareru, with its capital moving between Mottama and Bago (Pegu). It became rich on sea trade and Buddhism, was conquered by Toungoo in 1539, and revived briefly before ending in 1552.

Haripuñjaya.text: Haripuñjaya was a Mon kingdom in northern Thailand, centred on Lamphun, said to be founded by Queen Chamadevi. It remained a Buddhist centre until King Mangrai of Lan Na conquered it in 1292.

Hasanwayhids.text: A Kurdish dynasty of western Iran, c. 959-1015, ruling Dinavar, Kermanshah, Hulwan and Shahrizur under the overlordship of the Buyids. The state collapsed by 1015, and the Annazids replaced it.

Hashemite Arab Federation.text: The map label points to Arab Iraq, the medieval name for lower Mesopotamia in today's Iraq. In 1415 to 1439 it was a region of cities and farms along the Tigris and Euphrates, mostly under the Qara Qoyunlu. The name is not that of the 1958 federation.

Haudenosaunee.text: A confederacy of Native American nations in what is now New York State and nearby areas, also called the Iroquois. Its name means those who build the longhouse. It began as five nations, and a sixth, the Tuscarora, joined in the 1720s.

Hazaraspids.text: Kurdish atabegs of Greater Lur in the Zagros mountains of Iran, ruling from Idaj (Izeh) from the mid-12th century. The Timurids ended the dynasty in 1424.

Helvetic Republic.text: A French-backed republic that replaced the old Swiss Confederation in 1798, with a more centralised government. It lasted until Napoleon restored a looser federation, the Act of Mediation, in 1803.

Henan.text: A short-lived kingdom in northwestern Henan, China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE after Qin fell. Its king was Shen Yang, a former Zhao official, and it lay around the old heartland of the Zhou kings.

Hill Tippera (Tripura).text: A kingdom east of Bengal in present-day Tripura, India, called Hill Tippera in British records, with its capital at Agartala. It acceded to India on 13 August 1947.

Himyarite Kingdom.text: A kingdom in the southern highlands of Yemen that conquered the other South Arabian states and by the end of the third century CE ruled most of South Arabia. Its kings later adopted Judaism, and Aksum, across the Red Sea in Ethiopia, conquered it in the 520s CE.

Hindu Shahi kingdom.text: A dynasty ruling Kabul, Gandhara and northern Punjab, c. 875-1000, first from Kabul and later from Udabhanda (Hund) on the Indus. Its kings lost Kabul to the Saffarids in 870, then lost lands west of the Indus in 1001 and fell in 1026.

Hokuzan.text: The northern of Okinawa's three kingdoms in the 1300s, with its castle at Nakijin. It was the largest of the three but the poorest and most thinly peopled, and the king of Chūzan conquered it in 1416, a step toward uniting the island.

Honduras.text: A Central American country with coasts on both the Caribbean and the Pacific, home to the great Maya ruins of Copán. It became independent from Spain in 1821 and a separate republic after the federation ended. Its capital is Tegucigalpa.

House of Anjou-Sicily.text: A branch of the French royal family founded by Charles I of Anjou, who took the Kingdom of Sicily in 1266. A revolt called the Sicilian Vespers in 1282 cost the family the island itself, but they kept southern Italy, ruling from Naples as the Kingdom of Naples.

House of Ascania.text: A German princely family, also called the House of Anhalt, whose ancestral seats lay in the Anhalt region of Saxony-Anhalt near the Harz. Albert the Bear made it great in the 12th century, and its branches ruled Brandenburg, Anhalt and Saxe-Wittenberg, whose dukes became electors in 1356.

House of Bourbon.text: A French noble house descended from Robert, a son of King Louis IX, who in 1272 married Beatrix, heir to the Bourbon lands; their son became Duke of Bourbon in 1327. A later member, Henry of Navarre, became Henry IV in 1589, the first Bourbon king of France, and was crowned in 1594.

House of Habsburg.text: A Swabian noble family named after Habsburg Castle in present-day Switzerland. Count Rudolph became King of the Romans in 1273 and, after defeating Ottokar II of Bohemia in 1278, made his sons dukes of Austria; the family later ruled the Holy Roman Empire and Spain.

House of Hohenstaufen.text: A German royal and imperial dynasty that rose from the Duchy of Swabia in 1079 and held the German throne 1138-1254. Its best-known rulers were Frederick I Barbarossa, Henry VI and Frederick II.

House of Khalifa.text: The ruling family of Bahrain, an Anizah Sunni family from Arabia who took Bahrain in 1783. Their rule continued under British protection until independence in 1971.

House of Luxembourg.text: A dynasty of the late Middle Ages. Between 1308 and 1437 its members were German kings and emperors, and also kings of Bohemia, with one of them, Sigismund, king of Hungary and Croatia.

House of Tocco.text: A noble family of Italian origin that held the county of Cephalonia and Zakynthos from 1357, then used it as a base to take mainland lands in Epirus. Their holdings fell piece by piece to the Ottomans, who took the last of their islands in 1479.

House of Valois-Anjou.text: A cadet branch of the French royal family that ruled Anjou and Provence. Its members, starting with Louis I of Anjou, repeatedly claimed the crown of Naples, though success was brief and costly.

House of Wittelsbach.text: A Bavarian dynasty that held Bavaria from 1180 and the Rhine Palatinate from 1214; in later centuries its branches also ruled Holland, Sweden, Hungary, Bohemia and Greece. Three of its members were elected kings or emperors of the Holy Roman Empire.

Hoysala Kingdom.text: A South Indian dynasty that ruled most of Karnataka and parts of Tamil Nadu from about the 11th to the 14th century. It is famed for its richly carved temples at Belur and Halebidu, which became its later capital.

Hubaekje.text: Later Baekje, one of Korea's Later Three Kingdoms, founded in 892 by Gyeon Hwon in the southwest. It rivalled Silla and Taebong, and was conquered by Goryeo in 936.

Huguenots.text: French Protestants of the Reformed faith, drawn here in the 1620s when they held fortified towns in southwestern France. Their revolts ended when the royal army took La Rochelle in 1628 and the 1629 Peace of Alais removed their military privileges.

Hungarian Nationalists.text: Hungarians who rose against Habsburg rule in the 1848 to 1849 revolution, which Austria and Russia crushed. In 1867 a compromise made Hungary an equal partner in the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, which lasted until 1918. Dates on this entry are uncertain.

Hungarian People's Republic.text: The communist state of Hungary from 1949 to 1989. In 1956 Hungarians rose up against it, and Soviet troops crushed the revolt. It was replaced by a democratic republic in 1989.

Hungarian Republic.text: Hungary in the years after the First World War, when the 1920 Treaty of Trianon stripped it of about 70 percent of its old territory. Formally still a kingdom, it was run by the regent Miklós Horthy and joined the Axis powers in the Second World War.

Hungary.text: A Central European country on the Danube. Communist-ruled after the Second World War, it saw the 1956 uprising crushed by Soviet troops. It became a democracy again in 1989, and joined the EU in 2004. Its capital is Budapest.

Hussain Shahi Dynasty.text: The Hussain Shahi family of Arab descent, who ruled the Sultanate of Bengal from 1494 until 1538. It is shown here in its last years, when Bengal was taken by Sher Shah Suri after the fall of the capital Gaur.

Hwicce.text: The Hwicce were a small Anglo-Saxon people living around Worcester, Gloucester and Bath, formed after the Battle of Dyrham in 577 CE. They fell under Mercian control and became a sub-kingdom before being absorbed.

Hyderabad.text: The Nizam's princely state in the Deccan, one of the two largest in India along with Jammu and Kashmir. The Nizam did not accede in 1947, and the Indian Army took control between 13 and 18 September 1948 in Operation Polo.

Hyderabad State.text: A large princely state in southern India ruled by the Nizams, descended from Asaf Jah I, who founded it in 1724. India took it over in 1948, and its land is now in Telangana, Karnataka and Maharashtra.

Hyderabad State (Berar assigned).text: Berar, the Hyderabad lands west of the Wardha river, shown 1854-57 after the Treaty of 1853. The East India Company administered it, but formal sovereignty remained with the Nizam of Hyderabad.

Hyderabad State (the Nizam's dominions).text: The Nizam of Hyderabad's dominions in the Deccan of south-central India, 1799-1803. The Nizam had joined a subsidiary alliance with the British in 1798, and in 1800 he ceded his share of the Mysore conquests, the Ceded Districts, to them.

Hyderabad State (with Berar).text: The Nizam of Hyderabad's state in the Deccan, 1804-53, enlarged by the Treaty of Deogaon in 1803, which gave it Berar. In 1853 Berar was handed to the East India Company to pay for the troops it kept for the Nizam.

Hyksos.text: Foreign rulers of Egyptian Dynasty XV, c. 1650-1550 BCE, from the Near East who took over the Nile Delta and Middle Egypt. Their name means rulers of foreign lands. They governed from Avaris until the Theban kings drove them out.

Hán.text: A short-lived kingdom in southwestern Henan, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms Xiang Yu created in 206 BCE. Its king was Han Cheng, from the old Han royal house, whom Xiang Yu soon had killed. It is not the Hàn kingdom of Liu Bang.

I-Kiribati chiefdoms.text: The Gilbert Islands, now part of Kiribati, were settled long ago by the Austronesian I-Kiribati, whose Micronesian culture later absorbed Polynesian and Melanesian influences from Samoan, Tongan and Fijian invaders. The islands kept their own rule until Britain declared a protectorate over them in 1892.

Iberian Union.text: The period from 1580 to 1640 when one Spanish Habsburg king, beginning with Philip II, also ruled Portugal. It joined the whole Iberian Peninsula and both empires in one monarchy, and ended when Portugal rose in revolt and crowned John IV of Braganza.

Icelandic Commonwealth.text: An island republic with no king, c. 930 to 1262. Settlers from Norway set up the Althing, an open-air assembly, and it kept law until Icelanders accepted the Norwegian king in 1262.

Idalion.text: A city-kingdom in the middle of Cyprus, c. 600-451 BCE, ruled by its own kings such as Stasicyprus while paying tribute to Assyria and Persia. It is known for its bilingual inscription, found in 1869.

Idrisids.text: The first Muslim dynasty of Morocco, c. 788 to 974. Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet's family, fled the Abbasids and founded it, and his son Idris II made the new city of Fez its capital.

Ifat Sultanate.text: A Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa, based in the east of today's Ethiopia and stretching to the port of Zeila, in the late 1200s to early 1400s. It was led by the Walashma dynasty and spent much of its life in conflict with the Christian Ethiopian kings.

Ikhshidid dynasty.text: A dynasty of Turkic governors of Egypt, 935-969, who ruled almost independently of the Abbasid caliphs. Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid held Egypt and Palestine, later southern Syria with Damascus; the Fatimids took Fustat in 969.

Ikshvaku kingdom of Vijayapuri.text: The Andhra Ikshvaku kingdom of the eastern Krishna valley in India, c. 210-305 CE, which rose after the Satavahanas fell. Its capital Vijayapuri at Nagarjunakonda is known for its many Buddhist monuments; its royal dates are approximate.

Illyrian Kingdom.text: A kingdom of Illyrian tribes on the east side of the Adriatic, in today's Albania and Montenegro, which grew rich partly on piracy. Under King Agron and then Queen Teuta it became a strong land and sea power, and Teuta's wars with Rome ended with her submission around 227 BCE.

Imamate of Futa Jallon.text: A Fula Muslim theocracy in the highlands of Guinea, created by a jihad in 1725. Two lines of leaders called Almamys took turns governing from Timbo, with provinces under their own chiefs. France conquered it in 1896.

Imamate of Futa Toro.text: A Muslim state on the middle Senegal River in present-day Senegal and Mauritania, 1776-1859. Torodbe clerics overthrew the Denianke rulers and chose Abdul Kader Kan as the first almamy, or imam-ruler; France annexed it in 1859.

Imamate of Oman.text: A state in the interior of Oman, ruled by an elected Ibadi imam from Nizwa and separated from the sultan's coast by the Hajar Mountains. A 1920 treaty, signed at Seeb, left it self-governing until the sultan, backed by British forces, defeated it in the Jebel Akhdar War, which ended in 1959.

Imamate of Yemen.text: A state led by Zaydi imams, religious leaders of a branch of Shia Islam, in the highlands of Yemen. Imams claimed both spiritual and political rule, and their line lasted in some form from 897 until a republican revolution in 1962.

Independent State of Croatia.text: A puppet state in the Second World War, set up in 1941 under the Ustaše leader Ante Pavelić, backed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. It carried out terrible persecutions and ended in 1945.

Indo-Greeks.text: Greek-ruled kingdoms in the northwest of South Asia, in today's Pakistan, Afghanistan and northwest India, founded when Greco-Bactrian kings pushed south of the Hindu Kush. King Menander is best remembered, said in Buddhist texts to have debated the monk Nagasena.

Indo-Parthians.text: The Indo-Parthians were a kingdom in what is now Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan, founded in the 1st century CE by Gondophares. Taxila is thought to have been its capital, and tradition links Gondophares with the apostle Thomas. Kushan and later Sasanian conquests ended it.

Indo-Sasanian Empire.text: Also called the Kushano-Sasanians, this was a sub-kingdom set up by Persia's Sasanian Empire in Bactria (northern Afghanistan) after it seized lands from the declining Kushans in the 220s CE. Its governors called themselves King of the Kushans and are known mostly from coins; the Kidarites took most of it around 360–370.

Indore.text: The Maratha princely state of the Holkars in central India, its main block around Indore and Nimar, with detached parts such as Rampura-Bhanpura. It acceded to India in 1947.

Indore State (Holkar).text: The state of the Holkars, a Maratha dynasty, in Madhya Pradesh. After Mahidpur (1817) and the Treaty of Mandsaur (1818) it shrank to scattered districts under British protection; its capital moved from Maheshwar to Indore in 1818.

Indore State (Rampura–Bhanpura).text: The northern district of the Holkar state of Indore, around Rampura and Bhanpura, apart from Indore itself. It was a detached piece of the Maratha state of Holkar, lying between Mewar, Kota and Scindia's lands in Malwa.

Injuids.text: A Persian dynasty that ruled Shiraz and Isfahan in the 1300s. They had been managers of royal estates under the Mongols and became independent when the Ilkhanate broke up, until the Muzaffarids defeated them in 1357.

Iraqi Republic.text: Iraq after the 1958 revolution that overthrew its monarchy, ruled by a series of military and Ba'ath governments. Saddam Hussein dominated it from the late 1970s, and it fought a long war with Iran in the 1980s and invaded Kuwait in 1990.

Ireland.text: A country covering most of the island of Ireland, in northwest Europe, that broke away from Britain in 1922 as the Irish Free State, becoming a republic in 1949. The six counties of Northern Ireland remain in the United Kingdom.

Irish Catholic Confederation.text: The Catholic government of Ireland set up at Kilkenny in 1642 after the 1641 rebellion. It controlled much of the island and ran its own assembly, until Cromwell's invasion crushed it in 1649-52.

Irish Free State.text: A self-governing dominion of the British Empire, created in December 1922 after the Anglo-Irish Treaty. It covered most of Ireland, except Northern Ireland, and gave way to a new constitution in 1937.

Irukkuvel chiefdom (Kodumbalur).text: A small Sangam-age chiefdom around Kodumbalur in the Pudukkottai area of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-300 CE. It lay as a buffer between the Cholas and Pandyas, and historians debate whether it links to the later Irukkuvel line.

Isle of Man.text: An island in the Irish Sea between Britain and Ireland. In the 1300s it passed back and forth between English and Scottish control, and from 1346 the English held it through a series of lords. It is now a self-governing British Crown Dependency with its capital at Douglas.

Italian City-States.text: The rebel league of Italian peoples, such as the Samnites and Marsi, who fought Rome in the Social War of 91-88 BCE to win the rights of citizens. They set up their own capital, Corfinium, and Rome ended the war by granting citizenship.

Itza Mayans.text: A Maya people who made their capital, Nojpetén, on an island in Lake Petén Itzá, in today's northern Guatemala. Settled there since the 1400s, their kingdom stayed independent long after Spain conquered the rest of the region, finally submitting to Spanish rule in 1697.

Jabrid dynasty.text: A Bedouin dynasty of the Banu Jabr that ruled al-Hasa and al-Qatif in eastern Arabia from the early 15th century. They later held Bahrain and coastal Oman until the Muntafiq and Ottomans displaced them in the 1520s.

Jaemtland.text: A region in central Sweden, shown here from 947 to 1187. The Jamts long ran their own assembly, the Jamtamót, and had their own law; later tied to Norway, it became Swedish by the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645.

Jaffna kingdom.text: A Tamil kingdom in northern Sri Lanka, centred on the Jaffna Peninsula and ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty. It drew wealth from pearls, elephant exports and trade with South India, and the Portuguese ended its independence in 1619.

Jaintia Kingdom.text: A kingdom in the Jaintia hills of Meghalaya and the plains below at Jaintiapur in Sylhet, ruled by kings called Syiem. They used Jaintiapur as a winter capital and Nartiang in summer, until the East India Company annexed it in 1835.

Jaipur.text: A Kachhwaha Rajput princely state in Rajasthan, which included the Shekhawati chiefships. It acceded to India in 1947, and its capital, Jaipur, is now the capital of Rajasthan.

Jaisalmer.text: A Bhati Rajput desert princely state in the far west of Rajasthan, in the Rajputana Agency under the British. It acceded to India in 1947.

Jalayirid Sultanate.text: A Mongol-origin dynasty that ruled Iraq and western Iran after the Ilkhanate broke up in the 1330s. It held Baghdad and Tabriz, was shattered by Timur's invasions, and finally died out by 1432.

Jamaica.text: A Caribbean island nation, independent from Britain on 6 August 1962. It was a major sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans, and today it is known worldwide for reggae music and its sprinters.

Jammu and Kashmir.text: A large Himalayan princely state ruled by the Dogra maharajas, including Ladakh and the Gilgit region. Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India dated 26 October 1947, and Mountbatten accepted it the next day.

Janapada of Anga.text: An ancient kingdom in eastern India, in the area of Bihar and Bengal, listed among the sixteen great realms in Buddhist texts. Its capital Champa was a river port, and its king was defeated by Magadha's Bimbisara, who annexed it.

Janapada of Avanti.text: One of the sixteen great realms of ancient India, based in the Malwa region of today's Madhya Pradesh, with Ujjain as its northern capital. It was a strong kingdom in the Buddha's time, and Magadha eventually took it.

Janapada of Aśmaka.text: An ancient realm on the Godavari River, in what is now Telangana and Maharashtra, set far to the south of most of the sixteen great realms. Buddhist texts mention it, but it is little known.

Janapada of Aṅga.text: An early Indian state around Champa, near modern Bhagalpur in Bihar, drawn here c. 700-601 BCE. It lay east of Magadha, which later annexed it under King Bimbisara; its early dates are uncertain and no contemporary source describes its borders.

Janapada of Cedī.text: An ancient Indo-Aryan kingdom of central India, in the eastern part of Bundelkhand, counted among the sixteen great realms in Buddhist texts. Its people, the Caidyas, already appear in the Rigveda, where one of their kings is praised for his gifts.

Janapada of Gandhāra.text: An ancient kingdom in northwest South Asia, around Peshawar and Taxila in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan, one of the sixteen great realms. It fell to the Persian Empire in the 6th century BCE. Taxila later became a famous centre of learning.

Janapada of Kamboja.text: The Kambojas were a people of the far northwest of ancient India, on either side of the Hindu Kush, whose culture had Iranian as well as Indian ties. Indian texts list their land among the sixteen great realms.

Janapada of Kosala.text: A kingdom of the Ganges plain in northern India, one of the most powerful of the sixteen great realms in the Buddha's day. King Prasenajit ruled it from Shravasti, and Magadha absorbed it in the fifth century BCE.

Janapada of Kuru.text: The Kuru realm, in the area of Delhi and Haryana, was an old Vedic kingdom that shaped early Indian culture, and it provides the setting of the epic Mahabharata. By the Buddha's time it had shrunk and was just one of the sixteen great realms.

Janapada of Kāśī.text: A kingdom of the Ganges plain with its capital at Varanasi, which by the later Iron Age ranked among the strongest states of South Asia. Neighbouring Kosala conquered it for good shortly before the Buddha's lifetime, and Magadha later took it over.

Janapada of Magadha.text: A kingdom in the eastern Ganges plain, centred on Bihar south of the Ganges, that overshadowed and swallowed the other great realms of ancient India. Ruled first by the Haryanka kings, it later became the heartland of the Nanda and Maurya empires.

Janapada of Malla.text: A republic of two clan groups in northern India, among the sixteen great realms, ruled by an assembly of nobles instead of a king. Its town of Kushinagar is where the Buddha died. Magadha absorbed it.

Janapada of Matsya.text: An ancient Indo-Aryan kingdom in today's northeastern Rajasthan, one of the sixteen great realms. The Matsyas already appear in the Rigveda, and unlike several neighbours that turned into aristocratic republics they kept their kings until Magadha conquered them.

Janapada of Pañcāla.text: A kingdom in the Ganges-Yamuna plain of northern India, powerful in the late Vedic age and an ally of the Kurus. It was one of the sixteen great realms, with cities such as Kampilya and Ahichchhatra.

Janapada of Surasena.text: An ancient kingdom of northern India around Mathura, in the Braj region of Uttar Pradesh, counted as one of the sixteen great realms. Mathura later became a renowned religious and artistic centre.

Janapada of Vajji.text: A confederacy of clans in northeast India, including the Licchavis, governed by assemblies instead of one king. It was one of the sixteen great realms, and Magadha's king Ajatashatru conquered it.

Janapada of Vatsa.text: A kingdom of northern India ruled from Kaushambi by a branch of the old Kuru royal line, one of the sixteen great realms. Its king Udayana, a contemporary of the Buddha, is the romantic hero of many plays and tales; Avanti and later Magadha annexed it.

Jaunpur Sultanate.text: A Muslim kingdom in northern India, covering much of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, founded in 1394 by Malik Sarwar, a former minister of Delhi. It became a rich centre of learning and architecture until the Lodi sultans of Delhi finally conquered it in 1494.

Jesuit Reducciones.text: Mission towns that Jesuits built for the Guaraní people around the borders of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, starting around 1609. The Guaraní lived and worked in them under Jesuit guidance, until the Jesuits were expelled from Spanish lands in 1767-68.

Jhalawar State.text: A small Rajput state in south-east Rajasthan, created in 1838 by the British for the descendants of Zalim Singh Jhala, who had ruled Kota as regent for over forty years. Madan Singh was its first Maharaj Rana.
