Jiaodong.text: A short-lived kingdom on the Shandong peninsula in eastern China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by the warlord Xiang Yu in 206 BCE. Tian Rong of Qi soon conquered it and reunited the old Qi state.

Jibei.text: A short-lived kingdom in northern Shandong, among the Eighteen Kingdoms set up by the warlord Xiang Yu as the Qin empire fell apart in 206 BCE. Tian Rong, ruler of Qi, soon seized it and reunited the old Qi state.

Jin.text: A leading state of Zhou China in southern Shanxi, first called Tang, founded by a younger brother of King Cheng of Zhou. It was a major power until three of its noble families split it into Han, Zhao and Wei around 403 BCE.

Jinhan.text: One of the Samhan, the three loose confederations of chiefdoms in southern Korea, in the southeast, east of the Nakdong River. Its twelve small states eventually merged into the kingdom of Silla.

Jiujiang.text: A short-lived kingdom in central and southern Anhui, China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE. Its king, Ying Bu, a former Chu general, later surrendered and allied with Liu Bang, the future Han emperor.

Jodhpur (Marwar).text: The largest princely state of Rajputana, ruled by Rathore Rajputs, in western Rajasthan. Also called Marwar, it acceded to India in August 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Jolof Empire.text: A Wolof confederation in Senegal under the Burba of Jolof, formed c. 1360, including Waalo, Kajoor, Bawol, Sine and Saloum. Civil wars weakened it, and Sine and Saloum broke away in 1520.

Judea.text: The hill country around Jerusalem, where the Hasmonean family won independence from the Seleucids after the Maccabean revolt. Rome stepped in after 63 BCE, and Herod the Great later ruled as Rome's client king.

Junagadh.text: A Muslim-ruled princely state on the Kathiawar peninsula in Gujarat. Its Nawab acceded to Pakistan and fled on 26 October 1947; on 7 November the state council invited India to take over, and a plebiscite in February 1948 favoured India.

Kaabu.text: A federation of Mandinka kingdoms on the Upper Guinea coast, in present-day Guinea-Bissau and Senegal. Once Mali's westernmost province, it became independent as Mali declined, c. 1537, and fell in 1867 when Fula forces from Futa Jallon stormed Kansala.

Kaarta.text: A Bambara kingdom of the Massassi Coulibaly clan in the Sahel of western Mali, c. 1754-1854. Re-founded in 1754 after an earlier Kaarta was crushed by its rival Ségou, it stayed a rival of Ségou until El Hadj Umar Tall's jihad captured its capital Nioro in 1855.

Kachchhapaghatas of Gwalior.text: A Rajput dynasty ruling Gwalior and nearby Narwar and Dubkund, c. 1000-1196. They served the Chandelas until 1035, then ruled independently; Mahipala built the Sas-Bahu temple in 1096. Qutb al-Din Aibak took Gwalior fort in 1196.

Kadamba Empire.text: The Kadambas were the first native dynasty of Karnataka to use Kannada in government, ruling from Banavasi from about 345 CE. Around 540 the Chalukyas of Badami, once their vassals, conquered the kingdom, and the Kadambas lived on as minor vassal lines.

Kadi Burhan al-Din's state.text: A sultanate in central Anatolia (now Turkey) ruled from Sivas by Kadi Burhan al-Din, the Eretnid vizier, who took over the Eretnid lands in 1381. The Aq Qoyunlu killed him c. 1398, and Bayezid I annexed Sivas.

Kahuripan.text: A short-lived Hindu-Buddhist kingdom in East Java, c. 1019-1045, built by King Airlangga after the old Mataram kingdom collapsed. In 1045 he split it between his two sons, creating Janggala and Kediri.

Kakatiya Dynasty.text: A Telugu dynasty ruling the eastern Deccan, today's Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, in the 12th-14th centuries. Their capital was Orugallu (Warangal), and they began as feudal lords under larger powers.

Kakuyids.text: A Daylamite dynasty related to the Buyids that ruled Isfahan and Hamadan in Iran from about 1008. Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar, patron of Avicenna, founded it; Tughril took Isfahan in 1051, and later Kakuyids served the Seljuks at Yazd.

Kalaallit (Greenland Inuit).text: The Kalaallit, the Inuit of western Greenland, descendants of the Thule people who reached the island between about 1200 and 1400. They lived by hunting seals, narwhals and walruses along the coast, and Europeans did not settle in Greenland again until 1721.

Kalachuri kingdom of Mahishmati.text: A dynasty in central India, c. 550-622 CE, ruling Malwa, central Gujarat and northern Maharashtra from Mahishmati on the Narmada. Kings such as Krishnaraja and Shankaragana lost out to Chalukya invasions.

Kalachuri kingdom of Tripuri (Chedi).text: A dynasty ruling the Chedi country around Jabalpur on the upper Narmada in Madhya Pradesh, c. 850-979. Its kings, such as Kokalla I, served the Rashtrakutas and Pratiharas until they became independent, probably under Yuvarajadeva I.

Kalachuris of Ratnapura.text: A branch of the Tripuri Kalachuris that became independent towards the end of the 11th century, ruling the Chhattisgarh plains of India from Ratnapura (Ratanpur).

Kalachuris of Tripuri (Chedi).text: The core of the Kalachuri kingdom of Chedi on the upper Narmada and Son rivers in Madhya Pradesh, c. 1000-1211, ruled from Tripuri near Jabalpur. Under Lakshmikarna its power briefly reached far beyond.

Kalat (with Kharan, Las Bela and Makran).text: The princely state of Kalat in Balochistan, Pakistan, whose Khan headed a confederacy of Baloch chiefs including Kharan, Las Bela and Makran. Those three acceded to Pakistan first, and Kalat followed on 27 March 1948.

Kalinago (Island Carib) chiefdoms.text: The homeland of the Kalinago, or Island Caribs, a native people of the Caribbean whose islands ran from the Windward Islands to Guadeloupe. They raided European plantations and long defended their independence against English and French colonists, and Kalinago communities still live on Dominica.

Kalinga.text: An ancient region on India's east coast, in present-day Odisha. It was a prosperous maritime land until Ashoka the Mauryan emperor conquered it around 261 BCE, a war so bloody that he is said to have turned to Buddhism afterwards.

Kalmyk Khanate.text: A Mongol Oirat khanate on the lower Volga steppe, in today's Kalmykia in Russia, formed about 1630. The Kalmyks were by turns allies and raiders of Russia, and in 1771 many set off on a long trek back toward Dzungaria.

Kamarupa Kingdom.text: Kamarupa was the first known kingdom of Assam in northeast India, lasting from about 350 to 1140 CE. It was ruled by three successive dynasties, and the Chinese traveller Xuanzang visited it in the 7th century.

Kamata kingdom.text: A kingdom in lower Assam, north Bengal and Cooch Behar, which emerged from Kamarupa after King Sandhya moved his seat to Kamatapur. Alauddin Husain Shah of Bengal ended its Khen dynasty in 1498.

Kamerun.text: A German colony in Central Africa from 1884 to 1916, covering today's Cameroon and parts of its neighbours. After the First World War it was divided between Britain and France. The dates on this map entry look off.

Kampili Kingdom.text: A short-lived Hindu kingdom near Ballari in northeastern Karnataka, southern India, in the early 1300s. It fell in 1327 to the armies of the Delhi Sultanate under the Tughlaqs, and its fall is linked to the later rise of the great Vijayanagara Empire.

Kanak chiefdoms.text: The Kanak peoples, Melanesian islanders of New Caledonia in the southwest Pacific, lived in clan-based chiefdoms speaking many languages. France took the island in 1853, and Kanaks remain a large part of its population today.

Kannauj-Varman Dynasty.text: A kingdom centred on the city of Kannauj in northern India, drawn c. 732 to 771. Its first and best-known king, Yashovarman of the Varman dynasty, probably ruled c. 725 to 752. Kannauj was later held by the Ayudha rulers and became the prize fought over by the Pratiharas and other powers.

Kapisa.text: A region north of Kabul, in today's Afghanistan, around the old city of Kapisi near Bagram. It was once a kingdom in ancient times. On this map, 1475 to 1506, the label shows the area in the late Timurid era.

Karabakh Khanate.text: A khanate in the Karabakh region with its capital at Shusha (Panahabad), founded in 1748 under Panah Ali Khan. It was self-governing under nominal Iranian suzerainty after 1747, and came under Russian rule by 1805.

Karagwe.text: A highland kingdom between Rwanda and Lake Victoria in Tanzania, founded around 1450 according to its king-list. Under Rumanyika it was a hub of the caravan trade, and Speke and Grant visited in 1861.

Karamanli Dynasty.text: An Ottoman dynasty that ruled Tripolitania, in today's Libya, from 1711 to 1835, founded by Ahmad Karamanli. Though nominally Ottoman, they acted largely on their own and were known for piracy and tribute.

Karauli State.text: A Rajput princely state in eastern Rajasthan ruled by the Jadon dynasty from Karauli since the 14th century. It paid tribute to the Marathas in the later 18th century and signed a treaty with the East India Company on 9 November 1817.

Karkota Dynasty.text: The Karkotas ruled Kashmir and nearby lands from about 625 CE. Their king Lalitaditya Muktapida, in the 8th century, pushed far beyond Kashmir, and he is traditionally associated with the Martand Sun Temple. The dynasty declined by 855.

Karnats of Mithila (Tirhut).text: A dynasty ruling Mithila (Tirhut), between the Gandak and Kosi rivers in northern Bihar, India, founded by Nanyadeva in 1097. It ended when Ghiyath ad-Din Tughluq took Tirhut in 1324.

Kartids.text: A Sunni dynasty of Tajik origin that governed much of Khorasan from Herat in the 1200s and 1300s. They began as Mongol vassals, and Timur broke their power in 1381.

Kasanje Kingdom.text: An Imbangala kingdom in Angola, formed in 1620 by a band that deserted the Portuguese. It was a middleman in the slave trade between the Lunda lands and Luanda, and was absorbed by Portugal in the early 1900s.

Kashmir.text: Kashmir is a mountain region in South Asia. In the early medieval centuries it was an independent Hindu and Buddhist kingdom, noted for scholars and for the chronicle Rajatarangini, until Muslim rulers took over in 1339.

Kashmir and Jammu.text: A princely state formed in 1846, after Britain took the Kashmir Valley from the Sikhs and sold it to Gulab Singh, the Raja of Jammu. It lived under British protection until 1947, when its ruler joined India and war with Pakistan left the land divided and disputed.

Kashmiri Sultanate.text: A Muslim state in the Kashmir Valley. It began about 1320 with the Ladakhi noble Rinchan, who adopted Islam as Sultan Sadr-ud-Din; the Shah Mir dynasty ruled from 1339 and the Chaks from 1561. Mughal forces under Akbar took the valley in 1586.

Kastamonu.text: A town in northern Turkey that in the early 1300s was a base for Turkish rulers of the Candar family. It is now the seat of Kastamonu Province.

Kathiawar states.text: A grouping on the map of the many princely states of the Kathiawar peninsula in Gujarat, among them Nawanagar, Bhavnagar, Porbandar, Gondal, Morvi and Dhrangadhra. They all acceded to India in 1947.

Kathiri Sultanate.text: A sultanate in the Hadhramaut valley of eastern Yemen, founded in the late 14th century. It held much of the valley and took the port of al-Shihr in the 1460s. It lost ground to the rival Qu'aiti in the 19th century, and the Kathiri state of Seiyun survived until 1967.

Kathmandu.text: The Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, shown here as the old Malla-era kingdom around the city of Kathmandu. The valley was a trade crossroads between India and Tibet, and later became Nepal's capital.

Katyuri kingdom.text: A kingdom ruling Kumaon and western Nepal, c. 1000-1065, from Kartikeyapura (Baijnath), having moved there from Joshimath around 850. The dates follow one Wikipedia article whose accuracy is disputed.

Katyuri principalities (Kumaon).text: After a civil war among the sons of Virdeo, dated uncertainly to about 1065, the old Katyuri kingdom of the Kumaon hills (Uttarakhand, India) broke into rival branches at Baijnath, Dwarahat, Askot and other seats. Chand kings reportedly displaced the Dwarahat branch.

Kauaʻi chiefdoms.text: The chiefdoms of Kauaʻi, one of the main Hawaiian Islands, which stayed independent while Kamehameha I united the others. His invasions in 1796 and later were called off, and in 1810 its ruler Kaumualiʻi agreed to become his vassal, with the island to pass to Hawaii on his death.

Kazakhstan.text: The world's largest landlocked country, a land of vast steppes, which became independent from the Soviet Union in December 1991. Nursultan Nazarbayev led it for nearly 30 years. The capital moved from Almaty to Astana in 1997.

Kedah-Perlis District.text: A district on the northwest coast of the Malay Peninsula, in today's Malaysian states of Perlis and Kedah. Siam, which then ruled the region, separated Perlis from Kedah in the 1842 settlement. Britain took over Siam's rights there under the treaty of 1909.

Kediri Kingdom.text: A Hindu-Buddhist Javanese kingdom in East Java, c. 1042-1222, one of the two halves of Airlangga's realm. It is remembered for a golden age of Javanese literature, including the poem Bharatayuddha.

Keladi Nayakas (Ikkeri / Bednur).text: A Karnataka dynasty that governed for Vijayanagara and became independent after Talikota in 1565. They held the Shimoga and Chikmagalur plateau and much of the Canara coast, ruling from Ikkeri and later Bidanur until the 1760s.

Kelantan.text: A Malay sultanate in northeast Malaya, now a state of Malaysia, known as the Blissful Abode. It was under Siamese overlordship until 1909, when the British took over.

Kenmu Restoration.text: A short period, 1333 to 1336, when Emperor Go-Daigo ruled Japan directly after overthrowing the Kamakura shogunate. It collapsed when his general Ashikaga Takauji turned against him and set up a new shogunate in Kyoto.

Khadga Dynasty.text: The Khadgas were a Buddhist dynasty of Samatata and Vanga in Bengal, ruling from about 625 to 716 CE. They arose between the fall of Gauda and the rise of the Palas, and their first king was Khadgodyama.

Khairpur.text: A princely state in Sind, in present-day Pakistan, ruled by the Talpur Mirs. It acceded to Pakistan on 3 October 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Khanate of Kalat (Brahui confederacy).text: A Brahui confederacy in Balochistan, Pakistan, formed by the Ahmadzai khans, who united the Sarawan and Jhalawan tribes around Kalat. They were under Safavid, Mughal, Afsharid and Durrani overlordship in turn, and gained Kachhi in 1740.

Khanate of Kalat (Nasir Khan's khanate a.text: A Baloch khanate in present-day Pakistan, drawn here from 1758 to 1857. Mir Nasir Khan I freed Kalat from Durrani Afghan control in 1758 and brought Makran, Kharan, Las Bela and Kachhi under it, giving the khanate its greatest extent.

Khanate of Kazan.text: A Tatar khanate on the middle Volga, born from the breakup of the Golden Horde, founded in about 1438 or 1445 and covering today's Tatarstan and nearby lands, with its capital at Kazan. Its history was full of throne struggles, and the army of Ivan IV of Russia stormed Kazan in 1552.

Khanate of Khiva.text: An Uzbek khanate on the lower Amu Darya, in Khorezm, in what is now western Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. It lasted from 1511 to 1920 apart from a brief Persian occupation, became a Russian protectorate in 1873, and fell to a revolution after 1917.

Khanate of Kokand.text: Founded in 1709, a khanate centred on the Fergana Valley and reaching into parts of present Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Kazakhstan. Russia abolished it in 1876.

Khanates of the Caucasus.text: A set of small Persian-ruled khanates in the South Caucasus, such as Karabakh, Baku and Shirvan, each under a hereditary khan. They were conquered by Russia in the early 1800s.

Khandesh Sultanate (Faruqi).text: The Faruqi sultanate of the Tapti valley, in Maharashtra, India, ruled from Burhanpur. Akbar's forces forced its subordination in 1577, and Akbar annexed it in 1601 after the fall of Asirgarh.

Kharijites.text: The Kharijites were an early Islamic sect that rejected the caliphs' authority, and Berber followers rebelled across North Africa in the 700s. Here the name marks lands under Kharijite rule in the Maghreb c. 751 to 762, such as the Sufri state at Sijilmasa and Ibadi Tripoli.

Khasa Malla kingdom.text: A Himalayan kingdom in the Karnali basin of western Nepal with its capital at Sinja. It sometimes also ruled Purang and Guge, and it broke up into the Baise principalities in the late 14th century.

Khazaria.text: The Khazars were a Turkic people north of the Caucasus who built a trading empire from around 650 CE. Their ruling elite converted to Judaism, and the realm fell in the 10th century after attacks from the Rus.

Khmer Rouge.text: The communist regime of Pol Pot, called Democratic Kampuchea, which ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979. It emptied the cities and forced people into farm labour, and an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people died.

Khoshut Khanate.text: A Mongol Oirat khanate based in the Qinghai region on the Tibetan Plateau, founded by Güshi Khan in 1642. He backed the 5th Dalai Lama and the Gelug school's rise to rule Tibet. The Dzungars invaded and ended the khanate in 1717.

Kidarites.text: A nomadic dynasty named for their king Kidara, who held Bactria, parts of Central Asia and northern Pakistan during the 300s and 400s CE. Sasanian Persia and the Hephthalites ended their power.

Kilwa Sultanate.text: A Swahili city-state on Kilwa island in Tanzania, c. 1000-1505. At its height its authority reached along the Swahili coast; a sultan of 1178-1195 took Sofala from the Mogadishans, and the Portuguese took Kilwa in 1505.

Kindah Kingdom.text: A tribal kingdom of central and northern Arabia, c. 450-528 CE, ruled by kings of the Hujrid line such as Hujr Akil al-Murar. They served the kings of Himyar, and the kingdom collapsed after al-Harith ibn Amr died in 528.

Kingdom of Adiabene.text: A kingdom in northern Mesopotamia, in the old Assyrian heartland of northern Iraq. Its royal family, including Queen Helena, converted to Judaism in the first century CE, and it was a vassal of Parthia.

Kingdom of Africa.text: A strip of North African coast, around today's Tunisia, held by the Norman Kingdom of Sicily from the 1140s. Roger II took Mahdia in 1148, and the Almohads drove the Normans out by 1160.

Kingdom of Alamannia.text: Alamannia was the land of the Alemanni, a Germanic confederation that pushed past the Roman frontier in the 3rd century CE. It covered parts of southwest Germany, Alsace and northern Switzerland, and Clovis's Franks defeated them around 496. French and Spanish names for Germany come from them.

Kingdom of Alba.text: The medieval kingdom of Scotland, from the death of Donald II in 900 to the death of Alexander III in 1286. Donald was the first to be called King of Alba, and over time his successors added the Pictish north and other lands to their rule.

Kingdom of Allada (Ardra).text: An Aja kingdom on the Slave Coast in present-day Benin, called Great Ardra by Europeans, with ports at Offra and Jakin. It paid tribute to Oyo and was conquered by Dahomey in 1724.

Kingdom of Altava.text: A smaller Romanised Berber kingdom in northern Algeria, c. 579-700 CE, ruled from Altava after its predecessor's defeat in 578. Its king Kusaila killed the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi in 683 and forced the Arabs to leave Kairouan.

Kingdom of Amber (Jaipur).text: The Kachwaha Rajput kingdom of Amber, ruling from Jaipur, the planned city founded in 1727. Once a Mughal vassal, it paid tribute to the Marathas and accepted British protection in 1818.

Kingdom of Amber (Jaipur): Uniara tract.text: The Uniara area, a part of the kingdom of Amber (Jaipur) in eastern Rajasthan. Amber was a Kachwaha Rajput state that paid tribute to the Marathas and accepted British protection in 1818.

Kingdom of Araba (Hatra).text: An Arab kingdom around the caravan city of Hatra in northern Iraq, c. 150-241 CE, under Parthian protection. Its rulers called themselves kings of the Arabs; it beat back Trajan and Septimius Severus before Shapur I destroyed it.

Kingdom of Aragon.text: A kingdom in northeast Spain founded in 1035 by Ramiro I. It expanded south by taking Zaragoza in 1118, and later joined with Catalonia and Castile in the foundation of Spain.

Kingdom of Arles.text: Also called the Kingdom of Burgundy, formed in 933 when the two Burgundies were united. It lay in the Rhône valley and Provence, and was part of the Holy Roman Empire from 1032, but slowly drifted to France.

Kingdom of Armenia.text: A kingdom in the Armenian highlands, in today's Armenia and eastern Turkey, which grew from a Persian satrapy. Under Tigranes the Great it briefly ruled much of the Near East, and in 301 CE it became the first state to adopt Christianity.

Kingdom of Asturias.text: Asturias was a small Christian kingdom in the mountains of northern Spain, founded by Pelagius after the Muslim conquest of Iberia, c. 718 CE. It was the seed of the Reconquista, and later became the Kingdom of León.
Kingdom of Asturias.capital: Cangas de Onís; later Pravia; later Oviedo

Kingdom of Awadh (Oudh), reduced.text: A Muslim kingdom in the Gangetic plain of northern India centred on Lucknow, shown here from 1803 to 1856. A treaty of 1801 gave about half its land to the East India Company; the rest survived as a protected state until its last king, Wajid Ali Shah, was deposed in 1856.

Kingdom of Baguirmi.text: A sultanate on the Chari river south-east of Lake Chad, in present-day Chad, founded c. 1522. Long a tributary of Bornu, it was independent in the 18th century, then conquered by Wadai in 1805 and later by the warlord Rabih in the 1890s.

Kingdom of Bahrain.text: A small island country in the Persian Gulf, independent from Britain in 1971. It was one of the first Gulf states to find oil, and a causeway now links it to Saudi Arabia.

Kingdom of Bavaria.text: A German kingdom created in 1806 with Napoleon's backing, replacing the old electorate and based on Munich. It became a federated state of the German Empire in 1871, and the Wittelsbach monarchy ended in 1918.

Kingdom of Benin.text: The Edo kingdom of Benin City in southern Nigeria, ruled by Obas of the Eweka dynasty who replaced the earlier Ogiso rulers. Its early dates are traditional, and it lasted to the British conquest of 1897.

Kingdom of Bernicia.text: Bernicia was an Anglian kingdom in northeast England and southeast Scotland, with a capital at Bamburgh. Under King Æthelfrith it joined with Deira to create Northumbria, c. 604.

Kingdom of Bhutan.text: A mountain kingdom in the Eastern Himalayas between China and India, first united in the 1600s under the lama Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal. It has had a hereditary monarchy since 1907, and its capital is Thimphu.

Kingdom of Bithynia.text: A Hellenistic kingdom in northwestern Anatolia, in today's Turkey, whose ruler Zipoites took the title of king in 297 BCE. It stayed independent for over two centuries, until its last king, Nicomedes IV, left it to Rome in 74 BCE.

Kingdom of Bohemia.text: A medieval and early modern monarchy in central Europe, the forerunner of today's Czech Republic. Its king was a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and its crown lands at times included Moravia and Silesia.

Kingdom of Bosnia.text: A medieval Balkan kingdom that began as a banate. Its ruler Tvrtko I was crowned king in 1377. Strong for a time, it fell to the Ottomans in 1463, when the last king, Stephen Tomašević, was executed.

Kingdom of Breifne.text: The Irish kingdom of the Uí Ruairc (O'Rourkes) in Leitrim and Cavan, c. 1000-1256. Under Tigernán Ua Ruairc in the 12th century it pushed into Meath. In 1256 it split into West Breifne (O'Rourke) and East Breifne (O'Reilly).

Kingdom of Brittany.text: A Breton state in northwest France that won royal status in 851, when Erispoe defeated the Franks at Jengland and became its first king. Norse invasions and feuds over the throne followed, Vikings occupied the land after Alan the Great died, and it re-emerged in 939 as a duchy.

Kingdom of Brycheiniog.text: Brycheiniog was a small Welsh kingdom in mid-Wales, around today's Brecon, named after a ruler said to be Brychan. It lay between Wales's major kingdoms and the English, and the Normans took it in the late 11th century.

Kingdom of Bulgaria.text: The Bulgarian kingdom from 1908 to 1946. Its last tsar, Simeon II, was a child when a 1946 vote abolished the monarchy, after which Bulgaria became a communist state.

Kingdom of Bulungan.text: A small Muslim state in eastern Borneo, in today's North Kalimantan, founded in 1731 when its ruler converted and became sultan. It later became a special territory of Indonesia, so the span drawn here is only its early years.

Kingdom of Burundi.text: A Bantu kingdom in the African Great Lakes, ruled by a Mwami; Ntare I is traditionally said to have united its two centres c. 1680. By 1850 it had roughly modern Burundi's extent. It was assigned to German East Africa in 1890.

Kingdom of Butua (Torwa).text: A Kalanga kingdom of the Torwa dynasty on the south-western plateau of Zimbabwe, centred on Khami and famed for its gold. Changamire Dombo conquered it around 1683.

Kingdom of Calicut (the Zamorin).text: The kingdom of Calicut on India's Malabar coast, ruled by the Zamorin, a title for its king. A great spice port, it fought Portugal and the rival kingdom of Cochin for a century, and was conquered by Mysore in 1765-66.

Kingdom of Cambodia.text: A Southeast Asian country that became independent from France in 1953 under Norodom Sihanouk. It was home to the temples of Angkor. The Khmer Rouge ruled brutally from 1975 to 1979. Its capital is Phnom Penh.

Kingdom of Cappadocia.text: A kingdom in central Anatolia, in today's Turkey, that grew from a Persian province under its last governor, Ariarathes. Kings named Ariarathes ruled first, then the families of Ariobarzanes and Archelaus, until the Roman emperor Tiberius annexed it in 17 CE.

Kingdom of Castile.text: A Christian kingdom in northern Spain that grew from a border county, centred on Burgos. It expanded south during the Reconquista and was joined with León in 1230, and later became the core of Spain.

Kingdom of Ceredigion.text: Ceredigion, between the Teifi and the Dyfi, traditionally founded by Ceredig son of Cunedda. Its king Seisyll ap Clydog is regarded as the founder of Seisyllwg, which joined Ceredigion with Ystrad Tywi; the kingdom ceased to exist as a separate entity around 872.

Kingdom of Champasak.text: A Lao kingdom in the south of Laos along the Mekong, which broke away from the old Lan Xang kingdom in the early 1700s. It later became a vassal of Siam.

Kingdom of Cochin.text: A kingdom on the Kerala coast, with its capital at Kochi. It allied with the Portuguese from 1503 and was a Dutch protectorate from 1663, then came under British overlordship, remaining a princely state until 1949.

Kingdom of Cochin (Perumpadappu Swaroopa.text: A small principality on the Kerala coast that became free after the Chera Perumals fell in the 12th century. It rose to importance around Kodungallur and Kochi once the Portuguese arrived.

Kingdom of Commagene.text: A small Greco-Iranian kingdom on the upper Euphrates in southeastern Turkey. King Antiochus I built a mountaintop sanctuary on Mount Nemrut with giant statues of gods and himself. Rome annexed it for good in 72 CE.

Kingdom of Croatia.text: A medieval kingdom on the Adriatic coast of present-day Croatia. Tomislav is traditionally its first king, around 925. It had no fixed capital, with seats at Nin, Biograd, Knin and elsewhere, and in 1102 the crown passed to the Hungarian king Coloman.

Kingdom of Cyprus.text: A Crusader kingdom set up on Cyprus in 1192 by the French Lusignan family after the Third Crusade. It lasted until 1489, when Venice took over the island.

Kingdom of Dagbon.text: The Dagomba kingdom of northern Ghana, whose capital moved to Yendi after wars with Gonja c. 1700. It was a tributary of Asante from 1744 to 1874, and the Germans destroyed Yendi in 1896.

Kingdom of Dahomey.text: A Fon kingdom centred on Abomey in present-day Benin, founded c. 1600 by an offshoot of Allada's royal family. It conquered Allada (1724) and Whydah (1727) to reach the coast, and fell to France in 1892-94.

Kingdom of Dali.text: A Bai kingdom in Yunnan, southwest China, which followed Nanzhao and was founded in 937 by Duan Siping. Buddhism flourished there, and it lasted until the Mongols under Kublai Khan conquered it in 1253.

Kingdom of Dambadeniya.text: A medieval Sinhalese kingdom in Sri Lanka, founded by Vijayabahu III with its capital at Dambadeniya. It was a refuge kingdom in the 13th century after Polonnaruwa fell to invaders.

Kingdom of Damot.text: A medieval kingdom south of the Abay (Blue Nile) in what is now Ethiopia. It grew strong enough in the 13th century to make the Sultanate of Shewa pay tribute, until Emperor Amda Seyon conquered it in 1316-17.

Kingdom of Deira.text: Deira was an Anglian kingdom between the Humber and the Tees, in what is now Yorkshire, probably formed in the later 5th century. Its first securely known king, Ælla, ruled in the late 500s; after him it was joined with Bernicia to the north to make Northumbria, with York as a royal centre.

Kingdom of Denmark.text: The medieval Danish kingdom, which took shape in the Viking Age. Gorm the Old ruled from Jelling from c. 936, his son Harald Bluetooth won all of Denmark and brought Christianity, and in 1397 the Kalmar Union joined Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one crown.

Kingdom of Desmond.text: Deasmumhain, the MacCarthy kingdom of south Munster in Ireland, created in the partition of Munster in 1118. It held all of County Cork and most of Kerry until the Anglo-Normans conquered its eastern half in the late 12th century.

Kingdom of Desmond (MacCarthy Mór).text: What was left of Desmond after the Anglo-Norman conquest of its eastern half: the MacCarthy Mór kingdom of south Kerry and west Cork in Ireland. It survived until the death of Domhnall MacCarthy Mór in 1596.

Kingdom of Duklja.text: The medieval South Slavic kingdom of Duklja in what is now southeastern Montenegro. Its rulers gained the title of king in the 1070s, but later in the century it was overshadowed by Raška, the Serbian state to its north.

Kingdom of Dunoting.text: Dunoding was a small kingdom in northwest Wales around Meirionnydd, said to be named for Dunod, a son of Cunedda. It later sat under Gwynedd's authority as a sub-kingdom.

Kingdom of Dyfed.text: A post-Roman kingdom of the Demetae in Pembrokeshire and west Carmarthenshire, Wales, c. 410-919 CE, ruled by a dynasty of Irish Deisi origin. Hywel Dda absorbed it into Deheubarth around 920.

Kingdom of East Anglia.text: East Anglia was the kingdom of the East Angles in eastern England, home to the Sutton Hoo ship burial, probably of King Rædwald. Danish Vikings overran it in 869, after killing King Edmund.

Kingdom of Essex.text: Essex was the kingdom of the East Saxons in southeast England, founded in the 6th century and taking in London. A bishop was sent to London in 604, but its kings were usually under overlords such as Kent or Mercia, and in 825 its last king handed it to Wessex.

Kingdom of Etruria.text: A French client kingdom in Tuscany created in 1801, ruled by a Bourbon-Parma prince, with Florence as its capital. Napoleon annexed it to France in 1807.

Kingdom of Fiji.text: The first unified Fijian state, a monarchy from 1871 to 1874 with the high chief Ratu Seru Cakobau as king, while settlers held much of the real power. Heavy debts and unrest led Cakobau to cede the islands to Britain in 1874, making Fiji a colony.

Kingdom of Galicia.text: A medieval Christian kingdom in northwest Spain, closely linked with Asturias and León. Its kings were sometimes also kings of León, and its main pilgrimage site was Santiago de Compostela.

Kingdom of Gampola.text: A Sinhala kingdom in the central hills of Sri Lanka near Kandy, with its capital at Gampola. The Jaffna kingdom and the Vanni chiefs held the north.

Kingdom of Georgia.text: A medieval kingdom in the Caucasus, formed around 1008 under Bagrat III. It reached a golden age under Queen Tamar and later declined, and Russia annexed its eastern kingdom, Kartli-Kakheti, in 1801.

Kingdom of Gera.text: The last of the Oromo Gibe kingdoms in south-west Ethiopia to form, founded c. 1835 by Gunji between Gomma and Kaffa. It lasted until Dejazmach Besha Abua conquered it in 1887.

Kingdom of Germany.text: The eastern part of the old Frankish empire, which became the German kingdom. Henry the Fowler founded the Saxon dynasty in 919, and his son Otto I was crowned emperor in 962, creating the Holy Roman Empire.

Kingdom of Gomma.text: A small Muslim Oromo kingdom around Agaro in the Gibe region of south-west Ethiopia, c. 1780-1886. It arose in the 1700s and was entirely Muslim by 1841; Beshua Abue conquered it for Emperor Menelik II in 1886.

Kingdom of Gordyene.text: A mountain region on the upper Tigris in southeastern Turkey, south of Lake Van. It was a small kingdom under Parthian influence, then Armenian, Roman and later Persian overlordship, and is known only from scattered records.

Kingdom of Greece.text: Greece under its monarchy after the German occupation ended in 1944. A civil war between the government and the communists raged from 1946 to 1949. Bitter political divisions followed, and the military regime of the colonels abolished the monarchy in 1973.

Kingdom of Gumma.text: An Oromo kingdom of the Gibe region in south-west Ethiopia, c. 1770-1885. Its dynasty rose around 1770 and the kingdom was conquered by Menelik II in 1885, though a son of the last king, Firisa, kept resisting until 1902.

Kingdom of Gwent.text: Gwent was a Welsh kingdom between the rivers Wye and Usk in southeast Wales. It survived from the end of Roman rule until Norman lords overran it in the 11th century.

Kingdom of Gwynedd.text: Gwynedd was a Welsh kingdom in the northwest, strong because of the mountains of Snowdonia. Its rulers, notably Llywelyn the Great, led Welsh resistance to England, until Edward I conquered it in 1283.

Kingdom of Hanover.text: A German kingdom created in 1814 at the Congress of Vienna, once the Hanoverian lands were restored to George III. It shared a king with Britain until 1837, and Prussia annexed it in 1866.

Kingdom of Hejaz.text: A kingdom in western Arabia, containing Mecca and Medina, declared in 1916 by Sharif Hussein bin Ali in his revolt against the Ottomans. It ended in 1925 when Ibn Saud conquered it, creating what became Saudi Arabia.

Kingdom of Iceland.text: Iceland as a kingdom from 1918 to 1944, an independent state sharing a king with Denmark. It cut that last tie in 1944 by declaring itself a republic.

Kingdom of Imereti.text: A western Georgian kingdom around Kutaisi, set up in 1463 by a Bagrationi prince when the unified Georgian kingdom broke apart. For centuries it was fought over by Georgian and Ottoman forces, and Russia deposed its last king and annexed it in 1810.

Kingdom of Imerina.text: The Merina kingdom of Madagascar's central highlands, founded c. 1540 by Andriamanelo; his son Ralambo gave it the name Imerina. Andriamasinavalona divided it among four sons c. 1710, and it split into four rival parts that Andrianampoinimerina later reunited.

Kingdom of Iraq.text: A Hashemite monarchy created under British influence in 1921, which gained full independence in 1932. Faisal I was its first king. It ended in 1958 when army officers overthrew the monarchy in a coup.

Kingdom of Israel.text: The Israelite monarchy of the southern Levant. The united kingdom of Saul, David and Solomon is known mainly from the Bible and may have been small. The northern kingdom of Israel, with its capital at Samaria, lasted until Assyria conquered it around 722 BCE.

Kingdom of Jaisalmer.text: The Bhati Rajput kingdom of the Thar desert in Rajasthan, India, with its capital at Jaisalmer. Rawal Har Raj accepted Akbar's overlordship in 1570, and later it came under British protection.

Kingdom of Janggala.text: A Javanese kingdom in the northeast of East Java, created in 1045 when Airlangga split his realm between his two sons. It was the weaker twin beside Kediri, and sources about it are thin.

Kingdom of Jerusalem.text: The main Crusader kingdom, founded in 1099 after the First Crusade by Godfrey of Bouillon and lasting until Acre fell in 1291. Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187, after which the kingdom survived on the coast.

Kingdom of Jimma.text: The largest of the Oromo Gibe kingdoms in south-west Ethiopia, c. 1790-1884, a rich Muslim market state. Its king Abba Jifar I converted to Islam in 1830, and Abba Jifar II submitted to Emperor Menelik in the early 1880s.

Kingdom of Jolof.text: What remained of the Jolof state in Senegal after the battle of Danki in 1549, when Cayor, Waalo and others broke away. Jolof was left as a landlocked core under the Burba, and became part of French Senegal in 1890.

Kingdom of Jordan.text: A Middle Eastern kingdom ruled by the Hashemite family, with Abdullah I as its first king. It became independent from Britain in 1946 and has Amman as its capital.

Kingdom of Judah.text: The Israelite kingdom around Jerusalem in the hills west of the Dead Sea, c. 930-587 BCE, ruled by the House of David. It survived Assyria's destruction of Israel, but Babylon conquered it and destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple in 587/586 BCE.

Kingdom of Kaffa.text: A highland kingdom in south-west Ethiopia, bounded in the north by the Gojeb river, traditionally founded c. 1390. It reached the Omo under Tato Shagi Sherocho and was overrun in 1897 by Ethiopian forces.

Kingdom of Kakheti.text: An eastern Georgian kingdom centred on the province of Kakheti, ruled from Gremi and later from Telavi. It emerged in the 1460s when the Georgian kingdom split into three, and in 1762 it was merged with the neighbouring kingdom of Kartli.

Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti.text: A Georgian kingdom in the east of Georgia, in Kakheti and Hereti, c. 1014-1104, independent of the united Kingdom of Georgia. David IV annexed it in 1104.

Kingdom of Kandy.text: A hill-country kingdom in Sri Lanka founded in the late 15th century, with its capital at Senkadagalapura (Kandy). It lasted until 1815 and had intermittent access to the east-coast port of Batticaloa.

Kingdom of Kangra (Trigarta).text: A hill kingdom of the Katoch rajas in the old land of Trigarta between the Beas and the Ravi, c. 1044-1191, ruled from Nagarkot fort. Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Nagarkot in 1009, and a Ghaznavid garrison held it until the 1040s.

Kingdom of Kano.text: A Hausa kingdom around the walled city of Kano in northern Nigeria, c. 1000-1804. The Kano Chronicle starts with Bagauda around 999; it became Muslim under Yaji and Rumfa, and fell to the Fulani jihad in 1805-07. Early dates are traditional.

Kingdom of Kartli.text: An eastern Georgian kingdom around Tbilisi, formed in 1478 when the Kingdom of Georgia split into rival parts. Persian and Ottoman pressure repeatedly shook it, and it joined with Kakheti in 1762 before Russia annexed it in 1801.

Kingdom of Katsina.text: A Hausa kingdom in northern Nigeria and a terminus of trans-Saharan trade, whose best-known dynasty was founded by Muhammadu Korau. The jihad took it in 1805-06, and the old dynasty moved to Maradi.

Kingdom of Kazembe.text: An eastern Lunda kingdom in the Luapula valley of Zambia, founded c. 1740. Nominally tributary to the Mwaant Yaav but really independent, it was visited by Portuguese expeditions from 1796 and by David Livingstone in 1867.

Kingdom of Kebbi.text: A Hausa kingdom in north-western Nigeria, founded when Kanta Kuta broke away from Songhai in 1516-17. It became the leading power of western Hausaland, but revolts shrank it after c. 1715 and the Sokoto jihad defeated it; the dynasty lived on at Argungu.

Kingdom of Kent.text: Kent was a small Anglo-Saxon kingdom in southeast England, and the first to be Christianised after Augustine landed in 597 CE. King Æthelberht welcomed him, and Canterbury became England's religious centre. Mercia and then Wessex overshadowed it.

Kingdom of Khotan.text: A Buddhist kingdom on the southern Silk Road in the Tarim Basin, in the present-day Xinjiang region of China. Its people spoke an Iranian language, and Khotan was known for silk and jade until the Kara-Khanids conquered it in 1006.

Kingdom of Kotte.text: The Sinhala kingdom of Kotte in Sri Lanka, whose capital Parakramabahu VI moved to Kotte in 1412. It was one of several rival kingdoms on the island in this period.

Kingdom of Kotte (whole island).text: The Kotte kingdom at its greatest: Parakramabahu VI took the Jaffna kingdom in 1450 and brought the Vanni under Kotte, reuniting Sri Lanka until his death in 1467. A rebellion in 1469 then founded a rival hill kingdom.

Kingdom of Kumaon (Chand dynasty).text: A hill kingdom in Kumaon, now in Uttarakhand, ruled by the Chand rajas, whose capital was moved from Champawat to Almora. They sometimes paid tribute to the Mughals but stayed independent, until Nepal's Gorkhas conquered the kingdom in 1790.

Kingdom of Ladakh (Maryul, Namgyal dynas.text: A Himalayan Buddhist kingdom in Ladakh, ruled by the Namgyal dynasty from Shey and later Leh. After a war with Tibet it kept only the Minsar enclave under the 1684 Treaty of Tingmosgang, and the Dogra general Zorawar Singh's conquest ended the kingdom in 1842.

Kingdom of Laos.text: A landlocked kingdom in Southeast Asia that gained self-rule within the French Union in 1947 and full independence in 1953. Torn by civil war between royalists, neutralists and the communist Pathet Lao, it ended in 1975 when the last king gave up the throne.

Kingdom of Lazica.text: Lazica was a kingdom on the east Black Sea coast, in today's western Georgia, which depended on Byzantium. Persia and Byzantium fought over it in the 6th century, in the long Lazic War, and Byzantium absorbed it by the end of the 7th century.

Kingdom of León.text: A medieval Christian kingdom in northwest Spain, founded in 910 when the Asturian kings moved their court to León. It later led the Reconquista and was joined with Castile in 1230.

Kingdom of Libya.text: A North African kingdom that became independent in 1951 under King Idris I. Oil was found in 1959, and Colonel Muammar Gaddafi's coup overthrew the monarchy in 1969.

Kingdom of Lindsey.text: Lindsey was a small Anglian kingdom covering the north of today's Lincolnshire, between the Humber and the Wash, probably centred on old Roman Lincoln. Northumbria and Mercia took turns ruling it, and it lost its independence early, fading out by the 7th or early 8th century.

Kingdom of Lithuania.text: Lithuania between the world wars, an independent republic since 1918. Vilnius was held by Poland, so Kaunas served as its temporary capital. The Soviet Union took it over in 1940. The article linked here is about a medieval kingdom.

Kingdom of Loango.text: A Vili kingdom on the Atlantic coast north of the Congo's mouth, in Congo-Brazzaville and Cabinda. Once a vassal of Kongo, it grew into an independent trading power and stayed so until it signed treaties with France in 1883.

Kingdom of Lori (Tashir-Dzoraget).text: A Kiurikian Bagratid kingdom in northern Armenia, c. 979-1065, nominally a vassal of Ani. The Seljuks forced its king to accept their overlordship in 1064 and conquered it in 1111-13, but the dynasty kept Tavush and Matsnaberd afterwards.

Kingdom of Lower Burgundy.text: The kingdom of Lower Burgundy, also called Provence, in southeastern France around the Rhône valley. It was founded in 879 and merged with Upper Burgundy in 933 to form a single Kingdom of Burgundy.

Kingdom of Luang Phrabang.text: A Lao kingdom in northern Laos, named after the Phra Bang, a sacred Buddha statue that symbolised Lao sovereignty. It was a successor of Lan Xang and paid tribute to Siam before French rule.

Kingdom of Lunda.text: A confederation of chiefdoms in today's DR Congo, northeastern Angola and northwestern Zambia, with its core in Katanga. Local chiefs kept much freedom as long as they paid tribute to the paramount ruler, the Mwata Yamvo, a title tradition dates to about 1665.

Kingdom of Lysimachus.text: A kingdom carved out by Lysimachus, a bodyguard of Alexander the Great, who held Thrace, then western Anatolia, and finally Macedon. He fell at the Battle of Corupedium against Seleucus in 281 BCE, ending his realm.

Kingdom of Majorca.text: A kingdom of the Balearic Islands and lands around Perpignan, created in 1276 when James I of Aragon divided his realms between his sons. From 1279 its king was a vassal of Aragon, and in 1343 to 1344 Peter IV of Aragon conquered it, after which it stayed a separate kingdom under Aragon's king.

Kingdom of Manipur.text: The Meitei kingdom of Manipur, based in the Imphal valley and its surrounding hills, with its capital at Kangla. It raided deep into Burma under Garib Niwaz and suffered Burmese occupation in 1819-25, called the Seven Years Devastation.

Kingdom of Mann.text: The Norse-Gaelic kingdom of Mann and the Isles, centred on the Isle of Man. Its kings ruled the Irish Sea until 1266, when Norway handed the island to Scotland.

Kingdom of Mapungubwe.text: An early kingdom at the meeting of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers, on the borders of South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe, known mostly from archaeology. Its elite lived on Mapungubwe hill from c. 1220, and it faded around 1300 as trade shifted north to Great Zimbabwe.

Kingdom of Marwar.text: The Rathore kingdom of Marwar in Rajasthan, India, after Rao Maldeo recovered Jodhpur in 1545. The Mughals took Jodhpur fort in 1564, but Chandrasen held out in the Siwana hills until 1581.

Kingdom of Marwar (Jodhpur).text: The Rathore Rajput kingdom of Marwar, ruled from Jodhpur in western Rajasthan. It was once a Mughal vassal, paid tribute to the Marathas in the 18th century, and signed a protection treaty with the British in 1818.

Kingdom of Marwar (Maldeo).text: Marwar under Rao Maldeo, who made it the strongest Rajput state of his day by taking Nagaur, Ajmer and other places, and briefly Bikaner in 1542. Sher Shah Suri's victory at Sammel in 1544 ended this expansion.

Kingdom of Marwar (Mandore).text: The early Rathore kingdom of Marwar in Rajasthan, India, which moved to Mandore under Rao Chunda in 1395. After Rao Ranmal's murder at Chittor in 1438, Mewar held Mandore until Jodha retook it.

Kingdom of Maryul (Ladakh).text: The westernmost Tibetan kingdom, covering Ladakh from the Zoji La to Demchok, drawn c. 1000-1550. Its early kings include Lhachen Utpala and Lhachen Bhagan; the kingdom itself is dated c. 930-1842.

Kingdom of Matamba.text: A kingdom in Angola ruled by Queen Njinga from 1631, who combined it with the remnant of Ndongo after fleeing the Portuguese. Matamba stayed independent until it accepted Portuguese overlordship after war in 1744.

Kingdom of Meath (Mide).text: The midland kingdom of Mide in Ireland, c. 800-1172, held by the Clann Cholmain branch of the southern Uí Néill, whose kings were often High Kings of Ireland. After the Anglo-Norman invasion Henry II granted it to Hugh de Lacy.

Kingdom of Mercia.text: Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the English Midlands, which became the strongest in England in the 8th century under Æthelbald and Offa, who built Offa's Dyke. Viking invasions broke it up in the 9th century.

Kingdom of Mewar.text: The Rajput kingdom of Mewar in Rajasthan, India, ruled from Chittor and Kumbhalgarh. Rana Kumbha built Kumbhalgarh and fought Malwa and Gujarat, and Rana Sanga made it one of the strongest states in north India.

Kingdom of Mewar (Guhilas).text: The Rajput kingdom of the Guhila dynasty in Mewar, Rajasthan, c. 1000-1302, between the Aravalli hills and the Banas river. It fought the Paramaras, Chaulukyas and Chahamanas; Chittor fell to Alauddin Khalji in 1303.

Kingdom of Mewar (Rana Sanga).text: Mewar at its height under the Rajput king Rana Sanga, who led a Rajput alliance across Rajasthan and into Malwa, beating its sultan at Gagron in 1519. His hegemony ended when Babur's Mughal army defeated him at Khanwa in 1527.

Kingdom of Mewar (Sisodias).text: The Rajput kingdom of Mewar in Rajasthan, India, refounded when Hammir Singh of the Sisodia branch recovered Chittor in 1326. It later produced famous rulers such as Rana Kumbha and Rana Sanga.

Kingdom of Mewar (Udaipur State).text: The Sisodia Rajput kingdom of Mewar, ruled from Udaipur in southern Rajasthan. Once a Mughal vassal, it paid tribute to the Marathas, and came under British protection in 1818.

Kingdom of Mewar (Udaipur).text: The one great Rajput kingdom that long refused Mughal overlordship. Akbar took Chittor in 1568, and Maharana Pratap fought on after Haldighati (1576); the capital moved to Udaipur, founded in 1559, and his son Amar Singh I made peace in 1615.

Kingdom of Monaco.text: A tiny Mediterranean state on the French Riviera, ruled by the Grimaldi family since 1297. After 1815 it was placed under the protection of the Kingdom of Sardinia. Today it is a principality and the second-smallest country in the world.

Kingdom of Morgannwg.text: Morgannwg, once Glywysing, was a Welsh kingdom in the southeast, around today's Glamorgan. Norman knights conquered it in the late 11th century, but the area kept its Welsh name.

Kingdom of Mrauk U.text: A kingdom on the Arakan coast of western Myanmar, founded in 1429 and ruled from Mrauk U after a brief start at Launggyet. It grew rich on Bay of Bengal trade, took Chittagong, and lasted until Burma's king Bodawpaya conquered it in 1785.

Kingdom of Mysore.text: A kingdom in southern India ruled by the Wadiyar dynasty, a vassal of Vijayanagara until that empire's decline in the later 1500s. Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan dominated it from 1761 until Tipu died fighting the British at Srirangapatna in 1799.

Kingdom of Mysore (Srirangapatna).text: Mysore under the Wodeyars after they took Srirangapatna in 1610. Under Raja Wodeyar and Kanthirava Narasaraja I they expanded across the Kaveri country, turning a small principality into a regional kingdom.

Kingdom of Mysore (Wodeyar principality).text: The small Wodeyar principality around Mysore city in Karnataka, a feudatory of Vijayanagara. Its fortunes changed in 1610 when Raja Wodeyar took Srirangapatna from the Vijayanagara viceroy.

Kingdom of Mysore (restored Wodeyars).text: The Wodeyar kingdom of Mysore in southern India, restored in 1799 after Tipu Sultan's fall. The British put it back as a smaller, landlocked state under the child ruler Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, with Purnaiah as chief minister, and took over its administration in 1831.

Kingdom of Mysore under Chikka Devaraja.text: Mysore as expanded by Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar (1673-1704), who acquired Bangalore from the Mughals in the late 1680s and brought it close to its later core. From 1734 the Dalavayi brothers, and later Haidar Ali, ruled in the king's name.

Kingdom of Nagpur (Bhonsle).text: A Maratha kingdom of the Bhonsle family, centred on Nagpur in present-day Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh, 1818-53. It lost the Saugor and Narmada lands after the Third Anglo-Maratha War and was annexed by the British in 1853 when Raghoji III died without an heir.

Kingdom of Naples.text: The southern half of the Italian peninsula, ruled as a separate kingdom after the Sicilian Vespers revolt of 1282 sent the island of Sicily to a rival crown. Its kings came from Anjou and later Aragon, and it lasted formally until 1816.

Kingdom of Naples (Napoleonic).text: A French client kingdom in southern Italy from 1806 to 1815, set up after the Bourbon king of Naples sided against Napoleon. It was ruled first by Napoleon's brother Joseph and then by Joachim Murat.

Kingdom of Navarre.text: A kingdom centred on the largely Basque-speaking city of Pamplona and straddling the western Pyrenees, first called the Kingdom of Pamplona. After a union with Aragon ended in 1134 it had its own kings, then passed to the counts of Champagne and was joined to France in 1285-1328.

Kingdom of Ndongo.text: A Mbundu kingdom in the highlands of Angola between the Lukala and Kwanza rivers. Its ruler's title, ngola, gave Angola its name. After the Portuguese founded Luanda in 1576 it lost land and was left weakened.

Kingdom of Nepal (Thakuri dynasty).text: The Thakuri kings who followed the Licchavis in Nepal, c. 1000-1200, mostly around Nuwakot. Gunakama Deva is said to have founded Kantipur (Kathmandu). Some historians dispute the dynasty's existence; the Mallas followed.

Kingdom of Neustria.text: Neustria formed the western half of the Frankish realm, first stretching from the Loire to the Silva Carbonaria forest in northern France, with Paris, Orléans, Tours and Soissons among its cities. It often rivalled eastern Austrasia, and the Carolingian mayors eventually took control of it.

Kingdom of Northumbria.text: Northumbria was the Anglian kingdom stretching from the Humber into southern Scotland, formed by joining Bernicia and Deira. It had a golden age with Bede and the Lindisfarne Gospels, then was broken up by Viking raids and conquests from the late 8th and 9th centuries.

Kingdom of Norway.text: Norway left its union with Denmark in 1814, adopted its own liberal constitution, and was then forced into a looser union with Sweden under a shared king. It became fully independent in 1905 and is today a constitutional monarchy in northern Europe.

Kingdom of Numidia.text: A kingdom of the Numidian people in northwest Africa, in today's Algeria and Tunisia. Its famous kings were Masinissa, Rome's ally against Carthage, and Jugurtha, who fought Rome in the Jugurthine War. Rome annexed its eastern part after Caesar's victory at Thapsus in 46 BCE.

Kingdom of Osraige (Ossory).text: A small Irish kingdom between Leinster and Munster, in today's County Kilkenny, c. 800-1169. It was at its height under Cerball mac Dúnlainge in the 9th century and ended with the Anglo-Norman invasion of 1169.

Kingdom of Osroene.text: An Arab-ruled kingdom in Upper Mesopotamia, around Edessa in today's southeastern Turkey. A local dynasty, the Abgarids, ruled it, and Edessa became an early centre of Syriac Christianity. Rome deposed the Abgarids around 213 CE and made most of it a province.

Kingdom of Pajana.text: Almost certainly the Sultanate of Pajang in central Java, near today's Surakarta, drawn here from 1572 to 1587. Founded by Jaka Tingkir (Adiwijaya) as the successor of Demak, it gave way in the 1580s to Mataram, whose founder Sutawijaya seized the Pajang palace.

Kingdom of Pamplona.text: A Basque kingdom in the western Pyrenees, taking shape in the 820s under Íñigo Arista. It was the early form of the Kingdom of Navarre and held out between the Franks and the Muslims of al-Andalus.

Kingdom of Pergamon.text: A Greek kingdom of western Anatolia, ruled by the Attalid dynasty from the hilltop city of Pergamon. It was famous for its great library and the Pergamon Altar, and its last king, Attalus III, left it to Rome in his will in 133 BCE.

Kingdom of Pinya.text: A kingdom in central Burma that succeeded Myinsaing in 1313, ruled by Thihathu and his descendants. It was weakened when Sagaing broke away and by feuds among his sons, and after Shan raiders from Maw sacked it in 1364, Thado Minbya founded Ava in its place in 1365.

Kingdom of Polonnaruwa.text: A Sinhalese kingdom in Sri Lanka, ruled from Polonnaruwa, which spread across the island after the Cholas were driven out around 1070. Under Parakramabahu the Great it unified the island and fought campaigns in southern India and Burma.

Kingdom of Pontus.text: A Hellenistic kingdom on the south coast of the Black Sea, in northern Turkey, ruled by a dynasty of Persian descent from 281 BCE. Its greatest king, Mithridates VI, built a large empire and fought Rome in the long Mithridatic Wars, until Rome conquered Pontus in 63 BCE.

Kingdom of Powys.text: Powys was a Welsh kingdom in the east-central borderlands, from about the 5th century CE. Its early capital Pengwern may have been near Shrewsbury. English and Mercian pressure pushed its centre westward, and it split in 1160.
Kingdom of Powys.capital: Caer Guricon (Wroxeter); later Pengwern; later Mathrafal

Kingdom of Powys Fadog.text: The northern half of Powys, a Welsh kingdom, after it split in 1160. Its princes ruled from Castell Dinas Brân; Edward I of England's campaigns broke it in 1277, and the Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 abolished the last Welsh princely titles.

Kingdom of Powys Wenwynwyn.text: The southern part of the Welsh realm of Powys after its split in 1160, later named after its second prince, Gwenwynwyn. Often allied with England against rival Gwynedd, it lost its old royal seat at Mathrafal in 1212, and its last prince surrendered it to Edward I in 1283.

Kingdom of Rheged.text: Rheged was a Brittonic kingdom in northwest England and southern Scotland, centred perhaps on Carlisle by later legend. Its king Urien is praised in early Welsh poetry, and Northumbria annexed it before about 730.

Kingdom of Romania.text: A kingdom that began in 1881 under Carol I. After the First World War it gained Bessarabia, Bukovina, Banat and Transylvania, forming what was called Greater Romania. Its monarchy ended in 1947, when King Michael abdicated under communist pressure.

Kingdom of Rwanda.text: A Bantu kingdom in central Rwanda ruled by the Mwami, with early reigns dated from king-lists and uncertain. It grew to roughly modern Rwanda's size under Rwabugiri and became a German protectorate in 1897.

Kingdom of Sarawak.text: A kingdom on northwestern Borneo, founded in 1841 when the Englishman James Brooke was granted the territory by the rulers of Brunei. The Brooke family governed it as their own realm until 1946, when it was ceded to Britain as a Crown colony.

Kingdom of Saxony.text: A German kingdom from 1806, successor to the Electorate of Saxony, which joined the Confederation of the Rhine. It lost much of its land to Prussia in 1815 and lasted until 1918.

Kingdom of Scotland.text: The kingdom covering the northern third of Great Britain, traditionally founded in 843. It fought the Wars of Scottish Independence against England in the late 1200s and 1300s, and in 1603 its king, James VI, also inherited the English throne, joining the two crowns.

Kingdom of Seisyllwg.text: A small kingdom in west Wales, made of Ceredigion and the Tywi valley and said to be named after Seisyll, a king of the 7th or 8th century. In 920 Hywel Dda joined it with Dyfed to form the kingdom of Deheubarth.

Kingdom of Serbia.text: The Serbian state drawn here from c. 1188 for the medieval Nemanjić period, when it grew from a grand principality into a kingdom in 1217. The linked article covers the later modern kingdom, 1882-1918, with its capital at Belgrade.

Kingdom of Sicily.text: A kingdom of Sicily and southern Italy founded by Roger II in 1130 out of Norman conquests. It passed to Hohenstaufen and then Angevin rulers, until the Sicilian Vespers revolt of 1282 split the island, under Aragonese princes, from the mainland part ruled from Naples.

Kingdom of Sikkim.text: A Himalayan Buddhist kingdom ruled by the Chogyals, with early capitals at Yuksom and Rabdentse. Gorkha conquests in the 1770s-80s shrank it; Darjeeling was granted to the British in 1835. After Indian protection from 1950, it became a state of India in 1975.

Kingdom of Sindh (Chach dynasty).text: A kingdom in Sindh, now in Pakistan, c. 632-712 CE, ruled from Alor. Chach, a Brahmin who took the throne from the Rai dynasty, founded it; his son Dahir was killed when the Umayyad army of Muhammad ibn al-Qasim invaded in 712. The main source is the Chach Nama.

Kingdom of Sine.text: A Serer kingdom in Senegal ruled by the Maad a Sinig. It was part of the Jolof confederation until 1520, when it broke away and became independent, and it remained so until French colonial expansion ended its independence in the late 19th century.

Kingdom of Singapura.text: A small Malay kingdom on the island of Temasek, now Singapore, traditionally founded in 1299 by Sang Nila Utama. It is thought to have fallen between 1396 and 1398, but its story is known largely from later Malay tradition.

Kingdom of Sitawaka.text: A Sri Lankan kingdom carved out of Kotte in the partition of 1521, when Mayadunne took the Sitawaka share. It swallowed the Raigama kingdom in 1538 and became the main Sinhalese opponent of the Portuguese.

Kingdom of Sobrarbe.text: A legendary kingdom in the Pyrenees of northern Spain, said to have begun in 724 under García Ximénez and later called the first kingdom of Aragon. Historians do not treat it as real, so the dates drawn here, in the 820s, are loose.

Kingdom of Soissons.text: The Kingdom of Soissons was a Roman holdout in northern Gaul, led by Syagrius after the Western Empire fell. In 486 CE the Frankish king Clovis defeated him, marking an early step in the rise of the Frankish kingdom.

Kingdom of Sophene.text: A small Hellenistic-era kingdom between Armenia and Syria, in the upper Euphrates region of eastern Turkey, ruled by a branch of the Iranian Orontid dynasty. Tigranes the Great of Armenia conquered it around 95 BCE, after which it passed between Armenian, Cappadocian and Roman-backed rulers.

Kingdom of Sussex.text: Sussex, land of the South Saxons, was a small Anglo-Saxon realm on England's south coast, traditionally founded by Ælle around 477 CE. It was the last major kingdom to turn Christian, came under Mercian control by about 772, and was annexed by Wessex around 827.

Kingdom of Syrmia.text: A medieval territory between the Danube and Sava rivers, now split between Croatia and Serbia. From 1282 the Serbian king Stefan Dragutin ruled Syrmia, at first as a vassal of Hungary, and his son Vladislav II held it after him until he was defeated in 1324.

Kingdom of Syunik.text: An Armenian kingdom in southern Armenia, c. 987-1170, ruled from Kapan. The Seljuks took Kapan in 1104, and afterwards it was reduced to a few fortresses, such as Baghaberd, until 1170.

Kingdom of Tahiti.text: A Polynesian kingdom founded by Pōmare I, who united Tahiti, Moʻorea and nearby islands with British help and weapons. France made it a protectorate in 1842 and annexed it in 1880.

Kingdom of Thessalonica.text: A short-lived Crusader state in northern Greece set up in 1204 after the Fourth Crusade, a vassal of the Latin Empire. Its first king was Boniface of Montferrat, and it fell in 1224 to the Despotate of Epirus.

Kingdom of Thomond.text: Tuadmumu, the O'Brien kingdom of north Munster in Ireland, created with the 1118 partition of Munster. It held Clare, Limerick and north Tipperary until the Anglo-Normans took Limerick, then shrank to Clare and the lands west of the Shannon.

Kingdom of Thuringia.text: The Thuringian kingdom was a Germanic realm in central Germany, in the 5th and early 6th centuries CE, famed for its horses. The Franks conquered it in 531-532 after defeating King Herminafrid.

Kingdom of Travancore.text: A kingdom at India's south-western tip. After Marthanda Varma's conquests it reached roughly the extent it kept until 1949, ruled from Padmanabhapuram and from 1795 Thiruvananthapuram, and it accepted a subsidiary alliance with the East India Company.

Kingdom of Urartu.text: An Iron Age kingdom around Lake Van, in the Armenian highlands across eastern Turkey, Armenia and Iran. Known for fortresses, royal irrigation works and metalwork, and for fighting Assyria, it collapsed in the early sixth century BCE.

Kingdom of Vanand (Kars).text: A Bagratid Armenian kingdom around Kars in north-eastern Turkey, c. 963-1065, founded by Mushegh, brother of Ashot III of Ani. How independent it was from Ani is uncertain. Gagik-Abas ceded it to Byzantium in 1065.

Kingdom of Vaspurakan.text: A medieval Armenian kingdom around Lake Van, ruled by the Artsruni family. Its king Gagik I carried out building works on the island of Aghtamar in the lake, and its last king ceded the land to Byzantium in 1021.

Kingdom of Wessex.text: Wessex, the kingdom of the West Saxons, grew from a small southern realm to rule England. Alfred the Great held it against the Vikings, and his heirs united the English kingdom in the 10th century.

Kingdom of Westphalia.text: A French client kingdom in Germany ruled by Napoleon's brother Jérôme from 1807 to 1813, with only a loose link to the historic region of Westphalia. It fell after Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig.

Kingdom of Whydah.text: A Hueda kingdom on the coast of present-day Benin around Savi and Ouidah, the busiest slave port of the Bight of Benin c. 1700. It broke from Allada in the mid-17th century and fell to Dahomey in 1727.

Kingdom of Wogodogo (Mossi).text: The largest of the Mossi kingdoms, in present-day Burkina Faso, ruled by the Mogho Naba from Ouagadougou. Tradition places its founder Oubri in the 11th century, but the map follows the later dating of c. 1495. It lasted until French conquest in 1896.

Kingdom of Württemberg.text: A kingdom in southwestern Germany created in 1806 under Napoleon, now part of Baden-Württemberg. It joined the German Empire in 1871 and lasted until 1918.

Kingdom of Zamfara.text: A Hausa kingdom in north-western Nigeria between Kebbi, Gobir and Katsina. It was a tributary of Kebbi until it revolted c. 1715, lost its north and capital to Gobir c. 1756-62, and was absorbed by the Sokoto jihad c. 1805.

Kingdom of the Aurès.text: A Christian Berber kingdom in the Aurès mountains of Algeria, c. 484-703 CE, founded by Masties after revolts against the Vandals. Its last ruler, Queen Dihya (al-Kahina), resisted the Arabs until she was killed in 703.

Kingdom of the Gepids.text: The Gepids were a Germanic people who ruled the Carpathian basin around the Tisza and Danube after the Huns collapsed. In 567 CE the Lombards and Avars destroyed their kingdom, and the Avars took their land.

Kingdom of the Iberians.text: A medieval Georgian kingdom of the Bagrationi family, which emerged around 888 in Tao-Klarjeti, now mostly northeastern Turkey. It was an early step toward the later unified Kingdom of Georgia.

Kingdom of the Isles.text: A Norse-Gaelic sea kingdom of the Hebrides, the Isle of Man and nearby islands, from about 849 to 1265. Its kings controlled the Irish Sea lanes until Norway gave up the islands to Scotland in 1266.

Kingdom of the Suebi.text: The Suebi kingdom in northwest Spain, in Galicia and northern Portugal, began around 409 CE. It was one of the first Germanic realms in Iberia, and in 585 the Visigoths took it over.

Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.text: The largest state in Italy before unification, covering Sicily and all of southern Italy. It was formed in 1816 by merging the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily under a Bourbon king, and it fell in 1860 to Giuseppe Garibaldi's invasion.

Kiribati.text: A Pacific country of low coral atolls spread across a vast ocean area, formerly the Gilbert Islands. It became independent from Britain in 1979. It straddles both the equator and the International Date Line.

Kishangarh State.text: A Rajput princely state in Rajasthan founded in 1611 by Kishan Singh, a Jodhpur prince in Mughal service. It came under British protection on 26 March 1818. A rival line ruled from Rupnagar in 1756-81.

Kition.text: A Phoenician-influenced city-kingdom on Cyprus, c. 600-333 BCE, at today's Larnaca. Its kings, such as Baalmilk and Azbaal, ruled while it paid tribute to Assyria and Persia. Pumiathon was its last king.

Kizzuwatna.text: A kingdom on the Cilician plain of south-eastern Turkey, c. 1500-1400 BCE, independent between the Hittite Old and New Kingdoms. It switched sides between Hatti and Mitanni, then the Hittites absorbed it in the early 14th century BCE.

Knights Hospitaller.text: A Catholic military order that began as a hospital for pilgrims in Jerusalem. After losing the Holy Land it took Rhodes in 1310 and held it until 1522, then ruled Malta from 1530 until France seized the island in 1798.

Koch Bihar.text: The western half of the divided Koch kingdom, with Cooch Behar as its capital. It became a Mughal vassal in 1609 and was invaded in 1661-62. After a treaty of 1773 it was protected by the British East India Company.

Koch Hajo.text: The eastern half of the divided Koch kingdom, covering the north bank of the Brahmaputra up to the Bharali river, with Goalpara on the south bank. The Mughals conquered it in 1612-13.

Koch kingdom.text: The Koch kingdom of Assam and north Bengal, rebuilt by Biswa Singha from 1515 after the older Kamata kingdom collapsed. He founded the Koch royal line, and his son Nara Narayan took the kingdom to its greatest power.

Koch kingdom (Kamata).text: The Koch kingdom at its peak under King Nara Narayan and his general Chilarai, who made the Ahom, Manipur, Jaintia, Tripura and Kachari kingdoms pay tribute. It later split into the Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo branches.

Kolathunadu (Cannanore).text: A kingdom of north Malabar on the coast of Kerala, India, lying between the Chandragiri and Korapuzha rivers. Its rulers, the Kolathiri, held it from Ezhimala and later from Valapattanam, and it lasted well beyond the 16th century.

Kolhapur.text: A Maratha princely state of the Bhonsle line of Shivaji, the chief state of the Kolhapur and Southern Maratha Country agency, in Maharashtra. It acceded to India in 1947.

Kolli hills (Ori).text: A hill chiefdom in the Kolli Hills of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-170 CE, ruled by the chief Valvil Ori, a famous archer in Sangam poetry. Legend says it ended when Malaiyaman Kari killed Ori.

Kolli hills under the Cheras.text: The Kolli Hills of Tamil Nadu, drawn c. 170-300 CE under the Cheras, with the Chera ruler Perunjeral Irumporai said to have taken the hills after Ori's fall. The dates are approximate and rest on one scholar's chronology.

Kololo Kingdom.text: A kingdom on the upper Zambezi in present-day western Zambia, c. 1840-63. Sotho-speaking Kololo under Sebetwane conquered the Lozi and ruled from Linyanti, where David Livingstone visited them; the Lozi rose against them in 1864.

Kong Empire.text: A West African Dyula trading state, ruled by the Wattara family from Kong, in present-day Ivory Coast. Its power peaked under Seku Wattara, who extended it north; after he died in 1745 parts broke away, and Samori burned Kong in 1897.

Kongu Nadu (Kosar and local chiefs).text: A region of early Tamilakam in the upper Kaveri country, around today's Salem and Coimbatore, c. 300 BCE-150 CE, run by clans such as the Kosar. Kodumanal was a thriving industrial and trading centre here, but the map names no early dynasty.

Kongu under the Irumporai Cheras (Karuvu.text: Kongu country in western Tamil Nadu, drawn c. 150-300 CE under the Irumporai branch of the Cheras at Karur. The date follows one historian's chronology, and some inscriptions might put the change earlier.

Korean Empire.text: A Korean state proclaimed in 1897 by King Gojong, who took the title of emperor to show Korea's independence. It tried to modernise but lost its freedom to Japan, which annexed it in 1910.

Korean Jin.text: A confederation of small chiefdoms in the south of the Korean peninsula, south of the Han River, from about the 4th to 2nd centuries BCE. Its lands later split into the Samhan confederacies of Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan.

Kosovo.text: A small country in the Balkans, formerly a province of Serbia. NATO's 1999 air campaign ended Serbian control, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008. Many countries recognise it, but Serbia does not.

Kota State.text: A Rajput princely state in south-east Rajasthan. Once a Mughal vassal, it paid tribute to the Marathas, and its regent Zalim Singh ruled it for decades. It entered British protection by treaty in 1817-18.

Kotah (with Jhalawar).text: The princely state of Kotah in Rajasthan together with Jhalawar, which was carved out of it in 1838; the two formed the Kotah and Jhalawar Agency under the British. Both acceded to India in 1947.

Kourion.text: A city-kingdom on the south-west coast of Cyprus, c. 600-312 BCE. It kept its own kings, such as Stasanor and Pasicrates, while paying tribute to Assyria and then Persia. Its ruins are a major archaeological site.

Kuba Kingdom.text: A kingdom of the Kuba (Bushoong) in central DR Congo between the Sankuru, Lulua and Kasai rivers, united c. 1625 by Shyaam. It is famed for its court art and textiles. The kingdom still exists today under a king, the nyim.

Kutai Kingdom.text: The Muslim sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara on the Mahakam River in East Kalimantan, Borneo, Indonesia, which took over the older Hindu kingdom of Kutai Martadipura in 1635. The region's stone pillars with Sanskrit inscriptions, from the late 300s, are among the oldest in Indonesia.

Kutch (Samma-Jadeja chiefs).text: Kutch, in Gujarat, India, was held by Samma chiefs, later called Jadejas, from the 12th century. It was divided among branches until Khengarji I united it in 1549 and later moved the capital to Bhuj.

Kuttanad (attribution unknown).text: A backwater coastal region of Kerala south of the old port of Muziris, drawn c. 300 BCE-0 CE. Later tradition ties Kuttanad to early Chera kings such as Uthiyan Cheralathan, but the map leaves its rulers unattributed.

Kuttanad in the country of the Aioi.text: The Kuttanad coast of Kerala, drawn c. 100-300 CE under the Ay chiefs, whom Ptolemy calls the Aioi. The change from earlier maps may be real or may simply reflect a different source.

Kuwait.text: A small emirate at the northern tip of the Persian Gulf, ruled by the Al Sabah family since the 1750s. It gained independence from Britain in 1961, was invaded by Iraq in 1990, and was liberated in 1991.

Kyrgyzstan.text: A mountainous country in Central Asia, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. Traditionally its people were nomadic herders, and the epic of Manas is central to their culture.

Kénédougou Kingdom.text: A kingdom of the Senufo and Dyula people of the Traoré dynasty around Sikasso, in present-day Mali and Burkina Faso. It grew large from the 1820s, held out against Samori's siege of Sikasso in 1887-88, and fell to the French in 1898.

Lakhmid Kingdom.text: The Lakhmids were an Arab kingdom on the desert edge of southern Iraq, from about 268 to 602 CE. They guarded the Persian Sasanian frontier against other Arabs and Byzantium, and their court at al-Hira was a centre of poetry.

Lan Na.text: A Thai kingdom in the north of present-day Thailand, founded in the late 1200s with its centre at Chiang Mai. It was a rich Buddhist realm, but was under Burmese control for much of the time shown here, until the 1770s.

Lan Na Kingdom.text: A kingdom in what is now northern Thailand, founded in the late 1200s by King Mangrai. Its name means a million rice fields. It fought Ayutthaya as an equal in the 1400s, later weakened and fell under Burmese rule in 1558.

Lan Xang.text: The Lao kingdom of the million elephants, founded in 1353 by Fa Ngum. It was among the largest states in Southeast Asia, and its capital moved from Luang Prabang to Vientiane in 1560. In 1707 it split into two kingdoms, Luang Prabang and Vientiane, and Champasak broke away in 1713.

Land Chenla.text: Land Chenla, the northern half of Chenla, is the name Chinese records give to part of early Khmer Cambodia after the country split soon after 706 CE. While southern Water Chenla fell under Javanese power, Land Chenla held together, and under Jayavarman II it grew into the Khmer Empire, proclaimed in 802.

Landgraviate of Hesse.text: A landgraviate in central Germany, independent from 1264 under Henry the Child, with Marburg and Kassel. It gained Katzenelnbogen in 1479, and Philip the Magnanimous became a leader of German Protestants.

Langah Sultanate.text: A sultanate of the lower Punjab around Multan and Uch, in present-day Pakistan, founded, according to Firishta, by Rai Sahra and ruled by the Langah family. The Arghuns annexed it in 1528.

Laomedon.text: The territory held by Laomedon of Mytilene, one of Alexander the Great's generals, who received Syria when the empire was divided at Babylon in 323 BCE. Ptolemy of Egypt, who wanted Syria, soon sent an army and took it from him.

Laos.text: A landlocked country in Southeast Asia, run as a one-party communist state since 1975. The Mekong River runs along much of its western border. It was heavily bombed during the Vietnam War era.

Lapathus.text: A city-kingdom on the north coast of Cyprus, c. 600-312 BCE, at Lapethos. It kept its own kings, such as Praxippus, while paying tribute to Assyria and Persia, until the Ptolemaic takeover of Cyprus.

Later Gupta kingdom of Magadha.text: A dynasty that ruled Magadha in southern Bihar, and at times Malwa, from the 6th to 8th centuries, drawn here c. 647-750. It was subordinate to Harsha under Madhavagupta and independent under Adityasena.

Later Liang.text: Later Liang was a Sixteen Kingdoms state in Gansu, founded in 386 CE by Lü Guang, a general of Former Qin. It was ruled by the Di Lü family and ended in 403 when Later Qin forced its surrender.

Later Qin.text: Later Qin was a state founded in 384 CE by Yao Chang of the Qiang people, with its capital at Chang'an. It hosted the Buddhist translator Kumarajiva, then was conquered in 417 by the Eastern Jin general Liu Yu.

Later Western Liang.text: The Later Western Liang was a small Chinese state in the middle Yangtze, founded in 555 CE by Xiao Cha as a client of Northern Zhou and its successor Sui. It lasted until Sui took it over in 587.

Later Yan.text: Later Yan was a Xianbei state founded in 384 CE by Murong Chui, who revived the fallen Former Yan. It ruled much of northeast China until about 409, when the general Feng Ba's family took power.

Later Zhao.text: Later Zhao was a state in northern China started by the general Shi Le, a Jie leader, in 319 CE. It briefly dominated the north but declined into bloodshed after the brutal rule of Shi Hu, ending around 351.

Later Zhou.text: The last of the Five Dynasties in northern China, 951-960, founded by the general Guo Wei. Its second emperor, Chai Rong, was an able reformer; after his death the general Zhao Kuangyin took the throne and founded the Song dynasty.

Latin Empire.text: A Crusader state set up in 1204 when the leaders of the Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople. It was meant to replace the Byzantine Empire, but it survived only until 1261, when the Nicaean forces of Michael VIII Palaiologos retook the city.

Lavo Kingdom.text: Lavo was a Mon-Khmer realm of the lower Chao Phraya basin in central Thailand, centred on Lavapura, today's Lopburi. It was influenced by Dvaravati and later by the Khmer, and it eventually folded into Ayutthaya.

Lazica.text: A kingdom on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, in today's western Georgia, which rose after Colchis broke up. It was fought over by Byzantium and Persia, and in the Lazic War of 541-562 it sided with the Byzantines.

League of Lezhë.text: An alliance of Albanian lords formed at Lezhë on 2 March 1444 under Skanderbeg. Skanderbeg led it against the Ottomans, holding Krujë, until his death in 1468, though the alliance was fragile and began to fragment soon after it formed.

Lebanon.text: A small country on the eastern Mediterranean, with a mix of Christian and Muslim communities. It became independent from France in the 1940s, and a civil war lasted from 1975 to 1990. Its capital is Beirut.
