Leeward Society Islands chiefdoms.text: The island chiefdoms of the Leeward group of the Society Islands in Polynesia, including Raiatea, Tahaa, Huahine and Bora Bora. Captain James Cook first used the name Society Islands for this group, and the islands came under French rule in the late 1800s.

Lesotho.text: A mountain kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, independent from Britain in 1966 as the former Basutoland. It was founded in the 1820s by King Moshoeshoe I, who gathered peoples to defend themselves.

Li Zicheng.text: The area held by the rebel leader Li Zicheng, who helped topple the Ming dynasty in 1644 by taking Beijing. He proclaimed himself emperor of a short-lived Shun dynasty, but was driven out within weeks and died the next year.

Liaodong.text: A short-lived kingdom around the Liao River in northeastern China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu as the Qin dynasty collapsed in 206 BCE. Rival kingdoms soon absorbed it.

Libyan Arab Republic.text: Libya after 1 September 1969, when young army officers led by Muammar Gaddafi overthrew King Idris in a bloodless coup. Gaddafi used oil wealth to rule for over forty years and clashed often with the West.

Licchavi kingdom of Nepal.text: The Licchavi kingdom of the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, c. 400-879 CE, known from inscriptions; its best-remembered kings include Manadeva and Amshuverma. Tibet claimed overlordship in the mid-7th century, and the Thakuris followed.

Ligurian Republic.text: A French client republic created in 1797 that replaced the old Republic of Genoa. Napoleon controlled it, and he annexed it to France in 1805.

Limmu-Ennarea.text: An Oromo kingdom of the Gibe region in south-west Ethiopia, c. 1801-1891, on the old lands of Ennarea. It was the leading Gibe state under Abba Bagibo and was conquered by Shewa in 1891.

Linjiang.text: A short-lived kingdom in the middle Yangtze region of China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms set up by Xiang Yu as the Qin empire broke up in 206 BCE. It was swallowed up in the Chu-Han civil war.

Livonian Brothers of the Sword.text: A Catholic order of German crusading knights founded in 1202 by Bishop Albert of Riga to conquer Livonia, today Latvia and Estonia. After a crushing defeat by Samogitians and Semigallians at Saule in 1236, its survivors were taken into the Teutonic Order.

Livonian Conference.text: The loose confederation of Old Livonia, in today's Latvia and Estonia, made up of the Livonian Order of knights and several bishops' lands. Its states met in a shared diet from 1419 and formally united in 1435. The union ended in the Livonian War, around 1561.

Lohara Dynasty.text: A Hindu dynasty of Kashmir, founded in 1003 when Samgramaraja inherited the throne from Queen Didda; its main line ruled until about 1175. In its time the chronicler Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini, an early history of Kashmir.

Lombards.text: The Lombards were a Germanic people who settled on the middle Danube, in today's Austria, in the late 400s, and later moved into Pannonia in Hungary. After destroying the Gepid kingdom in 567, King Alboin led them into Italy in 568; Pavia became their capital in 572, and Lombardy still carries their name.

Lordship of Ferrara (Este).text: The early Este state around Ferrara in northern Italy, a papal fief whose ruler Obizzo II was acclaimed lord for life in 1264. Modena was added in 1288, and Ferrara became a duchy in 1471.

Lordship of Mantua.text: The Gonzaga state of Mantua in northern Italy, a lordship from Luigi Gonzaga's coup of 1328. It became a marquisate in 1433 and a duchy in 1530.

Lordship, later Principality of Piombino.text: A small coastal state in Tuscany, Italy, including part of the island of Elba, founded when Gherardo Appiani sold Pisa to the Visconti in 1399 and kept Piombino. It became a principality in 1594; Napoleonic France annexed it and gave it to Elisa Bonaparte in 1805.

Los Altos.text: A short-lived state in the western highlands of Guatemala, which also took in Soconusco, now in Mexico. It joined the Central American federation in 1838, was crushed by Guatemala in 1840, and briefly broke away again in 1848 to 1849.

Lower Burgundy.text: A Frankish kingdom of southeast France, formed in 879 when Count Boso of Vienne had himself crowned king. It combined Provence and the Rhône valley and was merged with Upper Burgundy in 933.

Lozi Kingdom (Barotseland).text: A kingdom of the Lozi people on the Barotse floodplain of the upper Zambezi, ruled by the Litunga. A rising in 1864 restored the kingdom, and Lewanika's agreements brought it under the British South Africa Company by 1899.

Lu.text: A Zhou-dynasty state in southwestern Shandong, founded by the Duke of Zhou's son Boqin, and the birthplace of Confucius. It was famous as a keeper of ritual and learning, and Chu conquered it around 249 BCE.

Luba Empire.text: A central African state of the Mulopwe kings in the Upemba depression and the Lomami and Lualaba country, in southern DR Congo. Its dates come from oral tradition. It grew greatly 1700-1860 and split in two in 1889.

Lucayan chiefdoms.text: The Lucayans were the Taíno-speaking people of the Bahamas, living in villages under local chiefs. They met Columbus in 1492, and within about thirty years nearly all had died or been taken away by the Spanish.

Lucayan chiefdoms (Turks and Caicos).text: The Lucayans, a branch of the Taíno peoples, lived on the Turks and Caicos Islands as well as the Bahamas, fishing and farming under local chiefs. The Turks and Caicos were resettled from Hispaniola around 1200. After Spanish contact in 1492, slave raids and disease emptied the islands by c. 1520.

Lunda Empire.text: A commonwealth in southern Katanga ruled by the Mwaant Yaav from Musumba, controlling some 150,000 square km by 1680. At its height it reached from the Kwango to the Lualaba, until Chokwe invaders sacked Musumba in 1887.

Luxembourg.text: A small landlocked grand duchy between Belgium, France and Germany. Restored after Napoleon's defeat in 1815, it won full independence in 1867 following the Luxembourg Crisis. Its capital, Luxembourg City, is one of the seats of the European Union.

Lydia.text: A rich Iron Age kingdom in western Anatolia, in today's Turkey, with Sardis as its capital. Its people made some of the world's first coins from gold, and its last king Croesus was defeated by Persia's Cyrus around 546 BCE.

Madagascar.text: A large island nation in the Indian Ocean off southeast Africa, independent from France since 26 June 1960. Its wildlife, such as lemurs, is found almost nowhere else on Earth. Most of its people speak Malagasy.

Madurai Sultanate (Ma'bar).text: A sultanate in Tamil Nadu, India, proclaimed in 1335 when Delhi's governor Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughluq. It ruled Madurai and parts of the old Pandya country, and Ibn Battuta visited in 1344.

Magadha - Haryanka dynasty.text: The ruling dynasty of Magadha in the Ganges plain, c. 544-413 BCE according to Buddhist tradition, though some scholars date it later. Bimbisara and his son Ajatashatru expanded the kingdom, and the capital moved from Rajagriha to Pataliputra.

Magadha - Shaishunaga dynasty.text: The ruling dynasty of Magadha after the Haryankas, c. 413-345 BCE in the traditional count. Its founder Shishunaga ruled from Rajagriha, with Vaishali as a second capital, and the dynasty was followed by the Nandas.

Magna Frisia.text: Magna Frisia, or the Frisian Kingdom, is a modern term for the Frisians' realm along the North Sea coast in the 7th and 8th centuries CE. Its kings Aldgisl, Redbad and Poppo resisted the Franks, who beat them at the Boarn in 734.

Mahajanapadas.text: The last of the great realms of northern India in the mid-fifth century BCE, as kingdoms such as Magadha grew and swallowed their neighbours. The earlier sixteen kingdoms and republics were slowly merging into fewer, larger states.

Mahan.text: The largest of the Samhan, three loose chiefdom confederations of southern Korea, covering the southwest and west-center of the peninsula. It had dozens of small states, and the kingdom of Baekje grew out of one of them.

Mahdids.text: A short-lived dynasty in Yemen, c. 1159-1174, that took the western Tihama coast from the Najahids. They were overthrown by the Ayyubids, who sent armies from Egypt.

Mahra Sultanate.text: A sultanate in eastern Yemen led by the Banu Afrar clan, ruling from Qishn, and also holding the island of Socotra from the 16th century. It accepted British protection in 1886 and lasted as a state until 1967.

Mahra Sultanate (Socotra).text: The island of Socotra as part of the Mahra Sultanate, whose Banu Afrar rulers held it from the 16th century after the Portuguese left. The island's main town was Hadibu, and the whole sultanate accepted British protection in 1886.

Maitraka Dynasty.text: The Maitrakas ruled the kingdom of Valabhi in Gujarat, western India, from about 475 CE until the late 700s. Their founder Bhatarka had been a Gupta governor, and their capital Vallabhi had a famous seat of learning compared with Nalanda. Arab sea raids weakened them, but how the dynasty ended is unknown.

Majeerteen Sultanate.text: A Somali kingdom in the far northeast of the Horn of Africa, roughly today's Puntland, with a strong trading network. It peaked in the 19th century under Boqor (King) Osman Mahamuud, became an Italian protectorate in 1889, and was absorbed into Italian Somaliland after a war in the 1920s.

Makuria.text: Makuria was a Christian kingdom in northern Sudan and southern Egypt. After beating back an Arab siege of Dongola in 652, it signed the Baqt treaty, which kept peace with Egypt for centuries. Mamluk attacks, civil war and Bedouin raids wore it down, and it probably collapsed in the late 1400s.

Makuria Kingdom.text: A Christian Nubian kingdom on the Nile, in today's northern Sudan and southern Egypt, whose old capital was Dongola. After a civil war in 1365 it shrank to a rump state that lost Dongola; its last recorded king lived about 1460, and it probably collapsed soon after.

Malaiyaman Nadu (Kari of Kovalur).text: A chiefdom in the middle Pennai valley of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, ruled from Kovalur by the Malaiyaman chiefs such as Tirumudi Kari. Sangam poets praised Kari for his generosity; Cholas and Adiyamans fought him.

Malawi.text: A long, narrow landlocked country in southeast Africa, independent from Britain in 1964 as the former Nyasaland. Much of its eastern border is formed by Lake Malawi. Hastings Banda ruled it as a one-party state for three decades.

Malaya.text: The Malay Peninsula and nearby islands. On this map the label covers the region around 1294 to 1351, a time of small Malay trading states before bigger sultanates arose. The modern country called Malaya existed only from 1948 to 1963, then merged into Malaysia.

Malaysia.text: A Southeast Asian country formed on 16 September 1963 by joining Malaya with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak. Singapore left in 1965. It lies partly on the Malay Peninsula and partly on the island of Borneo.

Maldive kingdom (Buddhist period).text: The early kingdom of the Maldives, a chain of coral atolls in the Indian Ocean, when its people were Buddhist. This lasted until the king converted to Islam in about 1153, after which the islands became a sultanate.

Maldives.text: A chain of low coral islands in the Indian Ocean southwest of India, independent from Britain in 1965. It was a sultanate for centuries and became a republic in 1968. It is the lowest-lying country on Earth.

Mali Federation.text: A short-lived union of Senegal and the Sudanese Republic (now Mali), two former French colonies, which became independent together in June 1960. It broke apart within two months over political disputes, and the two halves became separate countries.

Malta.text: A tiny island nation in the central Mediterranean, independent from Britain in 1964. Its harbours made it a vital naval base, and it was bombed heavily in World War II. It became a republic in 1974 and joined the EU in 2004.

Malwa Sultanate.text: A sultanate of central India ruled from Mandu. Humayun held it briefly in 1535-36; in 1537 Qadir Shah, a former Khalji officer, regained part of it, until Sher Shah Suri conquered it in 1542.

Mamertines.text: A band of mercenaries from Campania who seized the Sicilian city of Messina around 288 BCE and ruled it as their own. When Syracuse threatened them, they asked Rome for help in 264 BCE, which began the First Punic War.

Mamluk dynasty of Iraq.text: A line of mamluk pashas of Baghdad, of Georgian origin,, from Hasan Pasha in 1704, who governed Baghdad and Basra with near-complete autonomy under the Ottoman sultan. The Ottomans reconquered it in 1831, ending the dynasty under Dawud Pasha.

Manipur.text: A hill kingdom on the Burma frontier in north-east India, with its capital at Imphal. It acceded to India on 11 August 1947 and is now the state of Manipur.

Manipur (Kangleipak).text: The Meitei kingdom of the Imphal valley in north-east India, with its capital at Kangla, dated from 1110. It later continued as a princely state.

Mannaea.text: A kingdom south of Lake Urmia in north-western Iran, c. 850-616 BCE. It sat as a buffer between Urartu and Assyria, and the Medes absorbed it after 616 BCE. Its kings include Iranzu and Ullusunu.

Maravi.text: A Chewa confederacy of the Kalonga in central and southern Malawi. Kalonga Muzura defeated the rival Lundu in 1622, and Maravi forces reached the Zambezi and the coast. In the 18th century it split into chiefdoms.

Margraviate of Baden.text: A small German state in the Holy Roman Empire, around Karlsruhe in present-day Baden-Württemberg. This map phase shows it from 1772, after Charles Frederick reunited its two Baden lines in 1771, until 1802; he became an elector in 1803 and later a grand duke.

Margraviate of Baden-Baden.text: The Catholic half of Baden after the family's division in 1535, on the Rhine plain and in the northern Black Forest. Its seat was Baden-Baden, then Rastatt from 1705, and it passed to Baden-Durlach in 1771 when its line died out.

Margraviate of Baden-Durlach.text: The Protestant half of Baden after the 1535 split, with lands around Pforzheim and Durlach and in the Breisgau. Its capital moved to Durlach in 1565 and to the new city of Karlsruhe in 1718. It merged with Baden-Baden in 1771.

Margraviate of Brandenburg.text: An important imperial principality founded in 1157, centred on Brandenburg an der Havel and later Berlin. Poor and sandy at first, it became an electorate and the core of Prussia.
Margraviate of Brandenburg.capital: Brandenburg an der Havel; later Berlin

Margraviate of Meissen.text: A march on the middle Elbe in eastern Germany held by the House of Wettin from 1089. Silver found at Freiberg in 1168 made it rich, and Henry the Illustrious added Thuringia in 1247. Its Wettin rulers got the Saxon electorate in 1423, after which their lands were called Saxony.

Margraviate of Moravia.text: A land in today's eastern Czech Republic, held within the Bohemian crown and the Holy Roman Empire from 1182. In this period it was governed by margraves from the Luxembourg family, and it remained part of Bohemia's crown lands until 1918.

Mari (Lim dynasty).text: An Amorite kingdom on the middle Euphrates in eastern Syria, c. 1830-1761 BCE, ruled by the Lim dynasty. It is famed for its huge palace of Zimri-Lim and thousands of letters; Hammurabi of Babylon conquered it in 1761 BCE.

Marinid Sultanate.text: A Berber Zenata dynasty that ruled most of Morocco and at times parts of Algeria and southern Spain, from the mid 1200s to the 1400s. It governed from Fez and was known for its madrasas.

Marion.text: A city-kingdom on the north-west coast of Cyprus, c. 600-312 BCE, at today's Polis Chrysochous. It kept its own kings, such as Stasioikos II, while paying tribute to Assyria and Persia, until the Ptolemaic takeover of Cyprus.

Marquesan chiefdoms.text: The island chiefdoms of the Marquesas, in today's French Polynesia, first settled by Polynesian voyagers around the 10th century. Rival tribes often fought one another, and their carvers were famed for wooden ancestor figures; France claimed the islands in 1842.

Marquisate of Mantua.text: The Gonzaga state of Mantua in northern Italy as a marquisate from 1433 to 1530, before becoming a duchy. Federico II was its last marquis and first duke.

Marshall Islands.text: A Pacific country of coral atolls, administered by the United States after World War II. It gained self-government in free association with the US in 1986. The US tested nuclear bombs at Bikini and Enewetak atolls.

Marshallese chiefdoms.text: The Marshall Islands were settled by seafarers thousands of years ago, who built great sailing canoes and stick charts for navigation. Atolls were ruled by chiefs (iroij) until Germany took over the islands in 1885.

Marwanids.text: A Kurdish dynasty of Diyar Bakr in south-eastern Turkey, c. 990-1085, centred on Mayyafariqin and Amid (Diyarbakir). It held Ahlat and Manzikert for much of the time, and the Seljuks ended it in 1085.

Massina Empire.text: A Muslim state in the Inner Niger Delta of present-day Mali, founded around 1818 by the Fulani preacher Seku Amadu after he defeated the Bambara. It was ruled by religious law from its capital Hamdullahi until Omar Tall's forces destroyed it in 1862.

Mataram Kingdom.text: A Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Java, c. 716 to 1016, first in Central Java and later in the east. Its rulers built great monuments such as Borobudur and Prambanan, and the court later moved eastward to East Java.

Mataram Sultanate.text: A Javanese sultanate that became one of the strongest states in the Indonesian islands under Sultan Agung (r. 1613-1645). After revolts in the late 1600s it relied on Dutch East India Company help, and in 1755 it was divided into the courts of Surakarta and Yogyakarta.

Maukhari Dynasty.text: The Maukharis ruled from Kannauj in northern India after the Gupta empire declined, around 510 to 606 CE. They fought the Later Guptas and Hunas, and Harsha later made Kannauj his capital.

Mauretania.text: A kingdom of the Moors in northwest Africa, in what is now Morocco and western Algeria. Its king Juba II, raised in Rome, was a scholar who ruled as a Roman ally. Rome annexed the kingdom around 42-44 CE after King Ptolemy was killed.

Mauritania.text: A vast, mostly desert country in northwest Africa, independent from France in 1960. About 90 percent of it is Sahara, and its people include Arab-Berber and sub-Saharan groups. Its capital is Nouakchott, on the Atlantic coast.

Mauritius.text: A volcanic island nation in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar. It had no settled population until Europeans arrived, was ruled by the Dutch, French and British, and became independent in 1968. It was the only known home of the extinct dodo.

Mauro-Roman Kingdom.text: A Berber-Roman kingdom in western Mauretania, in modern Algeria, c. 430-578 CE. An inscription of 508 at Altava names Masuna as king of the Moors and Romans. Some historians count the military leader Garmul, killed by the Byzantines in 578, as a later king.

Maynila.text: A Tagalog city-state on the south bank of the Pasig River, where Intramuros stands in today's Manila, Philippines. It was a busy trading town ruled by rajas, and it ended when the Spanish took it in 1571 and made it their colonial capital.

Mayurbhanj.text: The largest of the Orissa feudatory princely states, in present-day Odisha, ruled from Baripada. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Mazyadid dynasty (Banu Mazyad).text: An Arab emirate of the Banu Asad between Kufa and Hit in Iraq, c. 961-1150, under first the Buyids and then the Seljuks. Al-Hilla, which began as their camp, became its capital; Sadaqa I (1086-1108) was its strongest ruler.

Menabe.text: The first Sakalava kingdom, on Madagascar's west coast, ruled by the Maroseraña dynasty, and rose under Andriandahifotsy in the 17th century. Radama I of Imerina ravaged it in 1820-22 and Merina forces later took its southern lands.

Mengujekids.text: A Turkish beylik (small emirate) in eastern Anatolia, in present-day Turkey, ruling Erzincan, Kemah, Divriği and Şebinkarahisar from c. 1072. The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum annexed the Erzincan line in 1228, while the Divriği branch lasted to 1277 as a vassal.

Mentawai peoples.text: The people of the Mentawai Islands, off the west coast of Sumatra in Indonesia. They lived in longhouses called uma, mostly by hunting and gathering, and are known for full-body tattoos that mark a person's role and status.

Mi'kmaq people.text: An Indigenous people of eastern Canada and Maine, whose homeland is Mi'kma'ki, including Nova Scotia. They hunted, fished and travelled the coast by canoe, and were among the first to trade with Europeans.

Michoacán.text: The homeland of the Purépecha (Tarascans) in western Mexico. Their state took shape around Lake Pátzcuaro from the 1200s and grew into an empire centred at Tzintzuntzan that rivalled the Aztecs. Its ruler Tanganxoan II submitted to the Spanish in the 1520s, and Michoacán is now a Mexican state.

Micronesia.text: The Federated States of Micronesia, a Pacific nation of four states (Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae) spread over hundreds of islands. It entered free association with the United States in 1986 and has been fully independent since 1990.

Min.text: A kingdom in Fujian, southeast China, one of the Ten Kingdoms in the years between the Tang and the Song. Founded by the Wang family, it was ended by the Southern Tang in 945.

Minaeans.text: A trading kingdom of South Arabia in the Jawf valley of today's Yemen, built around the towns of Qarnawu and Baraqish. The Minaeans worshipped their national god Wadd and ran caravan trade across Arabia and beyond; when and how their kingdom ended is still debated.

Minyue.text: A kingdom in what is now Fujian in southeast China, founded by members of the Yue royal family and lasting from about 306 to 110 BCE beside the Han empire. After its king turned against the Han, Han armies conquered it and moved its people north to the Yangtze region.

Mirdasid dynasty.text: An Arab dynasty of the Banu Kilab ruling the emirate of Aleppo in Syria, c. 1024-1080 on this map. Salih ibn Mirdas founded it, and the dynasty held Aleppo more or less continuously until 1080; some dates for its start are earlier, from 1014.

Mitanni.text: A Hurrian-speaking kingdom across northern Syria and southeastern Anatolia, c. 1550-1260 BCE, that was a great power and rival of Egypt and the Hittites. Its ruling class bore Indo-Aryan names, and Assyria finally swallowed it.

Moab.text: An Iron Age kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, in modern Jordan, c. 900-582 BCE. King Mesha's famous stone inscription records his revolt against Israel. It paid tribute to Assyria and later fell to Babylon.

Molossians.text: A Greek tribe of Epirus, in northwest Greece and southern Albania, whose most famous king was Pyrrhus of the costly victories. After they backed Macedon in its third war with Rome, the Romans reportedly enslaved some 150,000 Epirotes, mostly Molossians.

Montenegro.text: A small Balkan country whose mountain clans kept a large degree of self-rule under the Ottomans. Ruled by the Petrović-Njegoš family first as a church state and then as a secular principality, it won recognition in 1878, became a kingdom in 1910, and regained full independence in 2006.

Moriori people.text: The Polynesian people of the Chatham Islands, east of New Zealand. Their law of Nunuku, a tradition of settling disputes without killing, was a notable feature of their society, and in 1835 Māori invaders from mainland New Zealand devastated their community.

Mosquito Kingdom.text: A kingdom of the Miskito people on the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and Honduras, long under British protection. A treaty in 1860 gave the land to Nicaragua with local self-rule, and it was fully absorbed in 1894.

Mozambique.text: A country on the southeast coast of Africa, independent from Portugal in 1975 after a ten-year liberation war led by Frelimo. A destructive civil war followed from 1977 until 1992.

Mthethwa Paramountcy.text: A paramountcy of Nguni chiefdoms in what is now KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, c. 1780-1817. Dingiswayo turned it into a confederacy around 1811, including the then minor Zulu; after he died fighting the Ndwandwe, Shaka folded it into the Zulu kingdom.

Mthwakazi (Ndebele kingdom).text: The Ndebele kingdom in present-day Zimbabwe, 1840-93. Mzilikazi's Northern Ndebele settled between the Sanyati and Limpopo rivers after leaving the Transvaal and raided the Shona; the British South Africa Company invaded it in November 1893.

Mujahideen.text: The Afghan guerrilla groups that fought the Soviet army and its Afghan government from 1979 to 1989. Backed by Pakistan, the US and others, they saw the Soviets withdraw in 1989. After the government fell in 1992, the factions fought each other.

Musunuri Nayakas.text: Telugu chiefs who drove Tughluq forces out of Warangal c. 1336 and ruled Telangana, India. Kapaya later ceded Golconda to the Bahmanis and was overthrown by the Recherla Nayakas in 1368.

Muzaffarids.text: A dynasty that ruled central and southwestern Iran until 1393, when Timur destroyed their power. They rose as the Mongol Ilkhanate fell apart, and their court at Shiraz was the home of the poet Hafez.

Mycenaean Greece.text: The first advanced Greek civilization, in the Late Bronze Age, made of palace-states such as Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns, which kept records in the Linear B script. Its palaces were destroyed or abandoned in waves from about 1250 BCE, and the civilization had faded by c. 1050 BCE.

Myinsaing Kingdom.text: A central Burmese kingdom run by three brothers, Athinkhaya, Yazathingyan and Thihathu, who took power as the Pagan Empire fell apart. It beat back a Mongol army in 1300 to 1301 and ended in 1313, when Thihathu founded a new capital at Pinya.

Mysore.text: The princely state of Mysore in southern India, ruled again by the Wodeyar dynasty after the 1881 handback by the British. It was one of the largest states in the south and joined the Indian Union on 9 August 1947.

Mysore (under British commission).text: Mysore while the British ran it directly, 1831-81, with a commission seated at Bangalore. The state kept its identity and was handed back in 1881 to Chamarajendra Wadiyar X.

Mysore under Hyder Ali (with Bednur).text: Mysore in c. 1763-65, when Hyder Ali, the general who had made himself real ruler while the Wodeyar king was only a figurehead, seized Bednur, the Keladi kingdom, in 1763. It lay in the south Indian state of Karnataka.

Mysore under Hyder Ali (with Malabar).text: Mysore in c. 1766-75, a sultanate in southern India run by Hyder Ali while a Wodeyar king was still the nominal head. In these years he conquered Malabar on the west coast and Coorg, and held lands in Tamil Nadu such as Dindigul.

Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan.text: Mysore at its greatest, 1776-91, under Hyder Ali and then his son Tipu Sultan. A sultanate in southern India, it grew by taking Bellary, Gooty, Chitradurga and Cuddapah in the 1770s and fought several wars against the British and their allies.

Mysore under Tipu Sultan after the Treat.text: Mysore under Tipu Sultan after 1792, when the Treaty of Seringapatam stripped him of half his land. Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul and Salem went to the East India Company and other lands to its allies. The shrunken sultanate survived until his death in 1799.

Nabataeans.text: An Arab people of the southern Levant and northern Arabia whose kingdom grew rich from a far-reaching trade network, centred on the city of Petra in today's Jordan. The emperor Trajan annexed their kingdom in 106 CE and made it the Roman province of Arabia.

Nabhani Dynasty.text: An Arab royal house of the Azd tribe that ruled Oman as hereditary kings from 1154, when the Seljuks were expelled, until the Yaruba took over in 1624. They governed from interior strongholds such as Nizwa and Bahla, leaving the elected Ibadi imams a mainly religious role.

Najahid Dynasty.text: A Sunni dynasty of former Ethiopian slave-soldiers who ruled part of western Yemen from 1022 to 1158 from Zabid. They fought their Shi'a Ismaili neighbours, the Sulayhids, and their last ruler was killed in 1158.

Nakhichevan Khanate.text: A khanate based at Nakhchivan in the south Caucasus, self-governing after Nader Shah's death in 1747 under nominal Iranian suzerainty. It was annexed by Russia in 1827-28.

Nalyvaiko Uprising.text: A Cossack revolt against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth led by Severyn Nalyvaiko, lasting from 1594 to 1596. It was the second of a long run of Cossack uprisings in Ukraine, and the Polish crown won, leaving much of the right bank in ruins.

Namayan.text: A pre-colonial Philippine polity on the Pasig River near present-day Manila, also known as Sapa. A confederation of several barangays, it was probably strongest in the 11th-14th centuries and lasted until the Spanish arrived in the 1570s.

Namibia.text: A country on the southwest coast of Africa, home to the Namib Desert. South Africa ruled it for decades, and it won independence on 21 March 1990 after a long struggle led by SWAPO.

Nannan of Chenkanma (Cheyyar valley).text: A small Sangam-age chiefdom in the Cheyyar valley of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, ruled by a chief named Nannan from Chenkanma, today's Chengam. He is a different Nannan from the one in Ezhimalai.

Nannan of Ezhimalai (Pali).text: A Sangam-age chiefdom on India's south-west coast, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, run by chiefs titled Nannan from the hill fort of Pali. It stretched from near Badagara to Kasaragod and inland to Coorg.

Nanyue.text: A kingdom in southern China and northern Vietnam, founded around 204 BCE by the former Qin general Zhao Tuo. His family ruled from Panyu, today's Guangzhou, until Han armies conquered it in 111 BCE.

Nanzan.text: The southern of Okinawa's three kingdoms, one of the small island rivals of the 1300s. It lasted until the 1420s, when the king of Chūzan absorbed it and merged Okinawa into the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1429.

Nanzhao.text: A kingdom in present-day Yunnan, in southwest China, c. 738 to 902, ruled from capitals beside Erhai Lake. It grew strong between Tang China and Tibet by switching sides in their wars; after a coup in 902 and short-lived regimes, the Dali Kingdom rose in 937.

Nauru.text: A tiny island in the central Pacific, one of the world's smallest countries. It became independent in January 1968 after Australian, British and New Zealand administration. Its wealth came from phosphate, which mining nearly exhausted.

Nauruan clans.text: Nauru, a tiny island in the central Pacific, was settled about 3,000 years ago and held by twelve clans. Britain was the first outsider to find it, in 1798, and Germany annexed it in 1888.

Nawab of Awadh.text: A northern Indian kingdom ruled by Shia nawabs of Persian origin, founded by Sa'adat Khan around 1722. They became great patrons of the arts and moved their court from Faizabad to Lucknow; the last nawab was deposed in 1856.

Nawabs of Bengal.text: The hereditary Mughal governors of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, who were almost independent rulers by the early 1700s. Their capital was Murshidabad, and their power was broken after the East India Company won the Battle of Plassey in 1757.

Nayaks of Gingee.text: A Tamil Nayak kingdom, one of three under Vijayanagara with Madurai and Thanjavur, based at the great fort of Gingee. It held the land between the Palar and Kollidam rivers until Bijapur captured the fort in 1649.

Nayaks of Madurai.text: A Telugu-speaking dynasty that ruled much of southern Tamil Nadu from Madurai, starting around 1529 as governors for Vijayanagara. They became independent after 1565, rebuilt great temples, and set up the palaiyakkarar system of local chiefs; their line ended in 1736.

Nayaks of Thanjavur.text: A Telugu dynasty founded around 1532 by Sevappa Nayaka, first as a Vijayanagara governor and then as a virtually independent ruler of Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu. They were great patrons of temples, music and literature in Tamil, Telugu and Sanskrit, until Maratha rule began in the 1670s.

Ndwandwe.text: A Nguni kingdom in the north of present-day KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, c. 1780-1819, best known under its king Zwide. It destroyed the Mthethwa in 1817-18 but was then defeated by Shaka's Zulu in 1819-20.

Negeri Sembilan.text: A Malay state whose name means nine states, a federation of districts settled by Minangkabau people from Sumatra. Its ruler, the Yang di-Pertuan Besar, is chosen by chiefs, and the state is now part of Malaysia.

Negroponte.text: The island of Euboea off the Greek coast, called Negroponte by the Venetians and Lombards after the Fourth Crusade. Here it shows its early Latin-ruled period c. 1206-1209, before Venetian control.

Nelcynda coast under the Pandyas.text: The pepper-port coast around Nelcynda in Kerala, drawn c. 0-100 CE as under the Pandyas of Madurai, following the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a 1st-century guide. Ptolemy later places Nelcynda in Ay country, and its exact site is still debated.

Nepal.text: A Himalayan nation unified in 1768 by Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha, who made Kathmandu his capital. It was ruled by kings for centuries and became a republic in 2008.

Netherlands New Guinea.text: The western half of New Guinea, which the Netherlands kept as an overseas territory after Indonesia's independence in 1949, governing it from Hollandia (now Jayapura). After a dispute with Indonesia it passed to a UN authority in 1962 and to Indonesia in 1963.

New Caledonia.text: An archipelago in the southwest Pacific, home to the Kanak people and claimed by France in 1853. France used it as a penal colony from 1864 and mined its nickel, found the same year. It is still a French territory, with Nouméa as its capital.

New Hebrides.text: A group of South Pacific islands run jointly by Britain and France from 1906, a rare arrangement called a condominium. It became independent as Vanuatu in 1980.

Nguyễn dynasty.text: The last dynasty of Vietnam, founded by Gia Long in 1802 when he reunified the country. Its emperors ruled from Huế, and the French took control in the 1880s, though the dynasty lasted formally until 1945.

Nguyễn lords.text: The Nguyễn clan, who ruled southern Vietnam (Đàng Trong, called Cochinchina by Europeans) from around 1558 as nominal servants of the Lê emperors. They fought the Trịnh lords of the north for generations and pushed Vietnam south into the Mekong delta.

Ni-Vanuatu chiefdoms.text: The island communities of Vanuatu in the South Pacific, first settled about 3,000 years ago by Lapita seafarers and later joined by other Melanesian migrants. Great chiefs such as Roi Mata were buried in grand tombs, and Europeans first arrived in 1606.

Nias chiefdoms.text: Chiefdoms on Nias, an island off the west coast of Sumatra in Indonesia. Its culture is famous for megalithic stonework and for stone jumping, a coming-of-age ritual in which young men leap over a stone tower about two metres high.

Nicaean Empire.text: The largest of the Greek states formed after the Fourth Crusade, centred on Nicaea (İznik) in western Anatolia. Its emperors recaptured Constantinople in 1261 and restored the Byzantine Empire.

Nicobarese peoples.text: The Austroasiatic-speaking islanders of the Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal, living in coastal villages from farming, fishing and coconut growing. Their islands became part of British India in 1869 after Danish rule.

Nieuwe Republiek.text: A small Boer republic in present-day South Africa, declared in 1884 on land given by a Zulu king to Boer volunteers. It joined the South African Republic in 1888 and later became part of Natal.

Nitra.text: The Slavic center of Nitra, in present-day Slovakia, drawn here in the years around 900. It was an early Slavic stronghold and one of the oldest towns in the area, linked to Great Moravia.

Nizari Ismaili state (Girdkuh).text: Girdkuh was a mountain fortress in northern Iran, held by the Nizari Ismailis from 1096 as part of the Alamut state of Hasan-i Sabbah. It outlasted Alamut itself, holding out against the Mongols until 1270.

Nizari Ismaili state (Quhistan).text: The Quhistan region of eastern Iran, a second cluster of Nizari Ismaili fortresses from 1091. It belonged to the Alamut state founded by Hasan-i Sabbah, a network of castles ruled from Alamut until the Mongols destroyed it in 1256.

Nizari Ismaili state (Rudbar).text: The Rudbar valley around Alamut castle in northern Iran, the heart of the Nizari Ismaili state founded in 1090 by Hasan-i Sabbah. It was a network of mountain fortresses rather than one solid territory, and the Mongols took Alamut in 1256.

Nizari Ismaili state (Syrian castles).text: A string of Ismaili mountain castles in Syria, acquired from the 1130s, among them Masyaf, which became their centre. They were an outpost of the Nizari state of Alamut in Persia.

Nizhny Novgorod.text: A Russian town founded in 1221 where the Oka river meets the Volga. In the 1300s it was the capital of a principality, Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal, that rivalled Moscow before Moscow absorbed it. Today it is a large city of over a million people.

Nobatia.text: Nobatia was a kingdom in Lower Nubia, along the Nile in southern Egypt and northern Sudan, founded around 400. It turned Christian in 543, and sometime in the 7th century it was annexed by Makuria to its south.

Nogai Horde.text: A confederation of Mongol-descended Nogai tribes on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian seas. They were herders and horse-riders and fought as allies or rivals of Russia, Crimea and Kazan until Kalmyks and Russians pushed them out in the 1600s.

Norman Italy.text: The lands in southern Italy won by Norman adventurers and knights from around the year 1000. Starting as mercenaries, they carved out counties and duchies at the expense of Byzantines and Lombards, and in 1130 united them as the Kingdom of Sicily.

Norse.text: The Norse were the North Germanic peoples of Scandinavia, whose Old Norse speakers became famous as Viking seafarers, traders and raiders. This entry covers their homelands in the south of Scandinavia; Norse settlers later reached Iceland, Greenland and beyond.

Norse Greenland.text: Farming settlements of Norse colonists on Greenland's southwest coast, founded in the late 10th century by followers of Erik the Red. At most 2,000-3,000 people lived there, trading walrus ivory to Europe, and the colonies were abandoned in the 15th century.

North Macedonia.text: A small Balkan country that left Yugoslavia peacefully in 1991. A long naming dispute with Greece ended in 2019, when it adopted the name North Macedonia.

North Sea Empire.text: The union of England, Denmark and Norway under the Danish king Cnut the Great, who gained England in 1016, then Denmark (1018) and Norway (1028). It split after his death in 1035, and its last remnant ended when his son Harthacnut died in 1042.

North Yemen.text: The northwestern part of today's Yemen, ruled first by an imam as the Kingdom of Yemen. A revolution in 1962 made it the Yemen Arab Republic, and it united with South Yemen in 1990.

Northern Fujiwara.text: A noble clan that governed the Tōhoku region in the north of Honshū, Japan, in the 12th century, almost as an independent realm rich in gold and horses. They built temples such as Chūson-ji at their seat, Hiraizumi, and fell to Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1189.

Northern Liang.text: Northern Liang was a Sixteen Kingdoms state in the Gansu corridor founded by the Juqu family, of Lushuihu origin. A Buddhist-friendly court, it lasted from 397 to 439, when Northern Wei took it.

Northern Qi.text: Northern Qi was a northern Chinese dynasty from 550 to 577 CE, founded by Gao Yang, whose family had controlled Eastern Wei. It began as the strongest of China's three states, but violent or incompetent emperors weakened it, and the poorer Northern Zhou conquered it in 577.

Northern Yan.text: Northern Yan was a Sixteen Kingdoms state in Liaoning, formed around 407 CE when Gao Yun took the throne, followed by Feng Ba. It was crushed by Northern Wei in 436, and its last ruler fled to Goguryeo.

Norway-Denmark.text: Here the name covers the early Norwegian-Danish union of Magnus the Good, who ruled Norway from 1035 and Denmark from 1042 until he died in 1047. It is not the much later union of 1536 to 1814 that the linked article describes.

Nupe Kingdom.text: A kingdom of the Nupe people along the middle Niger in central Nigeria, ruled by the Etsu Nupe. Wikipedia places its origins in the mid-15th century, and a king-list dates this phase from 1531 until the Fulani jihad of the early 1800s.

Obotrites.text: A confederation of West Slavic tribes in present-day Mecklenburg and Holstein, on the Baltic coast of northern Germany. For decades they fought beside Charlemagne against the Saxons, beating them at Bornhöved in 798, and they were long at war with the kings of Denmark.

Odisha under the Bhoi dynasty.text: The Gajapati kingdom of Odisha under a new dynasty, after the minister Govinda Vidyadhara seized the throne in 1541. The state kept its centre at Cuttack and the same core territory, but the Bhoi rule was short and unstable.

Odrysian Kingdom.text: A powerful Thracian kingdom founded by Teres I in the early 400s BCE, uniting many tribes across what is now Bulgaria, northern Greece and European Turkey. Long an ally of Athens, it later split among rival kings, and Philip II of Macedon conquered them in 340 BCE.

Oghuz Turks.text: A large confederation of Turkic tribes on the steppes between the Caspian and Aral seas, drawn c. 750 to 1055. Some Oghuz moved south and west, and from them rose the Seljuks, who then conquered Persia and much of the Middle East.

Old Kingdom of Norway.text: The medieval kingdom of Norway, which began when kings such as Harald Fairhair united the western coast in the late 800s. Norway later joined Denmark and Sweden under a shared crown, ending its separate rule around 1400.

Oriental Republic of Uruguay.text: A small republic between Argentina and Brazil on the Río de la Plata. Both big neighbours wanted the land, but it became independent in 1828 after a war was settled with British mediation. Its capital is Montevideo.

Orissa feudatory states: Patna, Kalahand.text: A grouping on the map of the Orissa Tributary States, such as Patna, Kalahandi, Sonpur, Bamra, Keonjhar and Dhenkanal. Later part of the Eastern States Agency, they merged into India under agreements of December 1947 that took effect on 1 January 1948.

Ostrogothic Kingdom.text: The Ostrogothic Kingdom was a realm covering Italy and nearby lands under Theodoric the Great from 493 CE. It tried to blend Roman and Gothic ways, and collapsed in 553 after Byzantine reconquest under Justinian.

Ostrogoths.text: The Ostrogoths were a Gothic people who first lived north of the Black Sea, then served under the Huns, and in 493 CE took Italy under Theodoric the Great. Their kingdom fell to Byzantium in the early 550s after a long war.

Ottoman Tripolitania.text: The Ottoman-ruled coast of northern Libya around Tripoli, which was semi-autonomous for centuries. After the local Karamanli dynasty ended in 1835 the Ottomans ruled directly, until Italy invaded in 1911.

Oyo Empire.text: A Yoruba empire in today's western Nigeria and Benin, the largest Yoruba-speaking state. Famed for its cavalry and trade, it dominated its neighbours until it broke up in the early 1800s.

Pahang Sultanate.text: A Malay state on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, in today's Pahang, Malaysia, ruled by the Bendahara family from the royal town of Pekan. It broke from Johor in 1853; after a civil war, Wan Ahmad took power, was proclaimed sultan in 1881, and accepted a British Resident in 1888.

Palau.text: A small island country in the western Pacific, once ruled in turn by Spain, Germany, Japan and the US. It became independent in 1994, freely associated with the US, and its Rock Islands are a World Heritage Site.

Palauan chiefdoms.text: The village chiefdoms of Palau, an island group in western Micronesia settled around 1000 BCE. Villages were ruled by chiefs and rival alliances, until Spain claimed the islands in the 1800s and sold them to Germany in 1899.

Palestine.text: The State of Palestine, claiming the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza. It declared independence in 1988, and since the 1993 Oslo accords the Palestinian Authority has governed parts of the territory. Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as their capital, while Ramallah is the seat of government.

Palestinians.text: An Arab people native to Palestine, the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean. During the 1948 war, hundreds of thousands left or were forced from their homes, and many became refugees.

Panduvamshi kingdom (Dakshina Kosala).text: A dynasty ruling Dakshina Kosala, in present-day Chhattisgarh, c. 620-754 CE, from Shripura (Sirpur), after a period of petty chiefs. At times they also held parts of Utkala and Vidarbha.

Pandya Dynasty.text: The Pandyas were one of the three great Tamil dynasties of south India, ruling from Madurai, a land long known for its pearl fisheries. King Kadungon revived their power in the late 6th century CE, and they were a leading force in the south until the Cholas rose in the 9th century.

Pandya Empire.text: A Tamil dynasty of South India dating back to ancient times, ruling from Madurai, and one of the three great kingdoms of Tamilakam with the Cholas and Cheras. In the 13th century, the period shown here, it entered a golden age, and Marco Polo visited the kingdom in 1288 and 1293.

Pandya kingdom (Pandya Nadu).text: One of the three great Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam age, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, in the Vaigai and Tamirabarani valleys of southern Tamil Nadu. Madurai was its capital and Korkai its pearl-fishing port.

Panthay Rebellion.text: A revolt in Yunnan, southwest China, by Hui Muslims and other peoples against Qing rule. Its leader Du Wenxiu held the city of Dali from 1856 as the capital of a rival state, until Qing forces took it in 1872; the last resistance ended in 1873.

Papal States.text: The pope's own state in central Italy, lasting from 756 to 1870. It began when the Frankish king Pepin handed the pope land won from the Lombards, and it ended when the new Kingdom of Italy captured Rome.

Paphlagonia.text: A region on the northern Anatolian coast of the Black Sea, in today's Turkey, between Bithynia and Pontus. It was ruled by local dynasties and by larger neighbours, and fell under Pontus and then Rome.

Paphos.text: A city-kingdom on the south-west coast of Cyprus, c. 600-312 BCE, centred on Palaepaphos and later Nea Paphos. Palaepaphos was famous for its temple of Aphrodite. King Nicocles was among its last rulers.

Papua New Guinea.text: A country on the eastern half of New Guinea and nearby islands, with over 800 languages. It was run by Australia after the Second World War and became independent in 1975. Its capital is Port Moresby.

Paraguay.text: A landlocked republic in the middle of South America, Paraguay broke away from Spanish rule in 1811. Unusually for the Americas, most of its people speak both Spanish and Guaraní, an Indigenous language, and both have official status.

Paramara Dynasty.text: A Rajput dynasty ruling Malwa in west-central India from 948 to 1305. Its king Bhoja, himself a renowned scholar, was a great patron of poets and learning, and the last known king was killed by Alauddin Khalji's forces in 1305.

Parambu (Pari).text: A hill chiefdom at Parambu in Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-170 CE, placed by the scholar Sastri at Piranmalai. Its chief Vel Pari is praised in the poems, which give him 300 villages; the three great kings besieged the hill and killed him by treachery.

Parambu after Pari's fall.text: The hill of Parambu in Tamil Nadu after the death of its chief Vel Pari, c. 170-300 CE. Three great kings had besieged it, but no source says who held it afterward.

Partabgarh State (Pratapgarh).text: A Rajput princely state in southern Rajasthan, an offshoot of Mewar's Sisodia line, ruled from Deolia and from 1698 from Pratapgarh. A 1804 British treaty was cancelled, and a new one in 1818 made it a protected state.

Patani Kingdom.text: A Malay sultanate on the northern Malay Peninsula, in today's southern Thailand and northern Malaysia. Its golden age came under four queens from 1584, when it beat off several Siamese invasions; Siam conquered it in 1786 and ended its royal line in 1902.

Pate Sultanate.text: A Swahili sultanate on Pate island, Kenya, ruled by the Nabhani dynasty, which long vied with Lamu and Takwa for control of the nearby coast. Its attempt, allied with the Mazrui, to subject Lamu failed badly in 1813.

Patiala.text: The leading Sikh princely state of the Phulkian dynasty in Punjab. The small states of Nabha and Malerkotla lay in pockets within it, and its Narnaul district was far to the south. It acceded to India in 1947.

Patriarchate of Aquileia.text: A church state in northeastern Italy ruled by the patriarch of Aquileia, a bishop who was also a prince of the Holy Roman Empire. Venice conquered Udine in 1420, ending its worldly power.

Pekan of the Avi clan (Palani hills).text: A small chiefdom of the Sangam age in the Palani hills of Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-300 CE, ruled by Pekan of the Vel Avi family. Linking his lands to Palani rests on tradition and is only weakly supported.

Peloponnesian League.text: A military alliance of Greek city-states led by Sparta, c. 550-366 BCE. Members promised to support one another, and it fought the Athens-led Delian League in the Peloponnesian War of 431-404 BCE, which Sparta won.

Penang.text: An island off the west coast of Malaya, acquired by the East India Company in 1786 when Francis Light got it from the Sultan of Kedah. Its main city George Town became a free port and trading hub, and today it is a Malaysian state.

People's Democratic Republic of Algeria.text: A North African country that won independence from France in 1962 after a bitter seven-year war led by the National Liberation Front. It is one of the largest countries in the world by area, and the Sahara covers most of it.

People's Democratic Republic of Yemen.text: A Marxist state in southern Arabia, also called South Yemen, formed in 1967 when Britain left Aden. It was the only communist Arab country, and it united with North Yemen in 1990.

People's Republic of Angola.text: Angola after independence from Portugal in 1975, run as a one-party Marxist state by the MPLA. A long civil war against the UNITA movement, with Soviet, Cuban and US involvement, shaped these years.

People's Republic of Bangladesh.text: A South Asian country that broke away from Pakistan in 1971 after a nine-month war, with India's help. It was formerly East Pakistan, and its people are mostly Bengali. The delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra covers most of its land.

People's Republic of Bulgaria.text: The communist state of Bulgaria from 1946 to 1990, run by the Bulgarian Communist Party on the Soviet model. Todor Zhivkov led the party from 1954 until he was removed in 1989, and the one-party system gave way to democracy in 1990.

People's Republic of Kampuchea.text: The government of Cambodia set up in 1979 after Vietnamese forces overthrew the Khmer Rouge. Backed by Vietnam and the Soviet bloc, it was recognised by few countries and fought guerrillas until the early 1990s.

People's Socialist Republic of Albania.text: The communist state of Albania, led by Enver Hoxha from 1946 until 1985. It broke first with the Soviet Union and later with China, cutting itself off from the world in the name of self-reliance, until one-party rule ended in 1991.

Peoples of Vancouver Island.text: The Indigenous nations of Vancouver Island, Canada: the Kwakwaka'wakw in the north, the Nuu-chah-nulth along the west coast and Coast Salish peoples in the southeast. Spanish ships arrived in the 1770s, and James Cook spent a month at Nootka Sound in 1778, opening a trade in sea-otter furs.

Peoples of the Bismarck Archipelago and.text: The island peoples of the Bismarck Archipelago and Bougainville, off northeastern New Guinea in today's Papua New Guinea. Humans first reached these islands some 30,000 or more years ago, later joined by Lapita seafarers, and the islands had no European settlement until Germany annexed the archipelago in 1884.

Perdiccas.text: The lands controlled by Perdiccas, the general to whom the dying Alexander gave his ring and who ruled as regent of the empire. He tried to invade Egypt, failed, and was murdered by his own officers in 320 BCE.

Phayao Kingdom.text: A Tai kingdom in northern Thailand centred on the city of Phayao, from about the 1000s to the 1300s. In 1338 armies from Chiang Saen and Nan sacked it, and its lands were split, with Phayao itself annexed by the Lan Na kingdom.

Philistia.text: The coastal plain of southern Canaan, in today's Israel and Gaza, held by the Philistines, who ruled five cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. It appears in the Bible as Israel's rival and fell to Assyria and then Babylon.

Phoenicia.text: A string of Canaanite trading city-states on the coast of today's Lebanon, at their height from about 1200 to 332 BCE, with Tyre and Sidon the leading ones. Their sailors planted colonies across the Mediterranean, Carthage the most famous, and carried the alphabet.

Phoenician Colonies.text: Trading settlements founded by Phoenician cities such as Tyre around the Mediterranean, reaching as far west as Spain and Morocco. They gave sailors safe harbours and markets, and Carthage, founded by settlers from Tyre, grew from one of them into a power of its own.

Phrygia.text: An Iron Age kingdom in west-central Anatolia, in today's Turkey, famous in legend for King Midas and the Gordian Knot. It flourished until Cimmerian invaders sacked its capital Gordion around 675 BCE, after which Lydia dominated the region.

Pictland (kingdom of Fortriu).text: The Pictish kingdom of Fortriu in northern Scotland, c. 685-848, after its kings became rulers of all the Picts. Bridei son of Beli's victory over Northumbria at Dun Nechtain in 685 started this era; Fortriu is now placed around the Moray Firth.

Poles.text: The Polish nation's rebellion against Russian rule, the November Uprising, which began in Warsaw in November 1830 in Congress Poland. The rebels held out for about a year, but Russia crushed them in 1831 and in 1832 issued the Organic Statute, which ended Poland's autonomy.

Polish Armed Forces.text: Poland as it re-emerged in November 1918, after 123 years of being split among Russia, Prussia and Austria. Józef Piłsudski led the new state, which had to fight over its borders. The article linked here is about the modern army.

Polish People's Republic.text: Poland after the Second World War, a communist state with its capital at Warsaw. Its borders ran along the Oder-Neisse line in the west and roughly the Curzon line in the east; it was formally the Republic of Poland until the 1952 constitution.

Polyperchon.text: The territory held by Polyperchon, an old general of Alexander who became regent of Macedon in 319 BCE after Antipater died. Antipater's son Cassander challenged him and by 316 BCE held Macedon, leaving Polyperchon only strongholds in the Peloponnese such as Corinth and Sicyon.

Pomerania.text: The region on the southern Baltic shore, now split between Poland and Germany, drawn here c. 1139-1187. Its Slavic dukes, the Griffins, ruled it, and the area slowly became Christian and German-influenced.

Pontianak Kadriyah Sultanate.text: A sultanate on Borneo's west coast, founded in 1771 by Syarif Abdurrahman Alkadrie, son of a Hadhrami Arab cleric. Its capital, Pontianak, grew where the Landak and Kapuas rivers meet, and the sultanate formally ended in 1950.

Porus's kingdom (Pauravas).text: The kingdom of King Porus in the Punjab, c. 330-316 BCE, between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers. We know it only from Greek sources. Alexander beat Porus in 326 BCE, then restored him and gave him more land.

Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg.text: The church state of the archbishops of Salzburg in the Salzach valley, Austria, fully separate from Bavaria from 1328. It was rich from salt and gold and expelled its Protestants in 1731.

Prince-Bishopric of Liège.text: A Church-ruled state along the Meuse in present-day Belgium, 985-1795, where the bishop was also the prince. Notger built it up, and it stayed separate from the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands until France annexed it in 1795.

Prince-Bishopric of Montenegro.text: A theocratic state in the mountains of Montenegro, ruled by Orthodox bishops of Cetinje, a role hereditary in the Petrović-Njegoš family from 1697. Though nominally Ottoman, it was effectively independent; Danilo II turned it into a secular principality in 1852.

Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht (Nedersticht.text: The Nedersticht, the lower part of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht, roughly today's province of Utrecht, 1024-1528. The bishops were also temporal rulers and princes of the Empire; the emperor held the right of investiture until the Concordat of Worms in 1122.

Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht (Oversticht).text: The Oversticht, the northeastern part of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht, covering Overijssel and Drenthe, 1024-1528. Its ruler was the bishop of Utrecht, who was both a church leader and a prince of the Empire.

Principality of Abkhazia.text: A principality on the Black Sea coast of the western Caucasus, centred on Sokhumi. It arose as the Georgian kingdom broke up in the 1400s, and it fell under Ottoman, then Russian influence, until Russia took full control in the 1800s.

Principality of Achaea.text: A Crusader state in the Peloponnese of southern Greece, also called the Morea, founded in 1205 after the Fourth Crusade. For a time it was the strongest state in Greece; it lasted until the Byzantines took the last of it in the 1430s.

Principality of Albania (Thopia).text: A principality in central Albania held by Karl Thopia, who styled himself prince of Albania and took Durrës from the Angevins in 1368. His son Gjergj gave Durrës to Venice in 1392.

Principality of Andorra.text: A tiny country in the eastern Pyrenees, between France and Spain. It has two co-princes, the Bishop of Urgell and the French head of state, under an arrangement dating from a 1278 agreement. Its capital is Andorra la Vella.

Principality of Ansbach.text: A small Hohenzollern principality in Franconia, in today's Bavaria, ruled by the margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach. It split from Bayreuth in 1486, stayed a separate state for three centuries, and was sold to Prussia in 1791 before Bavaria took it in 1806.

Principality of Antioch.text: A Crusader state founded in 1098 around Antioch, on the northeastern edge of the Mediterranean. Smaller than neighbouring Edessa or Jerusalem, it survived until the Mamluk sultan Baibars captured Antioch in 1268.

Principality of Arbanon.text: The first Albanian state named in sources, ruled by Progon and his sons from Krujë. In 1208 Dhimitër Progoni described its land to Pope Innocent III as the mountain region from Shkodër to Ohrid. After 1216 it passed to other powers.

Principality of Bayreuth.text: A Franconian territory in northern Bavaria ruled by a Hohenzollern branch, first from Kulmbach and later Bayreuth. It separated from Ansbach in 1486 and lasted until 1791, when its last margrave handed both principalities to Prussia.

Principality of Beloozero.text: A Russian principality in the cold north, around Lake Beloye in Vologda region, from 1238 to the 1480s. Its capital Beloozero was one of the first towns named in the early Russian chronicle, and Moscow finally took the principality over.

Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.text: The southern Welf principality in Germany after the 1269 division, centred on Wolfenbüttel and the city of Brunswick. Its borders shifted with many family partitions, and it was annexed to the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1806.

Principality of Bulgaria.text: A state created in 1878 by the Treaty of Berlin as an Ottoman vassal after Russia's victory over the Turks. It united with Eastern Rumelia in 1885 and declared full independence in 1908 as a kingdom.

Principality of Calenberg.text: A principality of the Welf dynasty between the Deister hills and the Leine river in Lower Saxony, formed in the partition of 1495. The dukes moved their seat to Hanover in 1636, and in 1692 Ernest Augustus was raised to elector.

Principality of Capua.text: A Lombard principality in southern Italy centred on Capua, lasting about three centuries. It was often at odds with Naples, Salerno and Byzantium, and eventually fell to the Normans in the 1000s.

Principality of Chernigov.text: One of the largest and strongest principalities of Kievan Rus', centred on Chernihiv in what is now northern Ukraine, with lands also in Belarus and Russia. For a time it ranked second only to Kiev, and its princes came from the line of Sviatoslav, a son of Yaroslav the Wise.

Principality of Drutsk.text: A small Rus principality around the city of Drutsk, in present-day Belarus. It broke off from Polotsk after Prince Vseslav's death in 1101 and was ruled by a branch of his descendants.

Principality of Galicia-Volhynia.text: A strong Rus state in western Ukraine and neighbouring lands, formed in 1199 by joining Galicia and Volhynia. It became a kingdom in 1253 and was one of the three leading Rus states.

Principality of Guria.text: A small Georgian principality in the southwest, between the Black Sea and the Lesser Caucasus, whose Gurieli princes ruled it from the 1460s. It fought constant border wars with Georgian neighbours and the Ottomans, who took its coastline, until Russia annexed it in 1829.

Principality of Halych.text: A Rus principality in western Ukraine, also called Galicia, ruled from Halych, which is first recorded as a princely seat around 1124. Its nobles and townspeople had an unusual say over their princes, and in 1199 Roman the Great joined it with Volhynia into one state.

Principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen.text: A small principality in southwest Germany ruled by the Catholic Swabian branch of the Hohenzollern family, the same family as Prussia's kings. Prussia took it over peacefully in 1850.

Principality of Iberia.text: The Principality of Iberia was a Georgian realm in Kartli, run by presiding princes after Persia abolished the old monarchy around 580. Its princes steered between Byzantine, Persian and later Arab overlords, until the Bagratid family restored the kingship in 888.

Principality of Jersika.text: A Latgalian principality in eastern Latvia, based at a hill fort on the Daugava river, and an important state of medieval Latvia. Crusaders of Bishop Albert of Riga conquered it in the early 13th century.

Principality of Koknese.text: A small Baltic principality on the Daugava River in what is now Latvia, a vassal of Polotsk from the 1180s. Its prince Vetseke rebelled against Bishop Albert of Riga and fled after burning his castle, and by 1209 the crusading Brothers of the Sword held it.

Principality of Lichtenberg.text: A small German exclave on the Nahe river, far from the rest of the Saxe-Coburg lands that owned it from 1816. In 1834 the duke sold it to Prussia. Its lands are now split between Saarland and Rhineland-Palatinate.

Principality of Liechtenstein.text: A tiny Alpine principality between Austria and Switzerland, named for its ruling family, which was made a principality in 1719. It became sovereign in 1806, and its capital is Vaduz.

Principality of Lippe.text: A small German principality between the Weser river and the Teutoburg Forest, ruled by the House of Lippe, with Detmold as its capital. It became a principality in 1789 and lasted until 1918.

Principality of Lüneburg.text: The northern Welf principality in Germany, around the Lüneburg Heath, Celle and Uelzen, from the 1269 division. Its dukes moved to Celle in 1371, and Hanover inherited it in 1705.

Principality of Mingrelia.text: A principality in western Georgia, also called Odishi or Samegrelo, ruled by the Dadiani dynasty from lands around Zugdidi. It became an independent principality in 1557, accepted Russian protection in 1803 against stronger neighbours, and Russia abolished it in 1867.

Principality of Minsk.text: A Rus principality centred on Minsk, in present-day Belarus, set up in 1101 as an appanage of Polotsk. It was later drawn into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and was fully annexed by 1326.

Principality of Moldavia.text: A Romanian principality between the Carpathians and the Dniester river, formed in the 1300s. Stephen the Great defended it in the late 1400s. It later paid tribute to the Ottomans and joined Wallachia in 1859 to create Romania.

Principality of Monaco.text: A tiny city-state on the French Riviera, ruled by the Grimaldi family since they seized the Rock of Monaco in 1297. It is a sovereign principality today, almost entirely surrounded by France.

Principality of Nitra.text: A small West Slavic principality around Nitra, now in Slovakia, in the early 800s. A church was consecrated for its prince Pribina by the archbishop of Salzburg, and the land was absorbed by Moravia, perhaps around 833, when Pribina was driven out.

Principality of Orange.text: A small feudal state in southern France beside the Rhône, north of Avignon, made a principality in the 12th century. It passed to the House of Nassau in 1544, which is why William of Orange and the Dutch royal family bear its name.

Principality of Peremyshl.text: A small Rus principality centred on Peremyshl, today Przemyśl in southeastern Poland, in the Red Rus' lands near the Polish border. It was one of the western principalities of medieval Galicia, and joined Halych in 1141.

Principality of Pereyaslavl.text: A principality of Kievan Rus' around Pereiaslav on the river Trubizh in central Ukraine, usually handed to younger sons of Kiev's grand prince. It stretched east toward the steppe of the nomad Cumans, and the Mongols sacked its capital in March 1239.

Principality of Pinsk.text: A medieval principality centred on the town of Pinsk in today's Belarus, split off from the older Turov lands of Kievan Rus. In the early 1300s it passed peacefully into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, with Narimantas, a son of Gediminas, ruling Pinsk.

Principality of Polotsky.text: A Rus principality on the Dvina River in present-day Belarus, centred on Polotsk, one of the earliest-recorded East Slavic towns. It often defied Kiev, was strongest under Prince Vseslav (1044-1101), and from 1240 fell under Lithuanian overlordship.

Principality of Regensberg.text: A short-lived state created in 1803 for Karl Theodor von Dalberg around the city of Regensburg. It joined the Confederation of the Rhine and passed to Bavaria in 1810.

Principality of Reuss-Gera.text: A small principality in Thuringia in central Germany, ruled by the junior line of the House of Reuss with Gera as its seat. It was one of Germany's tiny states and lasted until 1918.

Principality of Rostov-Suzdal.text: A Rus principality in the northeast of the Rus lands, in today's central Russia. Yuri Dolgorukiy, traditionally credited with founding Moscow, shifted its seat in 1125 from Rostov to Suzdal, and his son Andrey moved it again to Vladimir in 1157.

Principality of Ryazan.text: A Russian principality that split from Chernigov by 1129 and fought repeated wars with its neighbour Vladimir. After the Mongols destroyed its old capital in 1237, the seat moved to Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky, now Ryazan, and it kept its independence until 1521.

Principality of Salerno.text: A Lombard principality in southern Italy that broke away from Benevento in 851 after a civil war. Centred on the port of Salerno, it fell to the Normans under Robert Guiscard in the 1070s.

Principality of Schwarzburg-Sonderhausen.text: A small principality in Thuringia in central Germany, ruled by a branch of the old Schwarzburg noble family. It was one of the many tiny states of the German Confederation. After 1909 the prince of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt ruled it as well, until monarchy ended in 1918.

Principality of Serbia.text: The early medieval Serbian principality, drawn c. 768 to 961, in the western Balkans. Its princes, such as Vlastimir, lived between the Byzantine and Bulgarian empires, and the state broke up after Prince Časlav died around 960.

Principality of Smolensk.text: A Rus principality on the upper Dnieper around Smolensk, independent from 1125. Lithuanian influence grew over it from the 1300s, and Vytautas of Lithuania finally incorporated it as the Smolensk land in 1404.

Principality of Svaneti.text: A small mountain principality in the Svaneti region of the Caucasus, in today's Georgia, created after the Kingdom of Georgia broke up. The Gelovani and Dadeshkeliani houses ruled it, and Russia annexed it in the 1850s.

Principality of Terebovlia.text: A small Rus principality in western Ukraine, set up around 1084 as an appanage for Prince Vasylko Rostyslavych. It lasted only a few decades before being absorbed into the larger principality of Halych.

Principality of Theodoro.text: A small Greek Orthodox principality in the mountains of southern Crimea, also called Gothia, ruled from the fortress town of Mangup. Seen as the last fragment of the Byzantine world, it held out until the Ottoman commander Gedik Ahmed Pasha took Mangup in 1475.

Principality of Tmutarakan.text: A Rus principality on the Taman peninsula and across the Kerch strait, c. 988-1094, cut off from Rus by the steppe. Mstislav ruled it and used it to win lands on the Dnieper's left bank in 1024; it drops out of Rus sources after 1094.

Principality of Transylvania.text: A semi-independent principality in what is now Romania, ruled by Hungarian princes from 1570 to 1711, mostly as an Ottoman vassal. It grew out of the Zápolya family's eastern Hungarian realm after the Treaty of Speyer and gave Protestants unusual religious freedom.

Principality of Turov.text: A principality of Kievan Rus in what is now southern Belarus, dating from the 900s. Its capital was Turov, and later it was often called Turov and Pinsk, before the area passed to Lithuania in the 1300s.

Principality of Turov and Pinsk.text: A Kievan Rus' principality from the 10th century in what is now Belarus and northern Ukraine, ruled from Turov, with Pinsk as another key town. In the early 13th century it came under Galicia-Volhynia, and in the 14th century it passed to Lithuania.

Principality of Upper Hungary.text: A short-lived Ottoman vassal state in 1682-85, ruled by Imre Thököly in what is now Slovakia and northeastern Hungary. It collapsed when the Habsburgs took back the area, and Thököly was captured by the Ottomans.

Principality of Valona.text: A small principality around Vlorë in southern Albania, set up in 1346 after Serbia's ruler Stefan Dušan made his brother-in-law John Komnenos Asen its lord. It became independent after Dušan died in 1355 and lasted until the Ottomans conquered it in 1417.

Principality of Valona and Kanina.text: A medieval principality in southern Albania around Vlorë and Kanina, founded in 1346 under Serbian overlordship. From 1396 it was held by Mrkša Žarković, then after he died in 1414 by Rugina, his widow. The Ottomans conquered it in 1417.

Principality of Vitebsk.text: A Ruthenian principality centred on Vitebsk, in present-day Belarus, founded in 1101. When its last prince died heirless in 1320, it passed to Lithuania, whose grand duke Algirdas had married his daughter.

Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal.text: A Russian grand principality in the northeast of the Rus lands, with its capital at Vladimir. After the Mongol invasion it fell under the Golden Horde and broke into more than a dozen appanages, and the princes of Moscow, one of them, slowly gathered the rest under their rule.

Principality of Volhynia.text: A western Rus principality in Volhynia, along the borders of today's Ukraine, Belarus and Poland, tradition says founded by Prince Vsevolod in 987. It later joined with Galicia to form a bigger state.

Principality of Waldeck and Pyrmont.text: A small German principality in the northern Hesse area whose counts dated back to the 1100s. It became a state of the German Empire and merged into Prussia in 1929.

Principality of Wallachia.text: One of the two main Romanian principalities, north of the lower Danube. It formed in the early 1300s under Basarab I, who beat the Hungarians. Wallachia later paid tribute to the Ottomans and joined with Moldavia in 1859 to form Romania.

Prome Kingdom.text: A small kingdom in central Burma, based on the city of Prome (Pyay), that lasted from 1482 to 1542. It claimed to continue the ancient Sri Ksetra kingdom and was swallowed by the rising Toungoo dynasty.

Protectorate of the Western Regions.text: Set up by Han China in 59 or 60 BCE, this office under a protector-general oversaw the oasis states of the Tarim Basin along the Silk Road, aiming to guard trade and keep the Xiongnu away. It was abandoned and revived several times, lasting on and off until 439.

Provisional Priamurye Government.text: The last White enclave of the Russian Civil War, set up in 1921 by a coup in Vladivostok and shielded by Japanese troops. In 1922 it even proclaimed a new tsar, but when the Japanese left that year the Far Eastern Republic's army won back most of its land.

Pskov Republic.text: A city-state in northwestern Russia that won independence from Novgorod in 1348. It ran its own affairs with an assembly called the veche, and it guarded Russia's western frontier against the Livonian knights until Moscow took it over in 1510.

Pudukkottai.text: The only princely state in the Tamil country, under the Madras government, in present-day Tamil Nadu. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Puebloans - Aztec Regional System.text: A network of Ancestral Puebloan settlements centred on the great houses of Aztec Ruins, by the Animas River in northwestern New Mexico, built in the 12th and 13th centuries. American settlers later named the site after the Aztecs by mistake; its builders were ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples.

Puebloans - Chaco Regional System.text: The Ancestral Puebloan world centred on Chaco Canyon in northwest New Mexico, c. 850 to 1150. It was linked by roads to many outlying settlements and is famed for huge stone buildings such as Pueblo Bonito.

Punjab hill states: Chamba.text: Chamba, a princely hill state in the western Himalaya (now Himachal Pradesh), under the Punjab government. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Punjab hill states: Mandi, Suket, Bilasp.text: A grouping on the map of Punjab hill states under the Punjab government: Mandi, Suket, Bilaspur, Sirmur and Nalagarh, in present-day Himachal Pradesh. They acceded to India in 1947.

Punjab states: Faridkot.text: Faridkot, one of the plains princely states under the Punjab government, in Punjab, India. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Punjab states: Jind.text: Jind, a Sikh princely state of the Phulkian family in Punjab and Haryana, India, founded in 1763. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Punjab states: Jind (Dadri).text: The Dadri district of Jind, a Sikh princely state of the Phulkian family. Dadri was a detached piece of the state, lying away from its main territory. The state acceded to India in 1947.

Punjab states: Kapurthala.text: Kapurthala, a princely state in Punjab, India, under the Punjab government. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Pyu City-States.text: The Pyu were a group of walled city-states in present-day Myanmar, flourishing between roughly the 2nd century BCE and the 11th century CE. Their Buddhist cities, such as Sri Ksetra, laid the ground for later Burmese culture.

Qabacha's sultanate (Multan and Uch).text: A short-lived sultanate in Upper Sindh and Multan, in present-day Pakistan. Nasir ad-Din Qabacha, governor for Muhammad of Ghor, became independent after 1206 and held it until Iltutmish took Uch in 1228.

Qara Qoyunlu.text: A Turkoman confederation, called the Black Sheep, that ruled Azerbaijan, Armenia, northwestern Iran and parts of Iraq from 1375. Its capital was Tabriz, and it was overthrown in 1468 by its rivals the Aq Qoyunlu.

Qarlugs.text: The Qarluqs, or Karluks, were a Turkic tribal confederation in Central Asia west of the Altai mountains. They helped decide the 751 Battle of Talas against Tang China, and later their descendants formed the Kara-Khanid state.

Qarmatians.text: The Qarmatians were a radical Ismaili Shia movement that ran a state in eastern Arabia, centred on al-Ahsa. In 930 they raided Mecca and took the Black Stone away, returning it about twenty years later.

Qasim Khanate.text: A small Tatar khanate inside the Russian state, around Kasimov on the Oka river in today's Ryazan region. It was created in 1452 when Grand Prince Vasily II of Moscow granted lands to the Kazan prince Qasim Khan, and it stayed dependent on Moscow until 1681.

Qasimids.text: The Zaydi Shia imams of Yemen's Qasimi line, who proclaimed their imamate in 1597 and had driven the Ottomans out of Yemen by 1636. Their state lasted until 1849.

Qataban.text: An ancient kingdom of South Arabia in today's Yemen, one of six old Yemeni states, which grew rich on the frankincense trade along the caravan road. Its capital was Timna, and in the late first century CE Hadhramaut and Himyar divided its lands between them.

Qatar.text: A small country on a peninsula in the Persian Gulf. In 1913 to 1915 the Ottomans still claimed it, then Britain protected it from 1916 until independence in 1971. Today it is a wealthy gas-producing monarchy with its capital at Doha.

Qatar Dynasty.text: The early rule of local Gulf Arab leaders on the Qatar peninsula, when it was a coast of pearl divers and traders under Ottoman and British pressure. An 1868 agreement with Britain first recognised Qatar as separate, and the Al Thani family has ruled since.

Qatar Protectorate.text: Qatar as a British protectorate, from 1916 until independence in 1971. Oil was struck there in the late 1930s, though production paused during the Second World War. Doha was its main town.

Qi.text: A powerful state of ancient China on the Shandong coast, founded in the Zhou conquest by Jiang Ziya. It grew rich on salt and iron, was the home of the Jixia Academy, and was conquered by Qin in 221 BCE.

Qocho Kingdom.text: A Uyghur kingdom around Turpan, now in Xinjiang, western China, founded in 843 by Uyghurs who had fled Mongolia. Its people mixed Buddhism, Manichaeism and Chinese culture, and its rulers later became vassals of the Mongols in 1209.

Quba Khanate.text: A khanate in north-eastern Azerbaijan, based at Quba, which became self-governing after Nader Shah's death in 1747 and grew powerful by absorbing the nearby Derbent Khanate. Russia took control in 1806.

Qutlugh-Khanids.text: A dynasty of Kerman in south-east Iran founded by Buraq Hajib, of Khitan origin. They were vassals of the Mongols, and the line ended in 1306/07.
