Rai kingdom of Sindh.text: A dynasty ruling Sindh in present-day Pakistan, c. 489-631 CE, from Alor. It is known almost only from the 13th-century Chach Nama, since no inscriptions survive, so historians debate how reliable its story is.

Rajahnate of Cebu.text: A trading kingdom on Cebu island in the central Philippines, ruled by a rajah. It traded with China and Southeast Asia, and in 1521 Ferdinand Magellan was welcomed here before he died in a battle nearby. Spain took the island in 1565.

Rajputana Agency (other states): Alwar,.text: A grouping on the map of smaller Rajputana Agency princely states: Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur, Karauli, Bundi and Tonk. All kept their own rulers under British overlordship until they acceded to India in 1947.

Rajputana Agency (other states): Dungarp.text: A grouping on the map of three small princely states of southern Rajasthan: Dungarpur, Banswara and Partabgarh. They were in the Rajputana Agency under the British and all acceded to India in 1947.

Rajputana Agency (other states): Kishang.text: Kishangarh, a small Rajput princely state in the Rajputana Agency, in present-day Rajasthan. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Rajputana Agency (other states): Sirohi.text: Sirohi, a small princely state in the Rajputana Agency, in the south of present-day Rajasthan. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Rajputana Agency (other states): Tonk (C.text: The Chhabra district of Tonk, a detached piece of the Pashtun-ruled princely state of Tonk, which lay in central India away from the main Tonk district. Tonk belonged to the Rajputana Agency and acceded to India in 1947.

Rajputana Agency (other states): Tonk (S.text: The Sironj district of Tonk, a detached piece of the Pashtun-ruled princely state of Tonk, which lay in central India away from the main Tonk district. Tonk belonged to the Rajputana Agency and acceded to India in 1947.

Rajputana Agency (other states): detache.text: Small detached tracts near Pirawa and Gangdhar belonging to Rajputana Agency princely states, which were interleaved with other states in the region. Like all the agency's states they acceded to India in 1947.

Ramadanid Emirate.text: A Turkmen emirate in Cilicia, southern Turkey, founded in 1352 by Ramazan Beg as the Armenian kingdom there weakened. Ruled from Adana, it was first a Mamluk protectorate, then largely independent, and from 1517 under Ottoman protection, lasting until 1608.

Rampura–Aligarh (Holkar's).text: The Rampura district, later called Aligarh, east of Tonk in Rajasthan, held by the Holkars, one of the great Maratha chiefs. The British gave it to Amir Khan in 1817.

Rasulid Dynasty.text: A Sunni dynasty that ruled Yemen from 1229 to 1454, from Taiz, and was well known for patronage of scholarship and for trade through the Red Sea ports. Its power faded in the 15th century.

Ratanpur (Haihaya kingdom of Chhattisgar.text: A Chhattisgarh kingdom ruled from Ratanpur by the Haihaya (Kalachuri) dynasty, with a related branch at Raipur. The dynasty later came under Maratha control and lost its independence.

Rawadid dynasty.text: A Kurdicised Arab dynasty that ruled Azerbaijan from Tabriz in the late 10th and 11th centuries, c. 984-1071. Wahsudan submitted to the Seljuk leader Tughril in 1054, and the Seljuks ended the line in 1071.

Recherla Nayakas (Velamas).text: Velama chiefs who killed Kapaya Nayaka in 1368 and dominated Telangana, India, from Rachakonda and Devarakonda. The Bahmanis took Warangal in the 1420s and later their forts; the end date is approximate.

Reddi kingdom.text: A Telugu kingdom in Andhra Pradesh founded by Prolaya Vema Reddi after the Kakatiyas fell in 1323, ruling coastal and central Andhra. Its capital moved from Addanki to Kondavidu.

Reddi kingdom of Rajahmundry.text: The branch of the Reddi dynasty that held the Godavari delta around Rajahmundry in Andhra Pradesh, India, after Kondavidu fell in 1424. The Gajapati king Kapilendra took it c. 1448.

Regency of Algiers.text: A semi-independent Ottoman province in North Africa founded in 1516 by the corsair brothers Aruj and Hayreddin Barbarossa. It became the centre of Ottoman power in the Maghreb until France conquered it in 1830.

Republic of Albania.text: A small Balkan country on the Adriatic coast. After the fall of its isolated communist regime it held its first multiparty elections in 1991, and it later joined NATO in 2009.

Republic of Amalfi.text: A maritime republic on the coast of southern Italy that traded across the Mediterranean in the 900s and 1000s. Led by its duke, it sank in importance after the Normans conquered it and Pisa sacked it in 1135.

Republic of Armenia.text: A small, mountainous country in the South Caucasus, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. In 301 Armenia became the first state to make Christianity its official religion.

Republic of Azerbaijan.text: A country on the Caspian Sea in the South Caucasus, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. Its capital, Baku, supplied a large share of Soviet oil in the Second World War, and oil still drives its economy.

Republic of Baden.text: A revolutionary government set up in Baden in May 1849, when Grand Duke Leopold fled Karlsruhe during the German revolutions. Prussian troops entered Freiburg on 7 July, and the last stronghold, Rastatt, surrendered on 23 July. The article linked here covers a later republic, 1918 to 1945.

Republic of Baja California.text: A would-be republic proclaimed at La Paz in November 1853 by the American adventurer William Walker and a small band of mercenaries. It was never recognised and never controlled the peninsula; facing Mexican resistance, Walker gave up in 1854 and surrendered to US forces.

Republic of Belarus.text: A landlocked country in Eastern Europe that became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. Alexander Lukashenko has been president since 1994, and the country remains closely tied to Russia.

Republic of Benin.text: A West African country on the Gulf of Guinea, independent from France in 1960 as Dahomey. In 1975 it took the name Benin from the Bight of Benin off its coast (itself named for the old Benin kingdom in Nigeria), and its Marxist rule ended in 1990.

Republic of Botswana.text: A landlocked country in southern Africa, mostly the Kalahari Desert, independent from Britain in 1966 as Bechuanaland. Led by Seretse Khama, it stayed democratic and grew rich from diamonds, becoming one of Africa's steady success stories.

Republic of Bulgaria.text: A Balkan country on the Black Sea. Its communist government fell in 1989, and the country became a democratic republic. It joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007.

Republic of Burundi.text: A small, landlocked country in the African Great Lakes region, independent from Belgium in 1962 as a kingdom. The monarchy was abolished in 1966, and ethnic violence between Hutu and Tutsi marked much of its later history.

Republic of Cabo Verde.text: A chain of volcanic islands in the Atlantic off West Africa, uninhabited until Portuguese settlement in the 1400s. It became independent in 1975 and is today one of Africa's more stable democracies.

Republic of Cameroon.text: A country in west-central Africa that became independent from French rule on 1 January 1960. In 1961 the southern part of British Cameroons joined it. It is nicknamed Africa in miniature for its varied landscapes and many languages.

Republic of Chad.text: A huge landlocked country in north-central Africa, independent from France in 1960. It stretches from the Sahara in the north to the savanna in the south, and decades of civil conflict marked its early history.

Republic of Chile.text: A long, narrow republic squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific. Chilean patriots first set up self-government in 1810, and independence from Spain was won in the following years under leaders like Bernardo O'Higgins. Its capital is Santiago.

Republic of Costa Rica.text: A Central American republic between Nicaragua and Panama, free of Spanish rule since 1821. After a brief civil war in 1948, its new constitution of 1949 abolished the army, making it one of the few countries with no standing military. Its capital is San José.

Republic of Croatia.text: A country on the Adriatic coast of southeastern Europe, which declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991 and fought a war until 1995. It joined the EU in 2013 and is famed for its coastline and islands.

Republic of Cuba.text: The independent Cuban state that began in 1902 after Spanish and American rule. Havana was its lively capital, and it ended in 1959 when Fidel Castro's revolution toppled the dictator Fulgencio Batista.

Republic of Cyprus.text: An island republic in the eastern Mediterranean, independent from Britain since 1960 with Greek and Turkish Cypriots sharing power. A coup and Turkish invasion in 1974 split the island, and Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004.

Republic of Côte d'Ivoire.text: A West African country, independent from France in 1960 under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who led it for 33 years. It became a major cocoa grower. The capital moved from Abidjan to Yamoussoukro, his home village, in 1983.

Republic of Djibouti.text: A small country on the Horn of Africa at the entrance to the Red Sea, independent from France in 1977. Its port is vital for shipping, and several foreign countries keep military bases there.

Republic of Ecuador.text: A country on the equator in northwestern South America, which left Gran Colombia and became a separate republic in 1830. It includes the Galápagos Islands and has Quito as its capital, with Guayaquil as its largest city.

Republic of Egypt.text: Egypt after the 1952 revolution toppled King Farouk, when it became a republic in 1953. Gamal Abdel Nasser took power and nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956, which led to a crisis.

Republic of El Salvador.text: The smallest country in Central America, on the Pacific coast between Guatemala and Honduras. It left the Central American federation and became a separate republic around 1841. Its capital is San Salvador.

Republic of Estonia.text: A Baltic country in northern Europe, first independent in 1918, taken over by the Soviet Union in 1940, and independent again in 1991. It is known for its digital government services.

Republic of Fiji.text: An island country of more than 300 islands in the South Pacific, independent from Britain in October 1970. Its population mixes indigenous Fijians and descendants of Indian workers brought to farm sugar cane.

Republic of Finland.text: A Nordic republic that became independent from Russia in 1917. A short civil war was fought in 1918 between Reds and Whites. Finland is known for its lakes and forests, and Helsinki is its capital.

Republic of Florence.text: A city-state in Tuscany, Italy, that began in 1115 when Florentines threw off the rule of the margraves of Tuscany. Guild members chose its leaders, and its banking wealth and art made it a European powerhouse. On this map it continues under the Medici until 1737.

Republic of Genoa.text: A maritime republic on the Ligurian coast of Italy, ruled by an elected doge. Its merchants and ships built a trading empire across the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, until Napoleon ended it in 1797.

Republic of Guinea-Bissau.text: A small West African country that declared independence from Portugal in 1973, after a guerrilla war led by Amilcar Cabral, who was killed that year. Portugal recognised it in 1974.

Republic of Iceland.text: An island republic in the North Atlantic, declared on 17 June 1944 when it ended its union with Denmark. It is sparsely populated, volcanic, and has Reykjavík as its capital.

Republic of Iraq.text: A country in the land of ancient Mesopotamia, home to Babylon. The US-led invasion of 2003 toppled Saddam Hussein, and years of insurgency followed. Today it is a federal republic with a Kurdish region in the north.

Republic of Kenya.text: An East African country that became independent from Britain in December 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, after the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s. It is known for its safaris and its long-distance runners.

Republic of Korea.text: South Korea, founded in 1948 in the south of the Korean peninsula, with Syngman Rhee as its first president. After war, coups and dictatorship, its economy grew at one of the fastest rates in the world, and it became a democracy in 1987. Its capital is Seoul.

Republic of Latvia.text: A Baltic republic that declared independence on 18 November 1918. The Soviet Union took it over in 1940, and Latvia became independent again in 1991. Its capital is Riga.

Republic of Lithuania.text: A Baltic country that declared independence from the Soviet Union on 11 March 1990, the first Soviet republic to do so. In the Middle Ages it was a great power in a union with Poland.

Republic of Lucca.text: A city-republic in Tuscany, Italy, independent from the 12th century. Under Castruccio Castracani (1316-1328) it briefly ruled much of western Tuscany. The French turned it into a principality in 1805.

Republic of Mali.text: A large landlocked West African country, independent from France in 1960. It lies on the lands of the medieval Mali Empire, and the old city of Timbuktu was a renowned centre of learning.

Republic of Moldova.text: A small country between Romania and Ukraine, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. A breakaway strip on its eastern edge, Transnistria, has been outside government control since a 1992 war.

Republic of Nicaragua.text: The largest country in Central America, with big lakes and many volcanoes. It became independent from Spain in 1821 and later left the federation of Central America. Its capital is Managua.

Republic of Panama.text: A Central American republic that broke away from Colombia in 1903 with American support. The United States then built the Panama Canal, which opened in 1914. Its capital is Panama City.

Republic of Peru.text: A republic on South America's Pacific coast, once the heart of the Inca Empire and the Spanish viceroyalty. Independence was proclaimed in 1821 by José de San Martín, and the war ended in 1824. Its capital is Lima.

Republic of Pisa.text: A maritime republic in Tuscany, Italy, that grew rich on Mediterranean trade. It was Genoa's great rival at sea, lost the naval Battle of Meloria in 1284, and fell to Florence in 1406.

Republic of Poland.text: A Central European country on the Baltic Sea. After the war it was communist-run until the Solidarity movement helped end that in 1989. It joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004. Its capital is Warsaw.

Republic of Ragusa.text: A merchant city-state around Dubrovnik in southern Croatia, ruled by a council of noble families. Its Latin motto said liberty should not be sold for any amount of gold, and it paid tribute to bigger powers to stay independent and wealthy until Napoleon's forces ended it in 1808.

Republic of Rwanda.text: A small, hilly country in Africa's Great Lakes region, independent from Belgium in 1962. In 1994 between half a million and a million people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in a genocide. The country has since rebuilt and is known for its mountain gorillas.

Republic of San Marino.text: A tiny republic entirely surrounded by Italy, on the slopes of the Apennines, and one of the world's oldest republics. By tradition it was founded in 301 by Saint Marinus, and it is still independent today.

Republic of Senegal.text: The westernmost country of mainland Africa, independent from France in 1960 after a short union with Mali. Its first president, the poet Léopold Senghor, ruled for 20 years and stepped down peacefully.

Republic of Serbia.text: A country in southeastern Europe that became fully independent in 2006 after Montenegro left their union. It was once a medieval kingdom, and Belgrade sits where the Sava meets the Danube.

Republic of Siena.text: A city-republic in southern Tuscany, Italy, ruled by merchant governments such as the Nine. After a siege in 1554-1555 it surrendered to Charles V's forces, and in 1557 it was handed to Cosimo de' Medici of Florence.

Republic of Singapore.text: A city-state on a small island off the tip of the Malay Peninsula. It became independent in 1965 after being separated from Malaysia, and under Lee Kuan Yew grew into one of the world's richest trading hubs.

Republic of Slovenia.text: A small, green country in central Europe that declared independence from Yugoslavia in June 1991. A brief ten-day war followed, after which it became a sovereign state, and it joined the EU and NATO in 2004.

Republic of Sudan.text: A country in northeast Africa that became independent in 1956 from Britain and Egypt. It was Africa's largest country until South Sudan split away in 2011. Its capital is Khartoum.

Republic of Suriname.text: A small country on the northeast coast of South America, independent from the Netherlands in 1975. It is the only independent country outside Europe where Dutch is the official language, and most of its land is rainforest.

Republic of Syria.text: Syria after it broke out of its union with Egypt in September 1961 following an army coup, ending the United Arab Republic. This short-lived republic lasted only until another coup in March 1963 brought the Ba'ath Party to power.

Republic of Tajikistan.text: A mountainous country in Central Asia, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. A civil war raged from 1992 to 1997. Most of its people speak a form of Persian.

Republic of Texas.text: An independent country that broke from Mexico in 1836 after the Texas Revolution, with Sam Houston as its first elected president. Mexico refused to recognise it. The United States annexed it in December 1845, and power passed to the new state government in February 1846.

Republic of The Gambia.text: The smallest country on mainland Africa, a narrow strip along both banks of the Gambia River, surrounded by Senegal except on its Atlantic coast. It became independent from Britain in 1965 and a republic in 1970.

Republic of Trinidad and Tobago.text: A two-island country in the southern Caribbean, independent from Britain in 1962 and a republic from 1976. Calypso music and the steelpan were born there, and it has important oil and gas reserves.

Republic of Tunisia.text: A North African country on the Mediterranean that became independent from France in 1956 under Habib Bourguiba. The 2010 to 2011 protests that began the Arab Spring started here. Its capital is Tunis.

Republic of Uganda.text: A landlocked East African country, independent from Britain in 1962. It takes in a large part of Lake Victoria and lies in the basin of the Nile. Idi Amin ruled it as a brutal dictator from 1971 to 1979.

Republic of Uryankhay.text: A breakaway state in Tuva, in southern Siberia, proclaimed in late 1911 as Qing rule collapsed during China's Xinhai Revolution. Encouraged by Russia, its leaders accepted Russian protection in 1914, when it became Uryankhay Krai. Tuva is now part of Russia.

Republic of Uzbekistan.text: A doubly landlocked country in Central Asia, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. The great Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva lie within it.

Republic of Venezuela.text: The first attempts at an independent Venezuela began in 1811, when leaders in Caracas broke from Spain. The young republic collapsed in 1812 under royalist attacks, and Simón Bolívar's revived republic of 1813 to 1814 also fell.

Republic of Vietnam.text: South Vietnam, a state in the southern half of Vietnam from 1955 to 1975, based in Saigon. It fought the communist north with American support, and it fell on 30 April 1975.

Republic of Yemen.text: A country in southern Arabia, formed in May 1990 when North Yemen united with communist South Yemen. A civil war in 1994 and another since 2015 have made it one of the poorest countries in the Middle East.

Republic of Zimbabwe.text: A southern African country, independent in April 1980 after a guerrilla war against white-minority Rhodesia. Robert Mugabe led it for 37 years. Great Zimbabwe, a medieval stone city, gave the country its name.

Republic of the Congo.text: A country on the west bank of the Congo River, independent from France in 1960 and often called Congo-Brazzaville. It was officially a Marxist state, the People's Republic of the Congo, from 1969 until 1992.

Republic of the Niger.text: A large landlocked West African country, mostly in the Sahara, independent from France in 1960. Most people live in the less dry south and west, where farming is possible, and it exports uranium ore.

Republic of the Philippines.text: An island country in Southeast Asia, named for King Philip II of Spain. It became independent from the United States in 1946 and has Manila as its capital.

Republic of the Rif.text: A republic in the Rif mountains of northern Morocco, led by Abd el-Krim after his fighters crushed a Spanish army at Annual in 1921. France and Spain then joined forces against it with huge armies, and Abd el-Krim surrendered in 1926.

Republic of the Rio Grande.text: A breakaway government in northeastern Mexico, set up in January 1840 by federalists opposed to Mexico's centralist rulers. After defeats by Mexican troops, its leaders made peace at Camargo in November 1840. Its own papers never actually called it a republic.

Revolutionary Roman Republic.text: A short-lived French sister republic in Rome that was proclaimed in February 1798 after French troops occupied the city. It fell in 1799 when Neapolitan and other forces took Rome.

Rewa.text: The largest princely state in Baghelkhand, in present-day Madhya Pradesh. It acceded to India in 1947. Like other princely states, it kept its own ruler under British overlordship until 1947.

Rhodes.text: The island republic of Rhodes in the Aegean, a rich trading city with a fine navy, famed for its Colossus statue. In 188 BCE Rome rewarded it with most of Lycia and Caria after the war with Antiochus III.

Rhodesia.text: A breakaway state in southern Africa, where the white-minority government under Ian Smith declared independence from Britain in 1965 to avoid Black majority rule. No country recognised it. It faced a guerrilla war and gave way to Zimbabwe.

Riau-Lingga Sultanate.text: A Malay sultanate in the Riau Islands of Indonesia, created in 1824 when the old Johor-Riau realm was split between Britain and the Netherlands. It was recognised by both powers, and the Dutch dissolved it in 1911.

Riograndense Republic.text: A rebel republic in southern Brazil, roughly today's Rio Grande do Sul, proclaimed in 1836 during the Ragamuffin War against the Brazilian Empire. Called the Piratini Republic, it fought nearly ten years before peace came in 1845.

Rohilkhand (Rohilla state).text: A state of Rohilla Afghan chiefs led by Ali Muhammad Khan in Uttar Pradesh, around Bareilly, Moradabad and Bijnor, effectively independent of Delhi by the 1740s. Awadh conquered it in 1774 with British East India Company help.

Romania.text: A country in southeastern Europe whose communist ruler Nicolae Ceausescu was overthrown and executed in the violent revolution of December 1989. It then moved to democracy and joined the EU in 2007.

Rotuman chiefdoms.text: Rotuma is a small volcanic island group north of Fiji, home to Polynesian people living in seven districts, each under its own chief. Rivalries among those chiefs led them to cede the island to Britain in 1881, and today it is a self-governing dependency of Fiji.

Rozvi Empire.text: A Shona state in present-day Zimbabwe ruled by the Changamire, who drove the Portuguese from the plateau in 1693-95. Its capital was Danangombe (Dhlo-Dhlo), and Nguni invasions in the 1830s ended it as a state.

Rugiland.text: Rugiland was a short-lived kingdom of the Germanic Rugii, on the north bank of the Danube in what is now Austria. It rose in the mid-5th century after the Huns' fall, and Odoacer destroyed it in 487.

Rustamid dynasty.text: An Ibadi Muslim dynasty in present-day Algeria, c. 777 to 909, founded by the Persian-born Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam. Its capital Tahert was known for learning and tolerance before the Fatimids overran it.

Ryazan.text: A Russian principality on the Oka river, southeast of Moscow, first formed in 1129 as Murom-Ryazan. Its princes allied with and fought the steppe peoples, and it stayed independent until Moscow annexed it in 1521.

Ryukyu Kingdom.text: A kingdom on Okinawa and the nearby Ryukyu Islands, formed in 1429 when the Chūzan king united the island. It traded between China, Japan and Southeast Asia, paying tribute to Ming China. Japan formally abolished it in 1879.

Saar Protectorate.text: A protectorate of France in the Saar region of western Germany, 1947-56, with its own constitution and government. It shared a customs and currency union with France; after voters rejected a European statute in 1955, the Saar joined West Germany in 1957.

Sabaeans.text: The people of Saba, or Sheba, a South Arabian kingdom in today's Yemen, rich from the frankincense and myrrh trade. A legendary queen of Sheba appears in the Bible; the kingdom lasted until Himyar took over around 275 CE.

Sacred Band of Thebes.text: The city of Thebes in central Greece, which briefly became the leading Greek power after beating Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE. It was known for the Sacred Band, an elite corps of 300 soldiers, which Philip II of Macedon wiped out at Chaeronea in 338 BCE.

Sagaing Kingdom.text: A small kingdom in upper Burma around the city of Sagaing, ruled from 1315 by a junior branch of the Myinsaing royal line. It broke free of Pinya's overlordship and lasted until about 1364, when Ava absorbed it.

Sai.text: A short-lived kingdom in northeastern Shaanxi, China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE. Its king was the Qin general Sima Xin. With Yong and Di it formed the Three Qins, which Liu Bang defeated.

Saint Kitts.text: An island in the eastern Caribbean, an old British sugar colony. From 1967 it was part of a self-governing association with Nevis and Anguilla, and it later became the main island of the independent nation of Saint Kitts and Nevis.

Saint Kitts and Nevis.text: The smallest country in the Americas by area, a two-island nation in the Caribbean. It became independent from Britain in September 1983. It was the first British colony in the Caribbean to be settled, in 1623.

Saint Lucia.text: A volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, famous for its twin Piton peaks. It was fought over by the British and French and became independent from Britain in 1979. It has produced two Nobel prize winners.

Saint Vincent.text: The main island of an eastern Caribbean group, a British colony that became a self-governing associated state in 1969. It gained full independence in 1979 as Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, with its capital at Kingstown.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.text: An eastern Caribbean country made of the main island of Saint Vincent and a chain of small islands, the Grenadines. It became independent from Britain in 1979.

Sajid Dynasty.text: An Iranian Muslim dynasty that ruled Azerbaijan and Armenia, c. 889 to 929, as governors of the Abbasid caliphs who became semi-independent. Their capital was Maragheh.

Salamis.text: The strongest city-kingdom of Cyprus on the east coast, c. 600-312 BCE, ruled by kings such as Evelthon, Onesilus and Evagoras I. It paid tribute to Assyria and Persia, and passed under Ptolemy's control.

Salamis (Tamassos).text: The city-kingdom of Salamis on Cyprus in 332-312 BCE, when it also held the territory of Tamassos. Its kings Pnytagoras and Nicocreon ruled under Persia and then Alexander; Ptolemy of Egypt then took control of Cyprus.

Salghurids.text: Turkmen atabegs who ruled Fars, in southern Iran, from Shiraz as a hereditary state. They were first vassals of the Seljuks, then the Khwarazmshahs and Mongols; the line ended in the 1280s after Abish Khatun's rule.

Sallarid dynasty.text: A Daylamite dynasty (the Musafirids) that took Azerbaijan in northwestern Iran in 941 under Marzuban ibn Muhammad. They ruled from Ardabil and later Tabriz until the Rawwadids replaced them in the 980s.

Saloum.text: A Serer-Wolof kingdom in Senegal ruled by the Buur Saloum from Kahone, founded c. 1494. It left Jolof's control in 1520 and held tribute-paying Gambia river chiefdoms, until French conquest in the late 19th century, after the wars of Maba Diakhou Bâ in the 1860s.

Saltukids.text: A Turkmen beylik centred on Erzurum in eastern Anatolia (now Turkey), founded after the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071. It lasted until the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum annexed it in 1202.

Sambuvaraya chiefdom (Tondaimandalam).text: A chiefdom of former Chola vassals in northern Tamil Nadu, India, whose chiefs issued records in their own regnal years in the early 14th century. Rajanarayana allied with Harihara I of Vijayanagara but was eventually overcome by it.

Samo's Empire.text: Samo's realm was the first recorded Slavic state in Central Europe, founded by a Frankish merchant named Samo who led a Slav revolt against the Avars in the 620s CE. It fell apart after he died in 658.

Samoa.text: A Polynesian island nation in the South Pacific, made of two large islands, Upolu and Savai'i, and several small ones. In 1962 it became the first Pacific island state to win independence, from New Zealand.

Samorian State (Wassoulou Empire).text: A Mandinka state built by Samori Ture on the upper Niger and Milo rivers in present-day Guinea and Mali, at its widest in the 1880s. Driven east by the French, he rebuilt it in northern Côte d'Ivoire until he was captured in 1898.

Samtskhe-Saatabago.text: A Georgian principality in the southwest, ruled from 1268 by the Jaqeli family as hereditary atabegs, a title meaning tutor. Its atabeg Qvarqvare II broke away from the Georgian crown in 1465; it became an Ottoman vassal in the 1540s, and its line ruled until about 1628.

Samudera Pasai Sultanate.text: A Muslim sultanate on Sumatra's northern coast, flourishing from the late 1200s into the early 1500s. Tradition credits Merah Silu, who converted and took the name Malik al-Saleh, with founding it, and it counts among the first Islamic states of Southeast Asia.

Saraikela and Kharsawan (Chota Nagpur st.text: Two small princely states of the Chota Nagpur region, in present-day Jharkhand, under Bengal in 1909 and later in the Eastern States Agency. They merged into India on 1 January 1948.

Sarbadars.text: A short-lived state in Khorasan, northeast Iran, set up in 1337 by rebels during the collapse of the Mongol Ilkhanate. The name means head on the gallows. Its leaders mixed dervishes and secular rulers, and its last ruler submitted to Timur in 1381.

Sasak kingdoms.text: Small kingdoms of the Sasak people of Lombok, Indonesia, drawn here until about 1740. The Sasaks, whose language and ancestry link them to the Balinese, became Muslim in the late 1500s and early 1600s, while rulers from neighbouring Bali, starting with Gelgel, repeatedly sought to dominate the island.

Satara State (Bhonsle rump).text: A small Maratha state around Satara in Maharashtra, set up by the East India Company in 1818 for Pratap Singh, a descendant of Shivaji, after the Peshwa fell. It was annexed in 1848-49 under the doctrine of lapse.

Satavahana Dynasty.text: A dynasty ruling the Deccan plateau and much of central India until about 224 CE. It grew rich from trade with Rome, used the Prakrit language on its coins, and supported Buddhist monuments such as the stupa at Amaravati.

Saxe-Altenburg.text: A small Saxon duchy in Thuringia, ruled by a branch of the Wettin family, and one of the smallest German states. It had around 200,000 people in 1905 and lasted until 1918.

Saxe-Coburg and Gotha.text: A German duchy in Thuringia and Bavaria, made from the lands of Coburg and Gotha in 1826. Prince Albert, husband of Queen Victoria, came from this ruling family, and the duchy lasted until 1918.

Saxe-Meiningen.text: A duchy in southwestern Thuringia, Germany, created around 1680 when the Ernestine duchy of Saxe-Gotha was divided among the sons of Duke Ernest the Pious. It was ruled by its own line of the Wettin family until monarchy ended in 1918.

Saxons.text: The Saxons were a Germanic people of northern Germany. Some of them sailed to Britain, while those who stayed fought Charlemagne for decades until forced to convert and submit by about 804. This entry shows their homeland.

Scandinavian minor kingdoms.text: Before Norway, Sweden and Denmark united, Scandinavia was a patchwork of small chiefdoms and kingdoms. This includes the Vendel period, c. 550 to 800 CE, known for rich boat burials and ornate metalwork, ahead of the Viking Age.

Second Athenian League.text: A sea alliance of Aegean Greek city-states founded in 378 BCE, led by Athens as a way to resist Sparta. Its members were promised that Athens would not take their land or tribute, but a revolt of allies in the 350s broke it up.

Second Polish Republic.text: The Polish state between the world wars, from 1918 to 1939. Poland regained its independence as the First World War ended, after being divided among its neighbours for over a hundred years, and was invaded by Germany and the Soviet Union in September 1939.

Second Syrian Republic.text: Syria after the French left in 1946. Its early years saw many military coups, and in 1958 Syria joined Egypt in the United Arab Republic. Damascus was its capital.

Sena Dynasty.text: A Hindu ruling house that took over Bengal after the Pala Empire and held much of eastern India from the late 11th into the 13th century. Vijaya Sena (1096-1159) built up its power; c. 1203-04 the Ghurid general Bakhtiyar Khalji seized its capital, though Sena kings held on in eastern Bengal.

Septinsular Republic.text: The Republic of the Seven Islands, an oligarchic republic on the Ionian Islands off Greece from 1800 to 1807. It was set up under Russian and Ottoman protection, with Corfu as its capital.

Serbia.text: The Kingdom of Serbia in 1918, which had fought hard in the First World War and then joined with Croats and Slovenes. In December 1918 it became the core of the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia.

Serbia-Montenegro.text: A union of Serbia and Montenegro, formed in 1992 as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and renamed in 2003. It dissolved when Montenegro voted for independence in 2006.

Serbian Despots.text: The last medieval Serbian state, the Despotate, which survived for decades after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Its first ruler Stefan Lazarević was given the title despot in 1402, and it fell to the Ottomans by 1459.

Serbian Empire.text: A medieval Balkan empire built by Stefan Dušan, who proclaimed himself tsar in 1345 and founded the empire in 1346. For a short time it was among Europe's strongest states, but after he died in 1355 it slowly fractured into rival lordships, ending with his son Uroš V's death in 1371.

Serbs.text: The Serbs, a South Slavic people, shown here in the years from the Serbian Revolution that began in 1804. Serbia grew from a self-governing principality into an independent state in the 1800s.

Seychelles.text: An island nation of about 115 islands in the Indian Ocean northeast of Madagascar. It was uninhabited until the 1700s, and became independent from Britain in 1976. It is famed for its beaches and giant tortoises.

Shaddadids.text: A Kurdish dynasty ruling Arran, between the Kura river and the Karabakh hills, c. 951-1075, first from Dvin and then from Ganja. The Seljuks took it in 1075, and a junior branch governed Ani until 1199.

Shailodbhava kingdom (Kongoda).text: A dynasty ruling Kongoda, part of today's Ganjam, Khordha and Puri districts of Odisha, c. 620-771 CE. After serving as vassals of the Guptas and others, Madhavaraja II took independence; the Bhauma-Karas later took the land.

Shaki Khanate.text: A khanate around Nukha (Shaki) in north-western Azerbaijan, self-governing after Nader Shah's death in 1747 under nominal Iranian overlordship. Russia absorbed the Caucasian khanates in the early 19th century.

Shan States.text: A group of small Tai principalities called möng, ruled by princes with the title saopha, in the hills of eastern Myanmar and nearby lands. They paid tribute to powerful neighbours, and the British later used the name Shan States for them in colonial Burma.

Sharabhapuriya kingdom (Dakshina Kosala).text: A dynasty ruling Chhattisgarh, then called Dakshina Kosala, with parts of Odisha, c. 555-590 CE. Its kings Sharabha, Narendra and Prasanna were at first vassals of the Guptas. Scholars disagree on its exact dates.

Shekhawati (Shekhawat chiefs under Amber.text: A region of chiefships north of Jaipur in Rajasthan, ruled by Shekhawat Rajput chiefs at Sikar, Khetri, Jhunjhunu and Nawalgarh. They governed their own estates but were tributaries of Amber (Jaipur).

Shilluk Kingdom.text: A kingdom of the Shilluk people on the west bank of the White Nile in present-day South Sudan, founded c. 1490 by tradition. Its ruler, the reth, is still seen as a sacred figure, and the kingdom pushed northward along the river until the 1860s.

Shirvan.text: A medieval state in the eastern Caucasus, lying between the Kura River and the Caspian coast in present-day Azerbaijan. Its Shirvanshah rulers, a Persianized dynasty of Arab origin, held it from 809, sometimes independently and sometimes as vassals of larger empires, until Safavid Iran took control in the 1500s.

Shirvan Khanate.text: A khanate in eastern Azerbaijan with its capital at Shamakhi, under nominal Iranian suzerainty after Nader Shah's death in 1747. Russia annexed it in 1820.

Shu Han.text: Shu Han was one of China's Three Kingdoms, founded in 221 CE by Liu Bei, who claimed to continue the Han dynasty. Based in Sichuan, with the strategist Zhuge Liang as its chief minister, it was conquered by Wei in 263.

Shunten Dynasty.text: The second dynasty in the traditional history of Okinawa, said to have begun in 1187 under Shunten, whose father was supposedly the Japanese adventurer Minamoto no Tametomo. It had three rulers, who were really paramount chiefs, and ended in 1259.

Sierra Leone.text: A West African country, independent from Britain in 1961. Freed Black settlers from London arrived in 1787, Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia founded Freetown in 1792, and later people freed from slave ships joined them. A brutal civil war ran from 1991 to 2002.

Signoria of Milan.text: The lordship over Milan, held by the della Torre from 1259 and by the Visconti after the victory at Desio in 1277. Under Azzone and his successors it spread across most of Lombardy.

Sikkim.text: A Himalayan kingdom, a British protectorate from the Treaty of Tumlong in 1861, with Tumlong as its capital until 1894 and then Gangtok. It did not join India in 1947, became an Indian protectorate in 1950 and an Indian state in 1975.

Silla.text: Silla began around 57 BCE as a small kingdom in southeast Korea and became the winner among Korea's Three Kingdoms. Allied with Tang China, it conquered Baekje and Goguryeo, then ruled most of the peninsula until 935.

Sind-Habbari Dynasty.text: An Arab emirate in Sindh, in present-day Pakistan, founded around 854 by Umar al-Habbari and ruled from Mansura. It acted almost independently of the caliphs until Mahmud of Ghazni conquered it in 1026.

Sind-Samma Dynasty.text: A Muslim dynasty of Sindh, now in Pakistan, founded in 1351 after it broke away from the Delhi Sultanate. Its rulers took the title jam, and they built up Thatta as a rich trading city before falling in the early 1500s.

Singhasari.text: A Javanese Hindu-Buddhist kingdom in East Java, 1222-1292, founded by Ken Arok, which replaced Kediri as the leading power on the island. Its last king, Kertanegara, was killed in a revolt, and his son-in-law founded Majapahit.

Sirohi State.text: A Deora Chauhan state around Mount Abu in Rajasthan, India. It suffered wars with Jodhpur, which claimed suzerainty, and sought British protection in 1817, with a treaty in 1823.

Sloboda Ukraine.text: A frontier region of northeastern Ukraine and southwestern Russia, settled in the 1600s by Ukrainian refugees on land granted by the Tsar. It was made a Russian governorate in 1765, and its main city was Kharkiv.

Slovak Republic.text: A client state of Nazi Germany in present-day Slovakia, 1939-45, declared on 14 March 1939 as Czecho-Slovakia broke up. It lost southern land to Hungary and ended when the Red Army took Bratislava in April 1945.

Slovakia.text: A central European country that became independent on 1 January 1993, when Czechoslovakia peacefully divided in two. It joined the EU in 2004 and is a mountainous land with many castles.

Small Horde.text: The Lesser Nogai Horde, a nomadic Muslim group of Mongol-Turkic herders who split from the main Nogai Horde in the 1550s and roamed the Kuban steppe of the North Caucasus. It declined under pressure from the Kalmyks and the Russian state.

Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.text: A communist federation led by Josip Broz Tito from 1945. It joined six republics, including Serbia and Croatia, and broke away from Stalin in 1948. After Tito died, it fell apart in violent wars in the early 1990s.

Socialist Republic of Romania.text: The communist state of Romania, in power from 1947. Nicolae Ceaușescu led it from 1965 until the revolution of December 1989, when he was overthrown and executed.

Socialist Republic of Vietnam.text: The reunified communist Vietnam, proclaimed in 1976 after North Vietnam's victory in the war and the fall of Saigon in 1975. It is ruled by the Communist Party, which began market reforms in 1986.

Soli.text: A city-kingdom on the north-west coast of Cyprus, c. 600-312 BCE, ruled by its own kings such as Aristocyprus and Pasicrates. It paid tribute to Assyria and Persia until the Ptolemaic takeover of Cyprus.

Solomon Islands.text: An island country in the southwest Pacific, made up of six main islands and more than a thousand smaller ones. Guadalcanal saw fierce fighting in World War II. It was a British protectorate and became independent in 1978.

Solomon Islands chiefdoms.text: The island communities of the Solomon Islands in the southwest Pacific, settled by Papuan peoples at least 30,000 years ago and later by Austronesian seafarers. Spanish ships arrived in 1568, Britain declared a protectorate in 1893, and the country became independent in 1978.

Somaliland.text: A self-declared state in northwest Somalia, formerly British Somaliland. It broke away in 1991 during Somalia's civil war and has run its own elected governments. Israel recognised it in December 2025, the first UN member to do so.

Somavamshi kingdom.text: A dynasty of Odisha, c. 882-1000 on this map, first holding western Odisha and then coastal Utkala after replacing the Bhauma-Karas. Its kings, such as Janamejaya I and Yayati I, ruled from Binka and later Jajpur.

Sonargaon Sultanate.text: A sultanate of eastern Bengal that broke from Delhi under Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah in 1338. He took Chittagong in 1340, and Ilyas Shah defeated the sultanate in 1352.

Song.text: A Zhou-dynasty state in eastern Henan, set up for descendants of the overthrown Shang kings so that they could continue their ancestor worship. It lasted until Qi conquered it in 286 BCE.

Soomra dynasty (Lower Sindh).text: A local dynasty of Lower Sindh in Pakistan, c. 1026-1343. It paid tribute to the Ghaznavids at first and later submitted to Iltutmish of Delhi. Dodo I and several kings called Hamir are listed; the early record is thin, and the Samma dynasty followed.

Sosso Empire.text: A West African kingdom in today's Mali, also called Kaniaga, that started out subject to the Ghana Empire, then broke away and conquered its former overlords. It peaked under King Soumaoro Kanté, who was defeated by Sundiata Keita of the rising Mali Empire.

South Sudan.text: The world's newest country, which split from Sudan on 9 July 2011 after a referendum. A civil war began in 2013 and has slowed its development. It lies in the Nile basin.

Southern Chu.text: A kingdom in present-day Hunan, China, from 907 to 951, one of the Ten Kingdoms. Founded by Ma Yin, it grew prosperous selling horses, silk and tea, and was conquered by the Southern Tang after quarrels over the throne.

Southern Liang.text: Southern Liang was a short-lived Sixteen Kingdoms state in the Gansu and Qinghai region, ruled by Tufa Xianbei princes from 397 CE. After wars with Later Qin and a famine it fell to Western Qin in 414. It is not the later Liang dynasty of southern China.

Southern Yan.text: Southern Yan was a Xianbei state in what is now Shandong, set up in 398 CE by Murong De after the fall of Later Yan's heartland. Its rule lasted only until 410, when the Eastern Jin general Liu Yu conquered it.

Soviet zone.text: The Soviet occupation zone of Germany, 1945-49, one of four zones set up after the May 1945 surrender, under the Allied Control Council in Berlin. The western zones became the Federal Republic in 1949, and the Soviet zone the East German state.

Sri Lanka.text: An island country in the Indian Ocean south of India, formerly called Ceylon. It became independent from Britain in 1948 and took its present name in 1972. A civil war lasted from 1983 to 2009.

State of Buenos Aires.text: A breakaway state formed in 1852, when the province of Buenos Aires overthrew the Argentine Confederation's authority there and refused to accept its constitution. It ruled itself until 1861, when its own victory at the Battle of Pavón led it to rejoin the Confederation.

State of Eritrea.text: A country on the Red Sea coast of the Horn of Africa. After a thirty-year war it broke away from Ethiopia, and a referendum in 1993 confirmed its independence.

State of Israel.text: A country on the eastern Mediterranean, declared independent on 14 May 1948 as the British mandate in Palestine ended. A war with its Arab neighbours followed at once. Jerusalem is its seat of government, though its status is disputed.

State of Kuwait.text: A small, oil-rich emirate at the top of the Persian Gulf, independent from Britain in June 1961. Iraq at first refused to recognise it, claiming it as Iraqi land. Saddam Hussein invaded in 1990, and a US-led coalition drove his army out in 1991.

State of Libya.text: The North African country that has been in turmoil since an uprising in 2011 ended Muammar Gaddafi's rule. Rival governments have competed for control in the years since.

State of Qatar.text: A small peninsula state in the Persian Gulf, independent from Britain in 1971. Huge natural gas fields made it among the richest countries per person, and it hosted the 2022 football World Cup.

Strathclyde.text: Strathclyde, also called Alt Clut, was a Brittonic kingdom around the River Clyde in southwest Scotland. It survived Vikings and Angles for centuries, and joined the Scottish kingdom in the 11th century.

Sukhothai Kingdom.text: A Siamese kingdom around the city of Sukhothai in north-central Thailand, founded in 1238 by Si Inthrathit after a revolt against Khmer-dominated overlords. It was largest under Ram Khamhaeng (1279-1298) and fell under neighbouring Ayutthaya's sway in 1438.

Sulayhid Dynasty.text: An Ismaili Shi'a Arab dynasty founded by Ali al-Sulayhi in 1047 that ruled most of Yemen at its height. It was an ally of the Fatimid Caliphate in Cairo and is remembered for peace and prosperity there.

Sulayhid dynasty.text: An Ismaili dynasty in Yemen, 1047-1138, founded by Ali al-Sulayhi as an ally of the Fatimids. At its height (1063-1067) it ruled most of Yemen; Queen Arwa later ruled and, from about 1087, moved the capital to Dhu Jibla.

Sultan of Yogyakarta.text: A Javanese court at Yogyakarta, founded in 1755 when Prince Mangkubumi became Sultan Hamengkubuwono I after the Treaty of Giyanti split Mataram. His house still rules the special region of Yogyakarta today.

Sultanate of Aceh.text: A sultanate at the northern tip of Sumatra, Indonesia, founded in 1496 and strong in the 1500s and 1600s. It fought Portuguese Malacca and Johor for control of Strait of Malacca trade in pepper and tin, and was a centre of Islamic learning until its sultan surrendered to the Dutch in 1903.

Sultanate of Agadez.text: A Tuareg sultanate of the Aïr massif in Niger, founded c. 1405 according to oral history, with its seat at Agadez soon after the town's founding. Songhai conquered it in 1500, and it was independent again from 1591.

Sultanate of Aussa.text: An Afar sultanate of the Mudaito dynasty in the lower Awash valley, Ethiopia, with its capital at Asaita. It stayed outside the Ethiopian emperors' control until the 1890s, then autonomous under Menelik until 1936.

Sultanate of Banjar.text: A Muslim sultanate in southern Borneo, Indonesia, founded by Raden Samudera (Surianshah) after a civil war around 1520-1526. When the Dutch meddled in its royal succession, resistance grew into the Banjarmasin War of 1859, and the Dutch abolished the sultanate in 1860.

Sultanate of Banten.text: A pepper-trading sultanate on the northwest tip of Java, Indonesia, founded in the 1520s with the help of Sunan Gunungjati and his son Hasanuddin. It was a major port in the late 1500s and 1600s, then was overshadowed by Dutch Batavia and ended in 1813.

Sultanate of Bengal.text: A Muslim kingdom that dominated the Ganges and Brahmaputra delta, in today's Bangladesh and West Bengal, from 1352. It grew rich on trade in rice and cloth, with mint towns across the delta, before Mughal rule took over in the 1570s.

Sultanate of Bima.text: A Muslim sultanate in eastern Sumbawa, Indonesia, whose people called it the land of Mbojo. Its sultanate began around 1621 and it lasted into the twentieth century.

Sultanate of Bone.text: A Bugis kingdom in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, that became a sultanate after adopting Islam in 1611 under pressure from its rival Gowa. Its prince Arung Palakka later sided with the Dutch East India Company against Gowa, helping to capture Makassar in 1669. Bone kept its independence until a Dutch military defeat in 1905.

Sultanate of Brunei.text: A Malay sultanate on the northern coast of Borneo that became a sovereign power around the 1400s and later spread along the coasts of Borneo and the Philippines. It lost much land to Western powers and Sarawak's Brooke rajahs, became a British protectorate in 1888 and regained independence in 1984.

Sultanate of Cirebon.text: A Muslim sultanate on the north coast of West Java, Indonesia, traditionally founded by Sunan Gunungjati in the 1400s after declaring independence from the Sundanese kingdom of Pajajaran. It later split into smaller courts in the 1600s.

Sultanate of Damagaram.text: A Muslim sultanate in south-east Niger, founded in 1731 near Mirriah by Kanuri aristocrats, at first a vassal of Bornu. It took over many of Bornu's western vassal states, made Zinder its capital, and fell to a French column in 1899.

Sultanate of Darfur.text: A Muslim sultanate in western Sudan around the Marra Mountains, ruled by the Keira dynasty from the 1500s or 1600s until the warlord al-Zubayr conquered it in 1874. It was revived in 1898 under Ali Dinar and finally conquered by Britain in 1916.

Sultanate of Gowa.text: A Makassarese sultanate in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, and the most powerful kingdom of the region in its day. It was a busy trading port, but the Dutch East India Company and Bugis allies broke its power with the 1667 Treaty of Bongaya.

Sultanate of Harar.text: The Muslim Adal Sultanate in its Harar phase, in eastern Ethiopia, drawn here for the mid-1500s. Adal was a Horn of Africa power that fought Christian Ethiopia, and in this century its imam Ahmad al-Ghazi invaded Ethiopia with muskets and cannon before its decline.

Sultanate of Hobyo.text: A Somali sultanate in central Somalia, set up by Yusuf Ali Kenadid sometime between the 1870s and 1884. It had an army, nobility and bureaucracy of its own, became an Italian protectorate in 1889, and was absorbed into Italian Somaliland in 1927 after a war.

Sultanate of Jambi.text: A Malay sultanate in central Sumatra, Indonesia, founded about 1615 after the region had broken away from Majapahit's old hold. It grew rich on pepper and lasted until the Dutch ended it in 1904.

Sultanate of Johor.text: A Malay sultanate founded in 1528 by Alauddin Riayat Shah II, son of the last Sultan of Malacca, after the Portuguese captured that city. It ruled southern Malaya, Singapore and the Riau islands, later split between British and Dutch spheres, and survives as the Malaysian state of Johor.

Sultanate of Kedah.text: A Malay state in the northwest of the Malay Peninsula, now in Malaysia. Its annals date the first sultan to 1136, though historians doubt this and Kedah may have stayed Hindu-Buddhist until the 15th century. It became a British protectorate in 1909.

Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara.text: A Muslim sultanate on the Mahakam River in East Kalimantan that annexed the older Kutai kingdom in 1635. It later became a Dutch East Indies vassal, and its authority ended in 1960.

Sultanate of Lahej.text: The Abdali sultanate in south-west Arabia, self-ruling from 1728 and independent of the Zaydi imams by 1740. It held Aden until the British took the port in January 1839, after which Lahej joined the Aden Protectorate.

Sultanate of Lakhnauti (Ilyas Shah).text: The northern and western parts of Bengal, centred on Lakhnauti (Gauda) and Satgaon, which were separate sultanates before Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah united all of Bengal in 1352.

Sultanate of Maguindanao.text: A Sunni Muslim sultanate on Mindanao, in the southern Philippines, traditionally dated from about 1515. Its sway ran from Zamboanga round to the Davao Gulf, and it traded with Dutch and British merchants while fighting off Spanish rule.

Sultanate of Mempawah.text: A Malay-Dayak kingdom on the west coast of Borneo, around the Mempawah River in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, named after the mempauh tree. In the 1700s the throne passed to Opu Daeng Menambun, a noble of Bugis descent, and under him Islam became the kingdom's official religion.

Sultanate of Mogadishu.text: A city-state sultanate that ruled Mogadishu and the Benadir coast of Somalia, founded in the mid-13th century. The traveller Ibn Battuta saw it at its height in 1331.

Sultanate of Palembang.text: A Malay sultanate in southern Sumatra, Indonesia, centred on the old river port of Palembang. Long ruled by lords tied to Java's Demak, it was proclaimed a sultanate in 1659; the Dutch captured the city in 1821 and abolished the sultanate in 1823.

Sultanate of Perak.text: A Malay sultanate in the west of the Malay Peninsula, whose first sultan, Muzaffar Shah, came from the royal family of Malacca after the Portuguese took that city in 1511. It is one of the oldest sultanates in Malaysia, and Perak still has a sultan today.

Sultanate of Sambaliung.text: A small Malay sultanate in the Berau area on the east coast of Borneo, in today's Indonesian East Kalimantan. It arose around 1810, when the Berau sultanate split in two after a succession dispute, the other half being Gunung Tabur. Both later came under Dutch influence.

Sultanate of Sambas.text: A Malay sultanate on the west coast of Borneo, in today's Indonesia. Founded in 1609, it lasted in various forms until 1956, and was one of several small Malay states along the coast.

Sultanate of Selangor.text: A Malay sultanate on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, founded by a Bugis-descended royal family in the 1700s. Britain first became involved during the Klang War under Sultan Abdul Samad, when the first British Resident was appointed, and Selangor is now a Malaysian state.

Sultanate of Shewa.text: A Muslim sultanate of the Makhzumi dynasty in Shewa, Ethiopia, c. 900-1284. Its 896 founding rests on one later chronicle entry, and its dates are very uncertain; the Walashma of Ifat deposed the dynasty in 1285.

Sultanate of Sukadana.text: The old Malay kingdom of Tanjungpura on the southwest coast of Borneo, in today's Ketapang region of West Kalimantan, Indonesia. It took the name Sukadana when its capital moved there after a ruler embraced Islam, and its court later moved again, to Matan.

Sultanate of Sulu.text: A Muslim Tausug sultanate based in the Sulu Archipelago of the southern Philippines, with lands in Palawan and northeastern Borneo. Founded in the 1400s, it broke free of Brunei in 1578 and grew rich on trade and slave raiding until Spain forced its surrender in 1878.

Sultanate of Terengganu.text: A Malay sultanate on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, founded in the 1720s. It lived under Siamese influence before British rule, and it is now a state of Malaysia with its own sultan.

Sultanate of Tuggurt.text: An oasis sultanate in Algeria of the Berber Banu Jallab, holding Touggourt and the Oued Righ. Hafsid Tunis and Ottoman Algiers sometimes demanded tribute, but it kept its own sultans until the French took Touggourt in 1854.

Sultanate of the Maldives.text: An Islamic monarchy of the Maldive Islands that began in 1153 when King Dhovemi converted from Buddhism and took a Muslim name. Six dynasties followed, and the sultanate lasted until 1968.

Sunda Kingdom.text: The Sunda Kingdom was a Hindu realm in western Java. It was based later at Pakuan Pajajaran near today's Bogor, and its trade in pepper brought in the Portuguese. The Banten Sultanate conquered it in 1579.

Surakarta Sunanate.text: A Javanese kingdom centred on Surakarta (Solo) in central Java, Indonesia, where the royal court moved in 1745. It was one of the two halves left after Mataram was divided in 1755, and its ruler was called the Susuhunan.

Surguja.text: A hill princely state on the Chota Nagpur plateau, ruled from Ambikapur, among the Central Provinces feudatories in 1909. It merged into India on 1 January 1948 and is now in Chhattisgarh.

Swaziland.text: The kingdom now called Eswatini, in southern Africa, ruled by the Swazi king. Britain took charge around 1903 after the Boer War, and it regained independence in 1968, renaming itself Eswatini in 2018.

Swiss Confederation.text: A country in central Europe that grew from an alliance of three mountain communities in 1291. Over centuries more cantons joined, and Swiss soldiers became famous. The modern federal state dates from 1848, with Bern as its capital, and it keeps a tradition of neutrality.

Syria.text: The Syrian Arab Republic, ruled from 1970 by Hafez al-Assad and then, after 2000, by his son Bashar. A civil war began in 2011, and in December 2024 rebels overthrew Bashar al-Assad, ending the family's rule.

São Tomé and Príncipe.text: A tiny country of two islands in the Gulf of Guinea, off Africa's west coast. Portugal developed it into a major sugar and cocoa colony. It became independent in 1975.

Tabal Kingdom.text: A group of small Luwian-speaking Neo-Hittite states in southeastern Anatolia, in Turkey's Cappadocia region, in the Iron Age. They paid tribute to Assyria and were annexed by it in the late eighth century BCE.

Taebong.text: A short-lived Korean state in the Later Three Kingdoms period, founded by Gung Ye, a rebel, in the north. It was overthrown in 918 by Wang Geon, who founded Goryeo.

Tagadur under Chera suzerainty.text: The Adiyaman chiefdom of Tagadur, today's Dharmapuri in Tamil Nadu, c. 190-300 CE under Chera overlordship. The change follows one historian's chronology, and the inscriptions may point to an earlier date.

Tahirid Sultanate.text: The Tahirids on this map were a Sunni dynasty of Yemen, not the earlier Tahirids of Khorasan. The brothers Amir and Ali bin Tahir seized Aden in 1454, and their sultans ruled from Zabid until a Mamluk expedition from Egypt overthrew them in 1517.

Tahitian chiefdoms.text: The chiefdoms of Tahiti in the Society Islands of Polynesia. Rival chiefs ruled the island's districts, and in the late 1780s the Pomare family began to unite the whole island under one ruler.

Taifa of Albarracín.text: A small Berber taifa kingdom in eastern Spain, centred on Albarracín and ruled by the Banu Razin, whose ancestors came over with the Muslim conquest. It lasted from 1012 to 1104.

Taifa of Algeciras.text: A tiny Muslim taifa in what is now southern Spain around Gibraltar, c. 1035-1058, one of the many small kingdoms that appeared when the Caliphate of Córdoba broke apart. It was absorbed by its stronger neighbour, Seville.

Taifa of Almería.text: A taifa kingdom around Almería on the southeast coast of Spain. The port was important for trade and silk, and it was ruled by several different dynasties until the Almoravids took it.

Taifa of Alpuente.text: A small taifa kingdom in eastern Spain, c. 1009 to 1106, centred on Alpuente. It arose when the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up and was ruled throughout by the Qasimids, a Berber family.

Taifa of Arcos.text: A small Berber taifa kingdom in southwest Spain around Arcos de la Frontera, ruled by a local family, the Banu Jizrun. The larger taifa of Seville took control of it around 1069.

Taifa of Badajoz.text: A taifa kingdom in southwest Spain and Portugal around Badajoz. Founded in 1009 by the Slavic freedman Sabur, it was ruled from 1022 by the Aftasids, until the Almoravids took it in 1094; it briefly revived in 1144-1150.

Taifa of Carmona.text: A Berber taifa kingdom in southern Spain around Carmona, near Seville, ruled by the Birzalid family. Seville took it around 1067, and the Almoravids held it later.

Taifa of Ceuta.text: A small taifa at Ceuta, across the Strait of Gibraltar in North Africa, c. 1061-1084. It grew out of the break-up of the Córdoba caliphate and was run by Berber rulers before the Almoravids took over.

Taifa of Córdoba.text: Córdoba was first ruled as a taifa, a small Muslim city-state, by the Banu Jahwar family from 1031, when the Umayyad caliphate ended there, until Seville took it in 1070. This map entry shows the Córdoba area in a later period, after Almoravid rule broke down in the 1140s.

Taifa of Dénia.text: A taifa kingdom on the Valencian coast of Spain that also held the Balearic Islands. Its ruler Mujahid built a fleet and raided the Mediterranean before the kingdom was absorbed by larger neighbours.

Taifa of Granada.text: A Berber taifa kingdom in southern Spain, ruled by an offshoot of the Zirid dynasty from 1013 to 1090. Thought the wealthiest of the taifas, it fell to the Almoravids in 1090, and the city later became the capital of the last Muslim state in Spain.

Taifa of Majorca.text: A small Muslim taifa kingdom on the Balearic island of Majorca, independent from 1076. A crusade of 1113-1115 overthrew it, after which the Almoravids occupied the island.

Taifa of Majorca (Banu Ghaniya).text: The Balearic islands from the 1140s, when the Banu Ghaniya, Almoravid governors, ruled Majorca as an independent emirate. It became the last Almoravid stronghold in al-Andalus, and the Almohads conquered it in 1203.

Taifa of Menorca.text: A Muslim-ruled state on Menorca. After James I of Aragon took Majorca, Menorca's leaders accepted Aragonese overlordship in 1231 by the Treaty of Capdepera and kept their own government as a vassal until Alfonso III of Aragon conquered the island in 1287.

Taifa of Morón.text: A small Berber taifa kingdom in southern Spain around Morón de la Frontera, ruled by the Banu Dammar. It arose when the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up in about 1010, and it was taken by the larger taifa of Seville in 1066.

Taifa of Murcia.text: A taifa kingdom in southeast Spain around Murcia, independent in several short periods from 1011. Stronger neighbours such as Seville and, from 1091, the Almoravids often ruled it, until Castile took over in the 1200s.

Taifa of Málaga (Hammudid).text: A taifa kingdom at Málaga in southern Spain, 1026-1057, held by the Hammudid claimants to the caliphate of Córdoba after it broke up. Badis of Granada annexed it in 1057; Málaga was later independent again briefly.

Taifa of Niebla.text: A taifa kingdom in southwest Spain, centred on Niebla, which was independent in three separate periods. It was absorbed by Seville in 1053, and survived until Castile took it in 1262.

Taifa of Ronda.text: A small Berber taifa in the mountains of southern Spain, 1039-1065, ruled by a family from the Banu Ifran tribe of North Africa. In 1065 the larger neighbour Seville swallowed it, under Abbad II al-Mu'tadid.

Taifa of Saltés and Huelva.text: A small Arab taifa kingdom in southwest Spain, centred on the island of Saltés beside Huelva. It was independent from about 1012 to 1051, when Seville took it over.

Taifa of Santa Maria do Algarve.text: A small Muslim taifa kingdom on the south coast of Portugal around Faro. Independent from about 1018, it was taken over by Seville in 1051.

Taifa of Seville.text: The Abbadid-ruled Arab kingdom of Seville, 1023-1091, grew from a break-away of the Córdoba caliphate into the strongest taifa in southern Spain and Portugal. Pressed by Castile, it called in the Almoravids from Morocco, who took it over.

Taifa of Silves.text: An Arab taifa in the western Algarve of southern Portugal near Cape St Vincent, with Silves as its capital. It first existed 1027-1063, was revived briefly c. 1145-1150, and was finally taken by the Almohads.

Taifa of Tejada.text: A short-lived taifa of the second taifa period, centred on Tejada in Huelva province of southern Spain. It was founded in 1146 and conquered by the Almohads in 1150.

Taifa of Toledo.text: A taifa kingdom in central Spain around Toledo, ruled by the Dhunnunids, a Berber clan. In 1085, after years of pressure, Alfonso VI of León and Castile took Toledo peacefully, ending the taifa.

Taifa of Tortosa.text: A taifa kingdom around Tortosa on the lower Ebro in Spain. It was first independent from c. 1010 under Slavic former slaves, passed to Zaragoza from 1060, and revived c. 1081. Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona conquered Tortosa in 1148.

Taifa of Valencia.text: A Muslim kingdom around Valencia in eastern Spain that became independent in about 1010. El Cid took the city in 1094, and after later periods of Almoravid and Almohad rule the Crown of Aragon won it for good in 1238.

Taifa of Zaragoza.text: A powerful Muslim taifa kingdom in northeast Spain, ruled first by the Banu Tujib and from c. 1038 by the Banu Hud. The Almoravids took it in 1110, and Aragon captured the city of Zaragoza in 1118.

Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.text: A rebel state in China led by Hong Xiuquan, who called himself the younger brother of Jesus. From its capital at Nanjing it ruled lands with nearly 30 million people and fought the Qing in a long, bloody war until its fall in 1864.

Takrur.text: A West African state on the Senegal River in present-day Senegal, strongest in the 11th and 12th centuries, in the age of the Ghana Empire. Takrur was among the first states in the region whose rulers took up Islam.

Talpur Dynasty.text: The Talpurs ruled Sindh, in today's Pakistan, after Mir Fateh Ali Khan Talpur overthrew the Kalhora rulers in 1783. The family split into branches; those at Hyderabad and Mirpur Khas fell to the British in 1843, but the Khairpur branch survived as a princely state until 1947.

Talysh Khanate.text: A khanate of the Talysh people on the Caspian coast of south-eastern Azerbaijan, with its capital at Lankaran. It was self-governing after 1747 under nominal Iranian suzerainty and was dissolved after the Russian conquest of the 1820s.

Tamassos.text: An inland city-kingdom of Cyprus, c. 600-345 BCE, ruled by kings such as Pasicyprus. It paid tribute to Assyria and later Persia; its wealth came mainly from the nearby copper mines of the island.

Tamna.text: Tamna was an island kingdom on Jeju, south of the Korean peninsula, which traded and paid tribute to neighbouring Korean states. Goryeo made it a vassal, and Joseon ended its autonomy in 1404. Jeju's islanders kept a distinct culture and dialect.

Tangier International Zone.text: A neutral zone around the Moroccan port of Tangier, run jointly by several foreign powers under a 1923 agreement instead of by a single colonial ruler. Apart from a Spanish occupation during the Second World War, it kept this status until it rejoined independent Morocco in 1956.

Tanzania.text: An East African country formed in 1964 when Tanganyika, independent from Britain in 1961, united with the island of Zanzibar. It contains Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, and the Serengeti plains.

Tarumanagara.text: Tarumanagara was an early Hindu-influenced kingdom in western Java, known from rock inscriptions of King Purnawarman in the 5th century CE. It is one of Indonesia's oldest known kingdoms, and faded away by about 669.

Taíno chiefdoms.text: The Taíno, an Arawak-speaking people who lived in chiefdoms across the Greater Antilles and the Bahamas. They were the first peoples Columbus met in 1492, and Spanish conquest, forced labour and disease reduced their numbers sharply.

Tehri Garhwal.text: A Himalayan hill kingdom in present-day Uttarakhand, India, shown 1815-1947. After the Anglo-Nepalese War the British kept eastern Garhwal and returned the lands west of the Alaknanda to Sudarshan Shah, who ruled from Tehri; it later became a princely state and joined India in 1947.

Teng.text: A small Zhou-era state in southern Shandong, ruled by a branch of the Ji family and squeezed between bigger neighbours such as Qi and Chu. It is known as the birthplace of the philosopher Mozi. Song destroyed the state around 297 BCE.

Teutonic Order.text: A Catholic military order founded c. 1198 in Acre as a hospital brotherhood for pilgrims. It later became a crusading army and built a state on the Baltic coast in Prussia, which lasted until 1525.

Texcoco.text: A city-state on the eastern shore of Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, home to the Acolhua people. In 1428 it joined Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan in the Aztec Triple Alliance, and became known for its learning.

Thebans.text: The city of Thebes and its allies in Boeotia, central Greece, in the 350s to 330s BCE. After Philip II of Macedon beat Thebes and Athens at Chaeronea in 338 BCE it lost its independence, and Alexander razed it in 335 BCE.

Thessaly.text: The plains of northern Greece. Across 1272-1332 they were held by local Greek rulers, first the Doukas family of Neopatras and then regional magnates who accepted Byzantine overlordship, until Catalan mercenaries seized part after 1318. Thessaly joined modern Greece in 1881, after Ottoman rule.

Third Hellenic Republic.text: Greece after the military junta fell in 1974. A referendum chose not to bring back the monarchy, and a republican constitution followed in 1975. Greece joined the European Communities in 1981.

Thracian Kingdom.text: The Thracian kingdoms of the Balkans, in today's Bulgaria and neighbours, ruled by Thracian kings who survived as Roman allies. Rome made Thrace a province in 46 CE after the last king died, ending Thracian independence.

Thuringian states.text: A map label for the Thuringii, a Germanic people of central Germany, in the later 5th century CE, before they formed a larger kingdom. It is not the later duchy or landgraviate of Thuringia.

Togo.text: A narrow West African country on the Gulf of Guinea, independent from France in 1960. Its first president, Sylvanus Olympio, was killed in a coup in 1963, and the Gnassingbé family has led the country for most of the years since.

Toltec.text: A culture of central Mexico centred on Tula, in the present-day state of Hidalgo, at its height c. 950 to 1150. The later Aztecs looked back on the Toltecs as master artisans and the model of civilization, though much of what they said about them was legend.

Tomaras of Delhi.text: A Rajput dynasty ruling Delhi and parts of Haryana, drawn here c. 1044-1151. Mahipala probably took Hansi and Thanesar from the Ghaznavids; Lal Kot in Delhi became the capital around 1052. The Chahamanas took Delhi around 1152.

Tomaras of Gwalior.text: A dynasty that took Gwalior in the 1390s as Tughluq feudatories and kept it against Delhi until Ibrahim Lodi's siege. Man Singh Tomar is its best-known ruler.

Tondai Nadu (Kanchi and the Tiraiyar).text: A Sangam-age chiefdom of northern Tamil Nadu, c. 300 BCE-282 CE, centred on Kanchi and ruled by the Tiraiyar line. Its best-known chief is Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan.

Tondo.text: A Tagalog and Kapampangan trading town on the Pasig River delta, in today's Manila, Philippines. Its paramount chief took the title lakan, and it shared in a monopoly on Chinese goods across the islands before the Spanish took over the Manila Bay towns from 1570 to 1571.

Tonga.text: A Polynesian kingdom of 171 islands in the South Pacific, united in 1845 by the warrior chief Tāufaʻāhau, who had been baptised George. Britain handled its foreign affairs from 1900 to 1970, but Tonga never gave up its sovereignty. Its capital is Nukuʻalofa.

Tonk (Amir Khan's grant from Holkar).text: A grant of land at Tonk in Rajputana given in 1806 to Amir Khan, a Pashtun commander serving the Maratha ruler Holkar. He held it as Holkar's general until 1817, when the British made him a nawab; it then became the princely state of Tonk.

Tonk (Holkar's pargana).text: The pargana of Tonk in Rajasthan, held from the 1750s by the Maratha chief Holkar. Amir Khan, a commander of Holkar, received it in 1806, and the British recognised his rule in 1817.

Tonk State.text: A princely state of six scattered districts in Rajasthan and central India, 1817-57. Amir Khan, a Pashtun commander who had served the Holkars, was recognised by the British as its first nawab in 1817. Its main part was at Tonk itself.

Tonk State (Aligarh).text: A detached district of Tonk State, the nawabate recognised by the British in 1817 for Amir Khan, a Pashtun commander. This piece, called Aligarh and also known as Rampura, lay in Rajputana, apart from Tonk itself.

Tonk State (Chhabra).text: A detached district of Tonk State, the nawabate recognised by the British in 1817 for Amir Khan. Chhabra was one of the pieces of the state lying in central India, far from the town of Tonk in Rajputana.

Tonk State (Nimbahera).text: A detached district of Tonk State, the nawabate recognised by the British in 1817 for the Pashtun commander Amir Khan. Nimbahera was one of its pieces in Rajputana, separate from Tonk itself.

Tonk State (Pirawa).text: A detached district of Tonk State, the nawabate recognised by the British in 1817 for the Pashtun commander Amir Khan. Pirawa was one of the pieces lying in central India, separate from the main Tonk district.

Tonk State (Sironj).text: A detached district of Tonk State, the nawabate recognised by the British in 1817 for the Pashtun commander Amir Khan. Sironj was one of the pieces lying in central India, far from Tonk itself.

Toucouleur Empire.text: A West African empire created by the jihad of El Hadj Umar Tall in what is now Mali and Senegal. Shown 1855-61, after he took Nioro, with Bambuk and Dinguiraye; the French stopped him at Médine in 1857, and a treaty in 1860 left him Kaarta and Ségou.

Travancore.text: A kingdom at the southern tip of India on the Malabar coast, from 1729 to 1949. Its ruler agreed to accede to India on 12 August 1947, and it merged with Cochin on 1 July 1949.

Travancore under Marthanda Varma.text: Travancore as built by Marthanda Varma (r. 1729-58), who turned Venad into a stronger state by annexing Attingal, Kollam and Kayamkulam. He also defeated the Dutch at the battle of Colachel in 1741.

Triarchy of Negroponte.text: A crusader lordship on the Greek island of Euboea, given to Lombard lords after the Fourth Crusade and shared among three baronies. It was under the Principality of Achaea and, from 1209, Venetian protection, with a Venetian official at Chalkis.

Trinidad peoples.text: The Indigenous peoples of Trinidad, in the southern Caribbean, among them the Nepoya, Shebaya and Yao. Columbus reached the island in 1498 and claimed it for Spain, and from 1511 Spanish slavers raided it for workers for the pearl fisheries of nearby Margarita.

Tripura (Twipra Kingdom).text: A kingdom of the Manikya dynasty in the Tripura hills and the plains toward Comilla, in today's Tripura and Bangladesh. It competed with Arakan and Bengal for Chittagong and Sylhet, and its rulers later governed from Agartala.

Trucial States.text: A group of small Arab sheikhdoms along the southeastern Gulf coast, bound by treaties with Britain from 1820. In 1971 six of them joined to form the United Arab Emirates, and Ras Al Khaimah followed in 1972.

Trưng sisters.text: Two sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, led a revolt in 40 CE against Chinese Han rule in northern Vietnam and ruled as queens for about three years. Han forces crushed them in 43, and they remain national heroines.

Trịnh lords.text: The Trịnh clan, who ruled northern Vietnam (Đàng Ngoài, or Tonkin) from 1545 to 1787 while the Lê emperors reigned only in name. Twelve Trịnh lords held real power and fought the southern Nguyễn lords for generations.

Tuamotu and Mangareva chiefdoms.text: Chiefdoms on the Tuamotus, the world's largest chain of coral atolls, and on Mangareva in the Gambier Islands, in today's French Polynesia. The islands lay within the sphere of Tahiti's Pōmare dynasty until France claimed them in the 19th century.

Tulunids.text: A dynasty of Turkic origin that ruled Egypt and Syria, c. 868 to 905, founded by Ahmad ibn Tulun. They were officially under the Abbasid caliphs but acted on their own, until Abbasid forces took the lands back.

Turk Shahis.text: The Turk Shahis were rulers of Kabul and Gandhara in the 7th to 9th centuries CE, from a Turkic line. They fought Arab armies for generations, until the Hindu Shahis replaced them around 822.

Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.text: A self-declared state in the northern third of Cyprus, proclaimed in 1983 after Turkey's 1974 invasion split the island. Only Turkey recognises it as a country.

Turkmenistan.text: A mostly desert country in Central Asia, independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. It sits on huge natural gas reserves and is known for its fiery Darvaza gas crater.

Tuvalu.text: A tiny Polynesian island country of nine low coral atolls in the Pacific, formerly the Ellice Islands. It split from the Gilbert Islands and became independent in 1978. Rising seas threaten its future.

Tuvaluan chiefdoms.text: The island communities of Tuvalu in the Pacific, first settled by Polynesians. Each atoll was led by its own chiefs, and in the 1800s Europeans began to visit and call the group the Ellice Islands. Tuvalu is now an independent nation.

Tuyuhun.text: Tuyuhun was a kingdom of Xianbei nomads around Qinghai, on the Tibetan plateau's edge, lasting from about 284 to 670 CE. It grew rich as a link on Silk Road routes, and Tibetan armies finally conquered it.

Tver.text: A Russian city on the Volga that became the capital of a rival principality to Moscow in the 1200s. Its princes fought Moscow for leadership of Russia, but Moscow's Ivan III annexed the city in 1485.

Twipra (Tripura) kingdom.text: The Manikya kingdom of the Tripuri people in what is now Tripura, India, established by Maha Manikya c. 1400. Under Ratna Manikya I the capital moved to Rangamati, today called Udaipur.

Tyrconnell (Tír Chonaill).text: The Gaelic lordship of the O'Donnells in what is now County Donegal, Ireland. It ended with the Flight of the Earls in 1607 and the Plantation of Ulster.
