Tây Sơn dynasty.text: A Vietnamese dynasty that began in 1771 as a peasant revolt by three Nguyễn brothers. It overthrew the Nguyễn and Trịnh lords and ruled Vietnam from 1778 until Nguyễn Ánh defeated it in 1802.

Udaipur (Mewar).text: The Rajput state of Mewar, ruled by the Sisodia family, the senior Rajput house, in the Aravalli hills of Rajasthan. It acceded to India in 1947.

Ugarit.text: A Bronze Age port kingdom on the Syrian coast, c. 1400-1185 BCE, at Ras Shamra. A vassal first of Egypt and then of the Hittites, it kept its own kings. Its tablets include an early alphabet; it was destroyed around 1185 BCE.

Ukraine.text: A large country in Eastern Europe that became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Ukrainian People's Republic.text: A Ukrainian state that declared autonomy in 1917 and independence in January 1918, with Kyiv as its capital. Its Directorate, in which Symon Petliura became the leading figure, fought the Bolsheviks and others in 1919. It lost the war by 1921, and Soviet Ukraine joined the Soviet Union in 1922.

Unified Silla.text: After conquering Baekje and then taking Goguryeo's southern lands following 668 CE, Silla ruled the centre and south of the Korean peninsula from Gyeongju, then one of the world's largest cities. Buddhism shaped its art, but revolts split the land in the late 9th century, and its last king submitted to Goryeo in 935.

Union of Utrecht.text: The 1579 agreement among northern Dutch provinces and cities to fight Philip II of Spain together. It acted as a sort of first constitution, and the north soon declared independence from Spain in 1581 and became the Dutch Republic.

United Arab Emirates.text: A federation of seven emirates on the Persian Gulf, formed in December 1971 as Britain withdrew (Ras Al Khaimah joined weeks later), led by Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi. Oil wealth funded fast growth, notably in the cities of Dubai and Abu Dhabi.

United Arab Republic.text: A union of Egypt and Syria, proclaimed in 1958 under Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser as a step towards a single Arab nation. Syria broke away after a coup in 1961, but Egypt kept the name until 1971.

United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg.text: A cluster of Rhineland territories (Jülich, Cleves, Berg, Mark and Ravensberg) united in 1521 by a marriage between two ducal houses. Based at Düsseldorf, it broke apart after 1609, when the last duke died childless and the War of the Jülich Succession began.

United Kingdom.text: A country in northwest Europe whose four nations are England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It once ruled a vast empire. It voted to leave the European Union in 2016 and left in 2020.

United Principalities of Moldavia and Wa.text: The union of the two Romanian principalities in 1859, when both elected Alexandru Ioan Cuza as their ruler. It was the first step toward modern Romania, which was fully independent by 1877 to 1878.

United Provinces of Central America.text: A federal republic formed in 1823 after Central America broke from Spain and then Mexico. It joined Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, but civil wars and rebellions wore it down until it broke apart between 1839 and 1841.

Upper Burgundy.text: A Frankish kingdom in the western Alps, covering parts of present-day Switzerland and eastern France. Rudolf I was crowned in 888, and the kingdom was merged with Lower Burgundy in 933.

Upper Burgundy and Italy.text: The combined realm of Rudolph II of Upper Burgundy, who campaigned for the crown of Italy in the 920s while ruling the western Alps. It was short-lived: Hugh of Arles drove him out of Italy in 926, and in 933 Rudolph gave up his Italian claims.

Uqaylid dynasty.text: An Arab dynasty of Mosul in northern Iraq, c. 990-1096, controlling much of the Jazira. It reached its height under Muslim ibn Quraysh (1061-1085), who held Aleppo from 1080. The Turkish commander Kerbogha took Mosul in 1096, ending the dynasty's rule.

Utpala Dynasty.text: A Hindu dynasty of Kashmir, founded by Avantivarman in 855 after the Karkota line. Its later years were dominated by Queen Didda, and in 1003 her nephew Samgramaraja began the Lohara dynasty.

Uyunid Emirate.text: An Arab dynasty of the Banu Abdul Qays tribe that ruled Eastern Arabia, in parts of today's Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, after defeating the Qarmatians with Seljuk help in 1077-78. Its capital moved between al-Hasa, Qatif and Awal, and it fell to the Usfurids in 1253.

Vaghela dynasty (Gujarat).text: A dynasty of Gujarat, India, whose generals Lavanaprasada and Viradhavala gained power under the Chaulukyas; Viradhavala's son Visaladeva took the throne around 1244. It ruled until Alauddin Khalji's conquest of 1299-1304.

Vakataka Kingdom.text: The Vakatakas ruled much of the Deccan plateau in central India from about 250 to 500 CE, alongside the Gupta empire, whose emperor Chandragupta II married a daughter into their family. The Buddhist caves of Ajanta were carved under their king Harishena.

Vandal Kingdom.text: The Vandal Kingdom was a realm of Vandals and Alans in North Africa, set up by King Gaiseric in 435 CE and based at Carthage from 439. Its fleet raided across the western Mediterranean and sacked Rome in 455, until the Byzantine general Belisarius conquered it in 533 to 534.

Vandals.text: The Vandals were Germanic peoples first named in the 1st century CE in what is now Poland; later one branch lived near Roman Dacia. Pushed by Goths and Huns, they crossed into Gaul in the early 400s and then Spain, before sailing to North Africa in 429 and seizing Carthage by 439.

Vanuatu.text: A Pacific island chain, once the New Hebrides, jointly ruled by Britain and France. It became independent in 1980. It is known for the land-diving ritual of Pentecost Island, where men leap from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles.

Vatican City.text: A tiny independent state inside Rome, the smallest country in the world. It was created in 1929 by the Lateran Treaties and is the home of the pope and the centre of the Catholic Church.

Venad (Kingdom of Quilon).text: The southernmost successor of the Chera Perumals in Kerala, India, covering Kollam (Quilon), Thiruvananthapuram and Nanjinad. Its king Ravi Varma Kulasekhara led a military expedition north as far as Kanchi in the early 14th century.

Venad (early Travancore).text: A kingdom at India's south-western tip, around Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari, from which Travancore grew. Nearby Kollam, Kayamkulam and the northern lands were separate chiefdoms until Marthanda Varma began absorbing them in 1729.

Venezuela.text: A country on the Caribbean coast of South America that became fully separate from Gran Colombia in 1830. Long dominated by military strongmen, it holds the largest known oil reserves in the world. Its capital is Caracas.

Vermont Republic.text: An unrecognised independent republic in New England that existed from 1777 to 1791. It was claimed by New York and New Hampshire, and it joined the United States in 1791 as the 14th state.

Vientiane.text: A Lao kingdom around the city of Vientiane on the Mekong, one of the successors of Lan Xang. It ended in 1827 when Siam crushed King Anouvong's rebellion.

Vijayanagara Empire (Aravidu dynasty, Ch.text: The last stage of the Vijayanagara Empire, reduced to the Chandragiri and Vellore country after civil war (Toppur, 1616) and the advance of Golconda and Bijapur. Vellore fell c. 1646, which is taken as the end.

Vijayanagara Empire (Aravidu dynasty, Pe.text: The later Vijayanagara Empire, after the defeat at Talikota (1565) and the sack of Hampi. The Aravidu kings ruled from Penukonda and then Chandragiri, still holding much of southern India and claiming overlordship of the Nayaks.

Viking settlements.text: The lands where Norse people from Scandinavia settled from the late 700s onward, from Ireland and England to Iceland and Greenland. They traded and raided by longship, founded towns such as Dublin, and eventually blended into local societies.

Vishnukundina kingdom.text: A dynasty ruling coastal Andhra between the Krishna and Godavari rivers, c. 420-624 CE. Its kings, such as Madhava Varma II, ruled first from Indrapalanagara and then Denduluru; Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas ended it.

Visigothic Kingdom.text: After Gothic wars with Rome, the Visigoths settled in southwest France in 418 CE and later spread over Spain. Their kingdom turned Catholic in 589, and collapsed after Muslim armies defeated and killed King Roderic in 711.

Visigoths.text: The Visigoths were a Gothic people who crossed into the Roman Empire in 376 CE to escape the Huns. They sacked Rome in 410 under Alaric, then settled in southern Gaul, forming a kingdom there and later in Spain.

Volga Bulgaria.text: Volga Bulgaria was a Bulgar state around the Volga and Kama rivers, a trade link between Russia, Scandinavia and the Muslim world. Its ruler adopted Islam by 922, and the Mongols destroyed it in 1236.

Waalo.text: A Wolof kingdom in the lower Senegal valley and delta, ruled by a king called the Brak. Its kings were dated from 1287, but it was part of the Jolof confederation until Danki in 1549. It lasted into the 1850s.

Wadai Empire.text: A sultanate east of Lake Chad, in today's Chad, founded in the 1600s when Abd al-Karim overthrew the Tunjur rulers. It was powerful on trans-Saharan trade routes until the French conquest around 1909-1912.

Warsangali Sultanate.text: A Somali sultanate of the Warsangali clan in Maakhir (Sanaag) on the Gulf of Aden coast, consolidated by Garaad Abdulle Mahmud I from 1613. It signed a protectorate treaty with Britain in 1886 and lasted until 1920.

Water Chenla.text: Water Chenla, the southern half of early Cambodia, covered the Mekong delta and coast after about 706 CE. It was exposed to attack by Javanese sea raiders, until Jayavarman II united the Khmer lands c. 802.

Wei.text: One of the seven great Warring States of China, formed when Jin split in three, lying on the Yellow River plain. It started as the strongest, but wars with Qin wore it down and Qin conquered it in 225 BCE.

West Berlin.text: The western half of Berlin, an island of the West surrounded by communist East Germany. The Soviets blockaded it in 1948 and 1949, and the Berlin Wall surrounded it from 1961 until 1989.

Western Chalukya Empire.text: A Kannada dynasty that ruled most of the western Deccan in the 10th to 12th centuries, from Kalyani. They fought the Cholas for control of the south and supported Kannada and Sanskrit literature.

Western Chu.text: The central realm of Xiang Yu, who took the title Hegemon-King of Western Chu in 206 BCE after Qin fell. He ruled from Pengcheng and was defeated by Liu Bang, the first Han emperor, in 202 BCE.

Western Ganga kingdom (Gangavadi).text: A kingdom of southern Karnataka, c. 350-554 CE on this map, centred on Gangavadi around Mysore and Bangalore. Its early kings, such as Konganivarma Madhava, ruled from Kolar and then from Talakad on the Kaveri.

Western Liang.text: Western Liang was a small Sixteen Kingdoms state at the far western end of the Gansu corridor, founded around 400 CE by the Han Chinese official Li Gao. It controlled Dunhuang and was conquered in 421 by Northern Liang.

Western Moghulistan.text: The western lands of the Moghul khans, a breakaway branch of the Chagatai Khanate, in the steppes and mountains north of the Tian Shan in today's Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan. In the early 1500s the Moghuls were losing these pastures to the Uzbeks and to Kyrgyz tribes, and shifted their rule south to the Tarim Basin oases.

Western Qin.text: Western Qin was a small state of the Xianbei Qifu clan in the Gansu region, in two phases, 385 to 400 and 409 to 431. It survived mainly by shifting between stronger neighbours, until the Xiongnu Xia state crushed it.

Western Sahara.text: A thinly populated desert territory on Africa's northwest coast, ruled by Spain until 1975. Morocco now controls most of it, while the Polisario Front, which seeks independence, holds a strip in the east.

Western Satraps.text: The Western Satraps were Saka (Scythian) rulers of western India, governing Gujarat and Malwa from about 35 to 415 CE. They traded with Rome through Indian Ocean ports and were finally conquered by the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II.

Western Wei.text: Western Wei was a short-lived northern Chinese state from 535 CE, set up in the Wei river valley with Chang'an as its capital. The general Yuwen Tai held real power, and his son replaced it in 557 with the Northern Zhou dynasty.

Western Xia.text: A kingdom of the Tangut people in northwest China, 1038 to 1227, with its own script. It held its own between the Song, the Liao and the Jin, and was destroyed by the Mongols in 1227.

Western Yan.text: Western Yan was a brief Xianbei state founded in 384 CE by Murong Hong, a survivor of Former Yan. His people took Chang'an in 385, then moved east to Zhangzi in 386. Later Yan destroyed them in 394.

Wey.text: A Zhou-dynasty state in today's northeastern Henan, spelled Wey to tell it from the larger Wei. Its first ruler was Kang Shu, King Wu of Zhou's younger brother; it shrank to a tiny lordship but lasted until the Qin dynasty ended it in 209 BCE.

Wihtgar.text: This entry is the small Jutish kingdom on the Isle of Wight, named for Wihtgar, who with Stuf is listed as its first king and said to have received the island in 534, though he may be legendary. Wessex's King Cædwalla conquered it in 686, killing Arwald, the last pagan Anglo-Saxon king.

Wu.text: A state at the mouth of the Yangtze, outside the Zhou cultural world, that rose to power in the Spring and Autumn period. Under King Helu, helped by the strategist Sun Wu, it beat Chu, but Yue conquered it in 473 BCE.

Wusun.text: A semi-nomadic steppe people who first lived near Dunhuang in China, then took over the Ili valley, on today's border of China and Kazakhstan, around 130 BCE. The Han empire made them allies against the Xiongnu, sending princesses to marry their kings.

Wuyue.text: A kingdom in present-day Zhejiang and Shanghai, China, from 907 to 978, one of the Ten Kingdoms. Founded by Qian Liu, it prospered and developed its own regional culture, and its last king submitted to the Song in 978 rather than face destruction.

Xia.text: This Xia is the Hu Xia, a state of the Xiongnu leader Helian Bobo, founded in 407 CE on the Ordos plateau. His walled capital Tongwancheng has surviving ruins. Northern Wei took it in 427, and the state ended in 431 when the Tuyuhun captured its last ruler.

Xionites.text: The Xionites, or Chionites, were nomads of Central Asia, living around Bactria and Transoxiana in the 4th and 5th centuries CE. After years of war with Persia's Shapur II, they became his allies against Rome in 358, and some scholars link them with the later Kidarites and Hephthalites.

Xu.text: A state of the Huaiyi people along the Huai River in northern Jiangsu and Anhui, independent of the Zhou court for centuries. Its power ended in 512 BCE when Wu conquered it.

Yadava Dynasty.text: A medieval Indian dynasty, the Seuna Yadavas, that ruled a large part of the western Deccan in Maharashtra, northern Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh. Their capital was Devagiri (today Daulatabad), and they fell to the Delhi Sultanate in the early 14th century.

Yamhad.text: An Amorite kingdom in northern Syria, c. 1810-1600 BCE, centred on Aleppo. In the 1700s BCE its kings Yarim-Lim I and Hammurabi I led the strongest state in Syria, with about twenty vassal kings, until the Hittites destroyed it.

Yan.text: An ancient state in northern China whose capital Ji stood where Beijing is now. It was among the seven great Warring States, and was conquered by Qin in 222 BCE after a failed attempt to assassinate the Qin king.

Yarubid dynasty.text: The imams of Oman from 1624 to 1742, who expelled the Portuguese from Muscat and their other coastal forts and united the country. They promoted farming and trade and made Oman a naval power.

Yatenga.text: The northern Mossi kingdom in present-day Burkina Faso, with its capital at Ouahigouya, founded by Naaba Kango. Its founding date is traditional, and it became a French protectorate in the 1890s.

Yaudheya Republic.text: The Yaudheyas were a warlike confederation in what is now Haryana, India, governed as a republic rather than by one king. They minted their own coins, and in the 4th century CE they submitted to the Gupta emperor Samudragupta, after which the republic slowly broke up.

Yenisei Kyrgyz.text: The Yenisei Kyrgyz were a Turkic people of the upper Yenisei in southern Siberia. They defeated the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 CE and for a time ruled a wide steppe area. Mongol rule absorbed them in the 13th century.

Yin.text: A short-lived kingdom in northern Henan and southern Hebei, China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE after Qin fell. Its king was Sima Ang, who sided with Liu Bang in the wars that followed.

Yong.text: A short-lived kingdom in central Shaanxi in northwest China, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms of 206 BCE. Its king was the Qin general Zhang Han. With Sai and Di it formed the Three Qins, which Liu Bang defeated.

Yue.text: A state in eastern China, around today's Zhejiang, that rose in the Spring and Autumn period and was famed for its swords. King Goujian conquered its rival Wu in 473 BCE, and Yue was in turn partitioned by Chu and Qi around 333 BCE.

Yuezhi.text: A nomadic people first recorded in the area of western Gansu in China. After the Xiongnu defeated them in 176 BCE, they moved west, and one branch settled in Bactria, where they founded the Kushan empire.

Yugoslav Partisans.text: The communist-led resistance to Germany and its allies in occupied Yugoslavia in the Second World War. Led by Josip Broz Tito, they grew into a big army and took power in 1945.

Yugoslavia.text: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was founded in 1918 and renamed Yugoslavia in 1929. Under the Serbian Karađorđević dynasty, it collapsed when Germany and its allies invaded in April 1941.

Zagwe dynasty.text: A medieval Christian dynasty in northern Ethiopia, famous for Lalibela, where its kings had churches carved out of solid rock. It ruled until 1270, when Yekuno Amlak took the throne.

Zaire.text: The name used by the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 1971 and 1997, under the dictator Mobutu Sese Seko. Mobutu held power for over thirty years until rebels under Laurent-Désiré Kabila drove him out in 1997.

Zambia.text: A landlocked country in southern Africa that became independent from Britain in October 1964 as the former Northern Rhodesia. It holds Victoria Falls, shared with Zimbabwe, and has long been a leading copper producer.

Zaporozhian Cossacks.text: Cossacks who lived beyond the rapids of the Dnieper in Ukraine, forming a self-governing military brotherhood with its centre at the Sich. They were famed fighters against Tatars, Poles and Turks, until Russia destroyed their Sich in 1775.

Zapotec Civilization.text: A civilization of the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico, whose state, centred on the mountaintop city of Monte Alban, came to dominate much of today's Oaxaca. The Zapotecs built ball courts and tombs, devised one of the first writing systems in Mesoamerica, and their descendants still live in Oaxaca.

Zaydi Alid dynasties.text: Shia Zaydi dynasties of Alid descent that ruled Tabaristan and neighbouring parts of northern Iran, squeezed between the Alborz mountains and the Caspian. The first emirate was set up in 864; the Samanids drove it out in 900, another Alid branch returned in 914, and the Samanids conquered the region again in 928.

Zayyanid dynasty.text: A Zenata Berber dynasty that governed the Kingdom of Tlemcen in western Algeria from about 1235 to 1556. They were squeezed between the Marinids, the Hafsids and later the Spanish and Ottomans.

Zazzau.text: A Hausa kingdom based at Zaria in northern Nigeria, a collection point for slaves sent north to Kano and Katsina. Amina, credited with campaigns in the late 16th century, does not appear in the king-lists, and whether she was queen is disputed.

Zeta under the Balšići.text: A principality around Lake Shkodër and the coast from Budva to the Buna, in Montenegro and Albania, ruled by the Balšić family from about 1362 to 1421. Shkodër and later Ulcinj served as its seats; it became fully independent as Serbian imperial authority weakened.

Zeta under the Crnojevići.text: A principality in upper Zeta, Montenegro, ruled from 1451 by Stefan Crnojević. Ivan Crnojević moved his court to Cetinje in 1482 and founded the Cetinje monastery in 1484; a printing press worked there under his son Đurađ.

Zhangzhung.text: An ancient kingdom of western Tibet, c. 500 BCE-644 CE, linked to the Bon religion. Tradition places its capital, the Silver Palace of Garuda, near Mount Kailash. Its early dates rest on tradition, and Tibet's empire destroyed it in the 7th century.

Zhao.text: One of the seven big Warring States of China, formed from the break-up of Jin, in northern China. King Wuling reformed its army by copying steppe nomad horse archers. Qin conquered it in 222 BCE.

Zheng.text: A Zhou-era state on the central plain of Henan, near the Zhou capital, and the strongest vassal state when the Eastern Zhou began. Its chancellor Zichan is famous for early written law codes; Han conquered it in 375 BCE.

Zhongshan.text: A small Warring States kingdom in what is now Hebei, founded by a people called the Baidi in the north China plain. Its rulers adopted Chinese culture and bronze-working, but Zhao conquered it in 296 BCE.

Zhu.text: A tiny state in southern Shandong, also called Zou, centered near modern Zoucheng. A neighbour of Lu, it survived for centuries among larger powers before Chu conquered it in the fourth century BCE.

Zimbabwe Rhodesia.text: A short-lived, unrecognised state in southern Africa in 1979, formed when Rhodesia's white government agreed to share power with Bishop Abel Muzorewa. It was rejected by guerrilla leaders and ended with Zimbabwe's independence.

Zirid dynasty.text: A Sanhaja Berber dynasty founded by Ziri ibn Manad, a Fatimid commander, that ruled Ifriqiya (Tunisia and neighbouring lands) from 972 to 1148. The Zirids ruled from Kairouan then Mahdia, and lost their coast to the Normans of Sicily.

Ziyadid dynasty.text: A Muslim dynasty that ruled the Tihama lowlands of western Yemen from 819 to 1018, from its capital Zabid. Its founder Muhammad ibn Ziyad, a descendant of the Umayyads, was sent by the Abbasid caliph to subdue rebel tribes, and his family went on to rule while accepting Abbasid overlordship.

Ziyarid dynasty.text: An Iranian dynasty from the Caspian coast that ruled Tabaristan and Gorgan from 931. Its founder Mardavij briefly held much of Iran, and the dynasty lasted until 1090 as a smaller state.

Zurayid dynasty.text: A Yemeni dynasty of the Banu Hamdan that held the port of Aden c. 1083-1174, at first as tributaries of the Sulayhids. They were Isma'ili Shi'a loyal to the Fatimid caliphs in Cairo, and in the end the Ayyubids took their lands and executed them.

Âu Lạc.text: A semi-legendary kingdom in northern Vietnam and part of southern China, said to have been founded in 257 BCE by Thuc Phan, who took the name An Duong Vuong. Tradition says he built the spiral citadel at Co Loa. Nanyue later conquered it.

Éire.text: The Irish state under the name Éire, adopted in the 1937 constitution. It stayed neutral in the Second World War, which it called the Emergency, and in 1949 was declared the Republic of Ireland.

Đại Việt.text: The Vietnamese kingdom called Đại Việt, here shown from the rise of the Mạc dynasty in 1527. The Mạc ruled the unified country briefly, then lost the north to the Lê and Trịnh by 1592, and kept only Cao Bằng until 1677; the drawn span later covers the Lê-Trịnh and Nguyễn era.
